parties:
Mirza Abdul Bari Beg and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Zahidannessa and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was obtained by judgment-debtors upon making an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against order dated 10-9-2000 passed by Senior Assistant Judge at Sadar in Rangpur Other Execution Case No.2 of 1997.

2. Short facts for disposal of the Rule are that, on 13-5-81 opposite party No. 1 and the predecessor of opposite party Nos. 2 to 7 as plaintiffs instituted Other Suit No. 246 of 1981 for declaration of title and partition for separate share in respect of 56 decimals of land described in schedule-A to the plaint. On 30-9-90 the suit was decreed on contest in the preliminary form and on 17-11-96 the preliminary decree made final. Then on 19-3-97 the decree-holder put the decree into execution in Other Execution Case No. 2 of 1997 for possession of the share as allotted.

3. On 6-1-98 the petitioners made an application under section 151 of the Code for stay of the execution proceedings and the said application was rejected on 24-5-98 by the execution Court, against the order, the petitioners moved this Division and obtained a Rule in Civil Revision No. 2151 of 1998. By an order dated 8-6-99 the Rule was discharged by this Division. Thereafter, on 22-6-2000 the petitioners made another application under section 151 of the Code for striking out from the prayer for execution the prayer for possession by removal of huts and trees. The decree-holders raised serious objections to such prayer and also made an application for issue of fresh writ of delivery of possession. Hearing the applications, the execution Court by its order dated 22-6-2000 rejected the execution proceedings altogether.

4. Then on 23-7-2000 the decree-holders made an application under section 151 of the Code for recall of said order dated 22-6-2000 and issue of a fresh writ of delivery of possession on the ground that the petitioners by suppressing the order dated 8-6-99 of this Division and through misrepresentation obtained the order. The application was opposed mainly on the basis that the decree was not passed for giving possession to the decree-holders by removing the judgment-debtors and, as such, the writ for delivery of possession could not be passed on the basis of such decree. Hearing the application, the execution Court found that in view of the order dated 8-6-99 of this Division, the application of the petitioners on 22-6-2000 was not maintainable, and had the order of this Division been brought to the notice of the Court, the Court would not have made such order on 22-6-2000 and the order was obviously obtained through mistake. Upon such views, by impugned order the execution Court recalled its earlier order dated 22-6-2000 and issued fresh writ for delivery of possession fixing 28-9-2000 for return.

5. Mr Mozibur Rahman, learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that in view of section 6 of the Law Reforms Ordinance, 1984 the executing Court erred in law in issuing the writ of delivery of possession. It appears that on this ground only the Rule was obtained. On the earlier occasion also the petitioners raised the very same objection in Civil Revision No. 2151 of 1998 against execution and this Division rejected such objection on the ground that the petitioners never stated in any applications before the execution Court that they had got any homestead in the land allotted to the share of the decree-holders and, as such, section 6 of the Ordinance had no manner of application. Needless, to say that a homestead and huts are not always the same. Moreover, the petitioners failed to produce any evidence to support their claim that there was any homestead on the land at the time the final decree was passed. The possibility of raising some thatched huts by a judgment-debtor after the final decree in order to resist the execution, as was submitted by Mr Shahidul Islam opposing the Rule, cannot be brushed aside. This question could only be raised and finally decided before the final decree was made. In the absence of all necessary facts, I am of the view that section 6 cannot be mechanically applied in an execution preceding which commenced on a lawful decree for partition. This Division therefore cautioned the execution Court not to go behind the decree. So, this submission fails.

<u>6. Then, Mr Rahman submits in opposing execution by removal of structures kuchcha or pucca in view of the provisions of Order XXI rule 35(3) of the Code. He also cites the decisions in the case of Md Islam vs Munshi Abdur Rahman, 6 DLR 81, Md Mokarram Ali Lasker vs Sekandarul Islam 17 DLR 673 and Ajiruddin vs Rahman Fakir 13 DLR (SC) 191. Mr Shahidul Islam, on the other hand, submits that in execution of a partition decree, the executing Court is quite competent to remove all obstacles put up on the way to execution. He cites the decisions in the cases of Safia Khatun vs Mahbubar Rahman 13 DLR 753 and that of Shah Abdul Hamid vs Prakash Chandra Nandi and another 38 CWN 832.</u>

7. Let me first see the decisions as cited by the learned Advocates. Case of Md Islam vs Munshi Aabdur Rahman is a Second Appeal which arose out of a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession after removal of the structures. Suit was decreed by the trial Court and on appeal, was affirmed by the appellate Court. Title was based on the basis of purchase in a revenue sale. A single bench held that by purchase in such sale, a purchaser purchased not the interest of the defaulting owner but that of the Crown subject to the payment of the Government assessment. What pass in such sale is the land and not the structures. In executing such decree for khas possession, Court on application is authorised to remove the person in occupation under Order XXI rule 35 of the Code but when the decree is silent as to the building situated on the land, it is not within the province of the Court to direct that be pulled down. Suit was found to be barred under Order II rule 2 of the Code. In the circumstances, the learned Single Judge held that provisions of rule 35(3) of Order XXI of the Code do not give power to the Court to direct demolition of structures kuchcha or pucca.

8. Case of Md Mokarram Ali Lasker v Sekandarul Islam is also a Second Appeal which was preferred by the decree-holder. Decree-holder obtained a decree for khas possession of a strip of land measuring an area of 25 decimals out of 43 decimals within the middle of the plot No. 1683. When the decree was put into execution, objection was raised under section 47 of the Code. Trial Court ordered for symbolical possession. Prayer for khas possession by demolishing the huts therein was rejected. On appeal, appellate Court in modification of the order, ordered that the decree-holder could take khas possession of the decreed land instead of symbolical possession but without demolishing the huts. Following the above decision of Md Islam, second appeal was dismissed and the appellate order affirmed.

9. Case of Ajiruddin vs Rahman Fakir is an appeal before the Supreme Court of Pakistan which was preferred by the plaintiff against the order of the High Court returning the memorandum of appeal for presentation before the proper Court. Suit was for partition. Issue was what should be the value of the suit for the purpose of jurisdiction. By a majority decision, it was held that value of the share of the plaintiff would be the value of the suit for jurisdiction. In deciding the issue, one of the learned Judges observed that when the plaintiff is out of possession of joint property the grant to him of separate possession of his partitioned share amounts to two reliefs:

1. joint possession of his share, and

2. the transformation of that joint possession into separate possession of his partitioned share.

10. In Safia Khatun vs Moulvi Mahbubar Rahman a decree sought to be executed was a part decree passed in favour of the decree-holder along with others against defendant No. 9 who was originally found to be a trespasser. Co-decree holders Nos. 2 to 10 then quitted decree-holder No. 1. Defendant 9 claimed to have acquired the interest of said co-decree holders. On such difference having arisen amongst the decree-holders, a single Bench held:

"In such circumstances I should think it safe for the ends of justice and in the interest of the parties to allow the application for execution to proceed in the manner as laid down in clause (2) of Order XXI rule 35 of the Code. After symbolical possession is given in that it will for the parties to have their claims and right of actual physical khas possession and peaceful enjoyment further determined according to law."

11. Shah Abdul Hamid vs Prokash Chandra Nandi and another; 38 CWN 832 In an appeal by defendant No. 81 in an execution case which arose out of a final decree in a partition suit. Some other defendants as co-sharers applied for possession of their share. A commissioner was directed by the Court to deliver possession. He delivered possession on 24th April, 1932. At the time of delivery of possession, it was found that there was within their share some huts belonging to the appellant. Thereupon, on 27th April, 1932 they again applied for fresh delivery of possession by removal of the appellant's huts. Appellant raised objection under Order XXI rule 35 of the Code. Objection was overruled by the Court and it passed an order for delivery of possession by removal of the huts. A Division Bench dismissed the appeal in the view that all the co-sharers had demanded actual possession of their shares and the Court by its final decree directed actual possession to be given.

12. Now I will see the law, which is Order XXI, rule 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure:

Decree for immovable property:

"(1) Where a decree is for the delivery of any immovable property, possession thereof shall be delivered to the party to whom it has been adjudged or to such person as he may appoint to receive delivery on his behalf, and, if necessary, by removing any person bound by the decree who refuses to vacate the property.

(2) Where a decree is for the joint possession of immovable property, such possession shall be delivered by affixing a copy of the warrant in some conspicuous place on the property and proclaiming by beat of drum, or other customary mode, at some convenient place, the substance of the decree.

(3) Where a possession of any building or enclosure is to be delivered and the person in possession, being bound by the decree, does not afford free access, the court, through its officers, after giving reasonable warning and facility to any woman not appearing in public according to the customs of the country to withdraw, remove or open any lock or bolt or break open any door or do any other act necessary for putting the decree-holder in possession. "

A mere look at the aforesaid provision shows that under sub-clause (1) a writ for actual physical possession can be straightaway sought and issued by the Court against persons occupying immovable property which is the subject-matter of decree provided such persons who are occupying the suit property are judgment-debtors or persons claiming through the former. Under sub-clause (2) when the decree is for a joint possession of immovable property a symbolical possession is to be delivered. Under sub-clause (3) where possession of any building or enclosure is to be delivered, the Court will put the decree-holder in possession by removing the judgment-debtor or any person claiming through him if necessary by breaking open the door or by any other means as situation demands.

13. Mr Rahman submits that provision of sub-clause (3) does not authorise an executing Court to order for possession by demolishing a homestead and he very much relied upon the decisions of a Single Bench in the cases of Md Islam and Md Mokarram Ali. In the case of Md Islam, as stated above, of course there was a building on the land sold in a revenue sale. But it was found on various decisions that in revenue sale only land passes not the building. Mainly, on that view and also on the finding that the suit was barred under Order II rule 2 of the Code the execution in respect of building was refused. But it was observed that rule 35(3) of Order XXI of the Code does not give power to the Court to direct demolition of structures kucha or pucca but without elaborating how 'the structure kucha or pucca' comes within the words any building or enclosure.' Similarly, in case of Md Mokarram Ali another Single Bench where no building was involved also relied upon said decision in Md Islam. In the case of Safia Khatun, a joint possession was ordered. But only in the case of Shah Abdul Hamid, a Division Bench of Calcutta High Court affirmed the order of the execution Court for delivery of possession by removal of the huts. On the point as raised, I could not find any other case.

<u>14. On close scrutiny of sub-rule (1) of Order XXI rule 35 of the Code, it appears to me that when a decree passed for possession of any immovable property, the executing Court is duty bound to deliver possession to the decree-holder. Here, possession conceived of is the actual physical possession. The words, 'any immovable property' will take in its sweep all properties as so defined and do not leave any doubt or controversy. Any other interpretation will render the decree of a competent Court of law for possession fruitless. Elaborating, if a judgment-debtor raises huts or structures or plants trees on the land allotted to the decree-holder in order to resist and frustrate the decree for possession, will the executing Court be powerless under the sub-rule to deliver possession to the decree-holder. My answer is no. I, therefore, cannot with due respect, share the view of learned single Judge in the case of Md Islam as that is not the correct statement of law. I find the principle on which the Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Shah Abdul Hamid affirmed the decree of the executing Court for possession by removal of the huts is based on correct interpretation of the law.</u>

15. Now, in the case before me, it is not disputed that the lot in occupation of the judgment- debtors was allotted to the decree-holder by exhausting all procedures after the preliminary decree for partition by metes and bounds. Any objection against such allotment that might be raised to such allotment must have been met with before the preliminary decree was made final. Once a final decree is passed on the basis of such allotment and after exhausting all procedures against such final decree by way of appeal or otherwise, when such decree was put into execution for possession of the lot allotted to the decree-holder and the application did not suffer from any defect, it is the duty of the executing Court to deliver possession to the decree-holder under sub-rule (1) of Order XXI rule 35 of the Code, and if necessary, by removing all obstructions or obstacles put up the judgment-debtors. It was correctly in the earlier revision, this Division cautioned that the executing Court has no jurisdiction to go behind the decree. On such view of the law and the facts, the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners have no substance. Impugned order of the executing Court does not suffer from any infirmity.

16. In the result, the Rule is discharged with costs; Impugned order dated 10-9-2000 of the executing Court is hereby upheld. Order of stay as was granted at the time of issue of the Rule is also recalled and vacated. The executing Court is directed to proceed with the execution by issuing again the writ for delivery of possession to the decree-holders.

End.

full_judgment:
In this Rule the plaintiff petitioner challenged order No. 14 dated 30-5-2001 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Sonagazi, Feni in Title Suit No. 46 of 2000 rejecting the petitioner's application for calling for the records of Title Suit No, 134 of 1958 and accordingly, the opposite party Nos. 1-4 were directed to show cause as to why the aforesaid order should not be set aside.

2. The plaintiff-petitioners case is that, they instituted Title Suit No. 46 of 2000 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Sonagazi against the opposite parties for a decree declaring that the Solenama dated 13-2-62 and the Sole decree dated 2-6-62 passed on the basis of the said Solenama in Title Suit No. 134 of 1958 of the 1st Court of Munsif, Feni, as shown in schedule 'Ka' to the plaint of the present suit is forged, fraudulent, false, collusive, ineffective, illegal, null and void and not binding upon the petitioners and also prayed for setting aside the said Sole decree.

3. The case of the plaintiff-petitioners, in short, is that the petitioners had no knowledge about Title Suit No, 134 of 1952 as they were never served with any summons of the said suit nor they have filed any vokalatnama in the said suit to contest the same and, as such, a solenama shown to have been filed therein on the basis of which the Sole decree was obtained is fraudulent, collusive and not binding upon them. It is the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 1-4 who practiced fraud upon the Court and filed the alleged Solenama by forging the thumb impressions and signatures of the predecessor of the petitioners, The predecessors of the petitioners having right, title, interest and possession in the suit property never knew about such Sole decree. The present defendant Nos. 1-4 recently brought Title Suit No. 30 of 2000 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Feni for partition of the land of the concerned khatian. On receiving the notice of that suit the petitioners came to know about Title Suit No. 134 of 1958 and about the solenama foiled therein allegedly by their, predecessors and the Sole decree dated 2-6-62 passed in the said suit. Their specific case is that the thumb impressions and the signatures of the predecessors of the petitioners contained in the solenama are all forged, false and, as such, the sole decree obtained on the basis of such false and forged document filed in Title Suit No. 134 of 1958 is illegal, void and not binding upon the present plaintiff-petitioners.

4. The defendant Nos. 1-4 filed written statement in the suit denying the material allegations of the plaint contending, inter alia, that the entire property originally belonged to three brothers, the predecessors of the petitioners and the contesting defendant opposite parties, the numbers of co-sharers being increased the names of all the co-sharers were not recorded in the Khatian. However, the subsequent purchasers instituted Title Suit No. 134 of 1958 wherein an application for addition of co-plaintiffs was filed on 19-2-1959 and subsequent thereto a solenama was filed on 13-2-1962 on the basis of which a sole decree was passed on 2-6-62. The parties to the decree are possessing their respective sahams on the basis of the said sole decree. The suit, being hit by limitation are res judicata, is thus liable to be dismissed.

5. However, the plaintiff-petitioners found it absolutely necessary to bring before the court the relevant materials of Title Suit No. 134 of 1958 upon which fraud and forgery were practiced by the predecessors of the defendant-opposite parties and obtained the so-called sole decree. The petitioners claimed that this is very much essential in the present suit and the original documents bearing the mark and elements of the fraud and forgery are necessary to prove the present case, thus an application was filed accordingly.

6. The learned Assistant Judge, upon hearing the parties and perusing the said application, was pleased to reject the same by his order dated 29-4-2001 holding that the plaintiffs will be able to prove their case upon obtaining and filing the certified copies of the relevant documents. The plaintiff-petitioners thereafter on 20-5-2001 filed another application stating the fact that the certified copy of all the documents have already been filed but the certified copy will not be of any assistance to prove the forgery and fraud practiced by the predecessor of the defendants because the original document contains concerned thumb impressions and the signatures, which cannot be ascertained from the certified copies. Accordingly, the plaintiff petitioner prayed for recalling the order dated 29-4-2001 and allow the application for calling for the record of Title Suit No. 134 of 1958,

7. The learned Assistant Judge by order No. 14 dated 30-5-2001 was pi eased to reject the said application holding that on 29-4-2001 an application with same prayer being rejected, there is no scope for entertaining the present application. Against the said order the plaintiff petitioners obtained the present Rule.

8. Mrs. Ferdousi Sahab, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the learned Assistant Judge committed an error resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in rejecting the application without considering that the alleged fraud cannot be determined or proved without the original document being produced before the Court. In that respect the solenama filed in Title Suit No. 134 of 1958 being the subject matter, where the allegation of fraud and forgery has been made, is the basis of the present suit and until and unless the original document is brought before the Court fraud and forgery cannot be proved in accordance with law, Thus the plaintiff-petitioners will not be able to succeed in the present suit. Accordingly, the rejection of application has caused error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. She further submits that the Court below misconstrued the law and fact and accordingly, observed in the earlier order that the certified copy will be sufficient to prove the plaintiffs case on the basis of the facts and circumstances of the case, such observation is not tenable in law.

9. No one appeared on behalf of the opposite parties but in the record a counter-affidavit filed by the opposite party Nos. 1-4 is found. The contention therein appears to be that the application once rejected, the trial Court rightly rejected the subsequent application as the earlier order was not challenged in any higher forum. Further contention of the opposite parties are that, the disputed solenama and decree being more than 30 years cannot be put under challenge at this belated stage and accordingly, the trial Court rightly rejected the same. It is further contended that Abdur Razzak, the predecessor of the plaintiff-petitioner Nos. 1-3 who was one of the signatories in the said solenama, executed long before 38 years, which cannot be challenged on the plea of practicing fraud, by the successors of the executant.

10. Heard the learned Advocate for the petitioner and perused the revisional application along with the annexures.

11. On the perusal of the same it appears that the present suit is for declaration that the solenama and the sole decree passed in Title Suit No. 134 of 1958 are forged, fraudulent and non binding upon the plaintiff and also for setting aside the said sole decree. The specific case of the plaintiff-petitioners is that fraud has been practiced by forging the thumb impressions and signatures of the predecessors of the present petitioners and the alleged solenama has been filed only to obtain a sole decree which is the subject matter of the present suit. To ascertain whether fraud and forgery has been practiced the original document is very much essential and accordingly, the application was filed for calling the record of the concerned suit containing the said original document The finding of the trial Court that the allegation of the plaintiff-petitioners can be proved by filing the certified copies of the documents seems to be a misconceived one because the certified copy of the document does not contain the original thumb impressions or signatures of the parties. Accordingly, it cannot be ascertained from the copies whether the same are genuine or forged. On perusal of the impugned order it appears that the same has been rejected on the ground that the same prayer was rejected earlier by order dated 29-4-2001 and, as such, there is no scope for entertaining the present application.

<u>12. It appears that the learned Assistant Judge erred in arriving at such decision on the face of the statement made by the plaintiff that the certified copy of the relevant papers have already been filed but tile same would not be any assistance to ascertain whether fraud has been practised or forgery has been committed. It is the settled principle of law that he who alleges fraud or forgery, burden lies upon him to prove the same. Accordingly, the plaintiff-petitioners by filing an application for calling for the record of the concerned case took reasonable steps to prove their own case of fraud and forgery and, as such, the application was rightly filed but the learned Judge erroneously rejected the prayer by passing the impugned order.</u>

13. Having given my anxious considerations to the materials on record and on hearing the learned Advocate for the petitioners, I am of the opinion that there is merit in the Rule and the impugned order should be set aside.

14. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute and the impugned order No. 14 dated 30-5-2001 be set aside and the application dated 20-5-2001 be allowed.

However, there will be no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against Order No. 177 dated 9-10-1995 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Faridpur, in Title Suit (Pre-emption Suit) No. 47 of 1978 rejecting the petitioners application under section 4 of the Partition Act for buying up the share of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1.

2. The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 47 of 1978 for partition of the suit property against the petitioner and opposite party Nos. 2-11 alleging, inter alia, that the suit property consists of three plots, namely, plot Nos. 29, 40 and 41 appertaining to RS Khatian Nos. 568 and 960 of Mouja No. 118, Faridpur Town, along with structures threreon which originally belonged to Narayan Chandra Tahbilder, predecessor in interest of defendant Nos. 4-9 to the extent of 1I3rd share, Bhupati Mohan Tahbilder, Reboti Mohan Tahbilder and Parbati Mohan Tahbilder, the three brother to the extent of 1/3rd share, and Ranajit Mohan Tahbildar and Horipada Tahbildar, two brothers, to the extent of other 1/3rd share. Thus, the three sets of Tahbildars owned the suit property. Khatian No. 568 consists of two plots, namely, plot Nos. 39 and 41, and Khatian No. 960 consists of one plot, namely, plot No. 40. There is a building consisting of twelve rooms standing on plot Nos. 39 and 40 and the land appertaining to plot No. 41 is used as pathway which lies to the east of the aforesaid building. The area of .1079 acres of land appertaining to lot No. 39 has been acquired by the Government in LA Case No. 3/1964-65 before the purchase made by the parties, that is, the plaintiff and the opposite party Nos. 1-3. The further case of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 is that Rajanit Mohan Tahbildar sold his 1/6th share of plot No. 40 along with structure thereon to the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 vide registered deed dated 5-10-1970. Thereafter Horipada Tahbilder, the other brother of Ranajit, sold 478 of land of plot No. 39 and .003-3/4 acres of land of plot No. 41 and .0100 acres of land of plot No. 40 along with the structures standing thereon to the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 by another registered deed dated 7-2-1974, and thus the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 became the owner of the land along with the structures thereon as described in schedule 'ka' of the plaint and was possessing the same by mutating his name and on payment of rent regularly. The defendants Nos.1-3 have purchased land along with the structures thereon out of the said property from the original owners. The defendant petitioner purchased. 10 178 acres of land of plot No. 39 along with the structures thereon from Ranajit Mohan Tahbildar by a registered deed dated 17-7-1969 and before purchase he was possessing the same as tenant under the Tahbildar brothers and at the time of selling the suit property to the plaintiff opposite party No.1 the Tahbildar brothers disclosed the fact to the plaintiff and asked the defendant petitioner to pay rent to the plaintiff opposite party, and accordingly, the plaintiff opposite party got possession of the suit land through tenant, namely, the defendant No. 1 petitioner. During the liberation war the defendant petitioner left the country and, as such, the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 took over possession and after the liberation of the country when the defendant petitioner came back to this country he restored possession of the suit land and he is in possession of the same and, as such, the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 filed the instant suit for partition of his share.

3. The defendant petitioner contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and that the plaintiff has got no possession in the suit property and the suit for partition without a prayer for khas possession is not maintainable. It is further alleged by the defendant petitioner in his written statement that all the joint properties of original owners having not been taken into hotchpotch of the suit, partition suit is not maintainable.

4. The defendant opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 also contested the suit by filing written statement and prayed for separate saham alleging that they have purchased 1/3rd share of the suit land from two other Tahbildar brothers and since their purchase they are in peaceful possession of the same.

5. It appears from the record that during the pendency of the suit an application under section 4 of the Partition Act was filed on 17-4-1986 by the defendant-petitioner and the said application was rejected by the trial Court and the defendant petitioner did not move the higher court against the aforesaid order. However, the trial Court after recording evidence and hearing the parties vide its judgment and decree dated 30-4-1986 decreed the suit in part in preliminary form on contest against the petitioner and opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 and ex parte against others without costs, and the trial Court found that the plaintiff opposite party No.1 is entitled to get a separate allotment for .0402 acres of land out of the suit khatian and also 1/6 the share of the building standing on the suit land, and defendant No.1 petitioner was given a separate allotment for .0402 acres of land out of the suit khatian and 1/6th share of the building standing thereon. Being aggrieved by the preliminary decree, the defendant petitioner preferred an appeal, being Title Appeal No. 121 of 1986 before the learned District Judge, Faridpur, and the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 also filed a cross objection thereto. The learned appellate Court below after hearing the parties dismissed the appeal of the defendant petitioner and allowed the cross objection filed by the plaintiff opposite party No.1 and accordingly. modified the decree by making allotment of .0298 acres of land with construction thereon in favour of the defendant petitioner and allotment of .0298 acres of plot No. 39.0200 acres of land of plot No. 40 and .0022 acres of plot No. 41 together with the construction thereon in favour of the plaintiff opposite party and allotment of remaining 1/3rd share of plot No. 39 and plot Nos. 40 and 41 together with the construction there on in favour of the plaintiff opposite party Nos. 2 and 3. The defendant petitioner being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below preferred a revisional being Civil Revision No. 596 of 1989 before this court in which Rule was issued but finally, the Rule was discharged vide judgment dated 14-5-1992. Thereafter, against the said Judgment the present petitioner moved the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 344 of 1992 which was dismissed by the Appellate Division by order dated 27-4-1993. Thus, the preliminary decree of the aforesaid partition suit reached its finality and the record of the case was sent back to the trial Court. Thereafter, on 30-5-1993 the defendant petitioner again fi led an application under section 4 of the Partition Act to buy up the share of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1. The learned trial Court heard the said application on 5-8-1993 and by its order dated 7-8-1993 rejected the same without entering into merits of the application solely on the ground that earlier also an application was filed by the defendant petitioner before the trial Court and the said application was rejected by the predecessor judge of the court and as such, rejected the same. It further appears that thereafter on 7-9-1993 the defendant petitioner filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for hearing his application filed under section 4 of the Partition Act on 30-5-1993 on merit and the said application along with written objection filed by the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 were also heard and disposed of by the trial Court vide its order No. 161 dated 6-4-1994 and the trial Court was pleased to reject the defendant petitioner's application as the trial Court did not find any merit in the said application. The defendant petitioner then moved this court in revision against the order No. 106 dated 17-4-1986, order No. 132 dated 7-8-1993 and order No. 161 dated 6-4-1994, being Civil Revision No. 2624 of 1994, and that revisional application was heard and disposed of vide Judgment dated 11-7-1994 whereby a single bench of this Court set aside the impugned orders and sent back the case to the trial Court for disposing of the application filed under section 4 of the Partition Act on merit. Thus, the learned trial Court after hearing the parties vide his Judgment and order dated 9-10-1995 rejected the said application dated 30-5-1993 and being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order dated 9-10-1995 the defendant petitioner moved this court in revision and obtained the instant Rule.

<u>6. Mr Khandkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant petitioner, submits that the finding of the trial Court that the defendant petitioner did not purchase any land appertaining to plot No. 40 of Khatian No. 960 is erroneous as the trial Court failed to construe the title deed Exhibit 'Ka' along with the Town Survey Map and the holding number as mentioned in Exbit 'Ka' which clearly shows that the defendant petitioner in fact purchased land appertaining to both the plot Nos. 39 and 40 of Khatian Nos. 568 and 960. The learned Advocate further submits that the defendant petitioner purchased 1/6th share of the undivided dwelling house of the Tahbildar family by registered deed as back as in 1969 and after his purchase the other members of the undivided Tahbildar family did not raise any objection against the said purchase nor did they come up with any application under section 4 of the Partition Act to buy up the share of the defendant petitioner and, as such, the defendant petitioner was accepted as a member of the Tahbildar family and by virtue of this he also stepped into the shoes of the other members of the Tahbildar family and thereby he is entitled to file an application under section 4 of the Partition Act to buy up the share of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1. The learned Advocate further submits that the finding of the trial Court that the house in question is not at all a dwelling house of the Tahbildar family is erroneous and contrary to materials and evidence on record and it was also not proper for the trial Court to arrive at such a finding relying on the notes appearing in the book, "Law on Partition ", Third Edition, published by Dhaka Law Reports, without citing the case law or elaborating the facts therein which has caused a failure in the decision occasioning a failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that the superior courts of this sub-continent liberally construed section 4 of the Partition Act, and in support of his contention he relies on the decision reported in 30 Indian Cases 936, 97 Indian Cases 416 and AIR, 1963 (Cal) 161.</u>

<u>7. Mr Md Nurul Haque, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party No. 1, on the other hand, submits that although the word 'family' has not been defined in the Partition Act, section 4 of the Partition Act has been interpreted by the superior courts of this Sub-continent and the interpretation given by the court shows that in order to constitute a 'family' persons ought to be related to each other through blood, and in the instant case the defendant petitioner, Haripada Saha, is not a person related to the Tahbildar family through blood and, as such, he is not a member of the Tahbildar family as contemplated in section 4 of the Partition Act. The learned Advocate submits that the trial Court in the instant case after proper assessment of oral as well as documentary evidence on record rightly arrived at the finding that the suit property is not a dwelling house of the Tahbilder family and, as such, section 4 of the Partition Act has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case and in support of his contention he refers to and relies on the decision reported in 58 CLJ 174.</u>

8. On a perusal of the impugned order it appears that the learned trial Court rejected the application of the defendant petitioner filed under section 4 of the Partition Act on three grounds. The learned trial Court arrived at a finding that from a perusal of the materials and evidence on record it cannot be said that the defendant petitioner has purchased any land appertaining to plot No. 40 of Khatian No. 960. The learned trial Court further observed that the structures standing on plot Nos. 39 and 40 was never the undivided dwelling house of the Tahbildar family, and in arriving at such a finding the learned trial Court observed that the members of the Tahbildar family after construction of the building in the said plot let out the same to different tenants and never used that house as their dwelling house nor anyone of them ever lived there. The learned trial Court also rejected the aforesaid application on the ground that the defendant petitioner by virtue of his purchase of a portion of the suit land in 1969 from Rajajit Tahbildar did not become a member of the undivided Tahbildar family although he has become a co-owner or co-sharer in the suit property.

9. From the contentions of the learned Advocate of both the parties it appears that the provisions of section 4 of the Partition Act can be applied to the present case only if the share which the plaintiff has purchased is a share in a "dwelling house belonging to an undivided family" and the defendant petitioner is a member of that undivided family. This expression "dwelling house belonging to an undivided family" appearing in section 4, Partition Act, has been borrowed from section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act and bears the same meaning. Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act has been designed to prevent a transferee, who is an outsider, from enforcing his way into a dwelling house in which the other members of the transferor's family have a right to live.

10. Before I enter into the merit of the Rule, let me summarise the law. The law on the point is that, the word 'family' as used in the section ought to be given a liberal and comprehensive meaning and it includes a group of persons related in blood who live in one house under one head or management, that it is not restricted to a body of persons who can trace their descent from a common ancestor; that it is not necessary for the members to constitute an undivided family that they should constantly reside in the dwelling house, nor is it necessary that they should be joint in mess; that it is sufficient if the members of the family are undivided qua the dwelling house which they own; that it is the ownership of the dwelling house and to its actual occupation which brings the operation of the section into play, and the object of the section is to prevent a transferee of a member of a family who is an outsider from forcing his way into a dwelling house in which other members of the transferor's family have a right to live. The expression "dwelling house belonging to an undivided family" refers to a family dwelling house. It does not mean any house or building for human dwelling belonging to an undivided family.

11. In view of the materials and evidence on record it is difficult to accept the first submission of Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, vide Ext 'ka' that his client purchased four rooms of the twelve-roomed building standing on plot No. 40 appertaining to Khatian No. 960. The same argument, it appears, was canvassed by Mr Mahbubuddin Ahmed before the Appellant Division in the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 344 of 1992 and their Lordships after taking into consideration the materials and evidence on record observed that, "However, we have considered the documents and the map ourselves, which was difficult though without the help of a survey knowing Advocate, to ensure that the petitioner was deprived of his legitimate share on the basis of the kabala but we find it almost impossible to hold that the schedule of the document can plainly be construed to include part of the structures standing on plot No. 40 as contended by the learned Advocate. I have already mentioned that the share of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 was increased and that of the defendant petitioner was reduced in the appeal by the learned District Judge and against that the defendant petitioner preferred a revisional application before this court wherein the Rule was ultimately discharged by a single bench of this court upholding the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below, and against that Judgment and decree of this court the defendant petitioner preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 344 of 1992 in which their Lordships of the Appellate Division observed as quoted above. Besides, it is crystal clear from Ext 'ka' that the defendant petitioner has purchased 1/6th share of Ranajit Mohan Tahbildar appertaining to plot No. 39 of Khatian No. 568. It is also clear from a perusal of Ext 'ka' that the defendant petitioner purchased land from plot No. 39 with the structure thereon and the finding of the trial Court on this point is based on materials and evidence on record. Besides, this point has been finally decided by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 344 of 1992 and, as such, there is no scope for Mr Mahbubuddin Ahmed to reagitate that the finding of the appellate Court is erroneous on that point.

<u>12. The second contention of Mr Ahmed is that the defendant petitioner purchased 1/6th share of the suit building in 1969 and after his purchase the other members of the Tahbildar family did not raise any objection and they did not file any application under section 4 of the Partition Act to buy up his share and, as such, he has been accepted by the members of the Tahbildar family as their family member and, as such, he has stepped into the shoes of the Tahbildar family qua the dwelling house. I have already pointed out that the word 'family' has not been defined in the Partition Act but section 4 of the Partition Act came up for consideration before the superior courts of this sub-continent and it is the consistent view that section 4 of the Partition Act should be liberally interpreted and in interpreting section 4 of the Partition Act the Allahabad High Court in one case held that the son-in-law of a Muslim family is a member of the family and in another case a married daughter of a Hindu family was considered to be a member of her father's family after the death of her father as she inherited some property through her father but in arriving at such decision the courts expressed their mind to the effect that in order to be a member of the family one has to be related somehow. In other words, there must be some sort of blood relationship and the applicant must be a member of the undivided family qua the dwelling house. In the case reported in AIR 1941 Patna 4;190 IC (1940) 117 it has been observed that section 4 makes a distinction between members of a family undivided qua the property under partition and transferees who are not members of such family. The words 'such family' in section 4 do not mean the family already referred to in the section without the qualification 'undivided'. Where, therefore, in a partition suit a transferee who is made defendant is descendant from the common ancestor of himself and the joint family, he cannot merely by that reason be said to be a member of 'such family' within the meaning of the section. It has been held in the case reported in 88 CWN, 147 that rights of co-sharers owning a dwelling house as members of an undivided family is distinguished from other co-sharers are somewhat special as is evident from section 41- of the Transfer of Property Act. The special rights have been enlarged by section 4 of the Partition Act wherein lies the importance of the term undivided family. Where it appears from evidence that the co-sharers were not agnates or cognates, they never lived together nor messed together, but were merely brought close by marriage, which by no stretch of imagination effected integration of their families but helped to continue their separate identifies, it cannot be held that there was any common bond or cementing factor bringing them within the fold of an undivided family. In the instant case, admittedly the defendant petitioner is not a member of the undivided Tahbildar family. But the moot question is, whether defendant No. 1 became a member of the undivided Tahbildar family simply by virtue of his purchase of a share of the suit property in 1969. The consistent view of the superior courts of this sub-continent is that in order to qualify to invoke the provisions of section 4 of the Partition Act one must fulfil the condition that he is a member of the undivided family and has a share in the property owned by the undivided family. If the contention of Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed is accepted then, in my opinion, the true import and tenor of section 4 of the Partition Act will be exploded and the intention of the legislature to protect the members of the undivided family will be enlarged to a great extent and, in fact, there will be no difference between the members of undivided family and the co-sharer of the property. It, thus, appears that the learned trial Court on due consideration of the materials and evidence on record has rightly arrived at a finding that the defendant petitioner is not a member of the undivided Tahbildar family qua the dwelling house and, as such, he is not entitled to invoke the provisions of section 4 of the Partition Act. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed relied on three decisions but, in my opinion, they do not at all help him. Both the courts below considered these decisions and concurrently found that they are not attracted in the facts and circumstances of the present case.</u>

<u>13. The learned trial Court found as a matter of fact that the house in question is not a dwelling house of the Tahbildar family and in arriving at such a finding he relied on Exhibit 'Ka' through which the defendant petitioner purchased the share in the suit property and it is clear from the description given in the sale deed that the property is described as দোকানঘর. Moreover, the trial Court found on a perusal of the materials and evidence on record that the building in question was never used by the Tahbildar family as their residence. There is no evidence at all to show that any member of the Tahbildar family ever lived in the house and it is found after the construction of the building they let it out to different tenants and with that finding the learned trial Court observed that a house which has not actually been used by the undivided family for a number of years is not a dwelling house. It is true that the learned trial Court without going through the decisions simply by relying on the commentaries made in the book 'Law on Partition' published by DLR arrived at such a finding, but I have myself gone through the relevant decisions and it appears that the view taken by the trial Court is absolutely correct. The judicial view is that the expression 'dwelling house belonging to an undivided family', in fact, refers to the family dwelling house. It does not mean any house or building for human dwelling belonging to an undivided family. In the instant case there is no evidence to the effect that it was a family dwelling house but it transpires from evidence that the building was always in the occupation of the tenants. It, thus, appears that the learned trial Court rightly observed that the property in question is, therefore, not a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family within the meaning of section 4 of' the Partition Act. In the case reported in AIR 1953 (Pat) 344. it has been observed that the expression 'dwelling house belonging to an undivided family' in section 4(1) refers to the family dwelling house and not to any house or building for human dwelling belonging to an undivided family. Thus a house which is in the occupation of tenants cannot be said to be family dwelling house. In the instant case the trial Court on consideration of the materials and' evidence on record found that the building in question was never used by the undivided Tahbildar family as their dwelling house and in that view of the materials, section 4 of the Partition Act has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. It, thus, appears that finding of the trial Court that the defendant petitioner does not answer the description of a member of an undivided family as contemplated in section 4 of the Partition Act nor the property in question has ever been used as a dwelling house by the original owners, namely, Tahbildar family, is backed by evidence and materials on record. In this connection we may also refer to the decision reported in AIR 1950 (Cal) 111 wherein it has been observed by the Calcutta High Court that 'undivided family' means simply a family not divided qua the dwelling house; in other words, a family which owns a dwelling house and has not divided it. The essence of the matter is that the house itself should be undivided amongst the members of the family who are its owners. The emphasis is really on the house which imparts to the family its character of an undivided family. I, therefore, do not find any illegality in the impugned order.</u>

14. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

Send down the LC Records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Abdur Rouf J: This appeal, by leave by the Government of Bangladesh, defendant No.5 and the Joint Secretary, Ministry of Works and Urban Development, Government of Bangladesh, defendant No.4 of Title Suit No.142 of 1986 of the First Court of Subordinate Judge Dhaka, in a suit for specific performance of contract for sale of the suit property, is from the judgment and order dated June 16, 1994 passed in First Misc. Appeal (briefly FMA) No.416 of 1990 dismissing the appeal, preferred by the appellants and affirming thereby the judgment and order dated June 4,1990, passed by the aforesaid court of the learned Subordinate Judge dismissing Misc. Case No.14 of 1988, filed by the appellants under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, for setting aside the ex parte decree passed on January 4, 1987 in the aforesaid title suit.

2. Plaintiff-respondent No.1 Mashiur Rahman instituted the suit stating, inter alia, that defendant No.1 Hanif Brothers, a partnership concern, and defendant No.2. Mr. Abdur Rouf, its Managing Partner, as the owner of the suit property, measuring 15.5 Kathas of land and a building standing thereon, on plot. No.49 Block No. CES(A). Gulshan Model Town, Dhaka, had entered into an agreement with him on July 5, 1974 to sell the same at a consideration of Taka 4,80,000.00 and on that date they on receipt of Taka 2,00,000.00 in cash from him executed a deed of agreement and promised thereunder to deliver possession thereof after registration of the sale deed, which was to be executed after obtaining permission from the then Dhaka Improvement Trust (briefly DIT) now RAJUK defendant No.3, procuring an income tax clearance certificate from the relevant authority and liquidating all other liabilities in respect of the suit property. On different pretext those defendants, received on June 4, 1976 further amount of Taka 1,00,000.00 and again on September 13,1979 Taka 1,00,000.00 and lastly, on October 3,1982 Taka 55,000.00 from the plaintiff and acknowledged the receipts of those amounts by signing on the back of the deed of agreement. The plaintiff thus paid to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in total a sum of Taka 4,55,000.00 leaving a balance only for Taka 25,000.00. Subsequently when the plaintiff pressed for the registration of the sale deed those defendants on November 22, 1984 refused to execute and register the sale deed. Hence on June 2, 1986 the plaintiff filed the suit.

3. The defendant appellants by filing on September 20,1986 a joint written statement had been contesting the suit denying the material allegations of the plaintiff made in the plaint. Their case, inter alia, is that the where about of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 were not known during and after the war of liberation and, as such, the suit property has been declared an abandoned property and that the suit is barred under the provisions of the President's Order No.16 of 1972, and Ordinance LIV of 1985 and that the suit is also barred by limitation. According to them the alleged deed of agreement is a forged and fabricated document and the same has been fraudulently created to grab the suit property illegally. Respondent No.4, the then Dhaka Improvement Trust, now RAJUK, as defendant No.3, had also been contesting the suit by filing another identical written statement denying the allegations of the plaintiff, stating therein that the suit property has correctly been listed as abandoned property and accordingly it has been so published in the Official Gazette.

4. Since 8-1-87 after several shifting’s of the date for setting the date of hearing, briefly SD December 26, 1987 was ultimately fixed for SD. Thereafter upon an application, filed by the plaintiff under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, on an off-date, i.e. on December 2, 1987 the trial Court re-fixed December 26, 1987 as a date of peremptory hearing of the suit, which date had earlier been fixed for SD. On December 26, 1987 the plaintiff filed hajira but the defendants did neither file hajira nor took any step. The trial Court then fixed January 4, 1988 for ex parte hearing of the suit. On that date the suit was taken up for hearing. After examining the plaintiff and marking some documents as exhibits, it was decreed ex parte.

5. On March 6, 1988 the appellants filed the Misc. Case, noted earlier, under Order IX rule 13 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the said ex parte decree stating, inter alia, that the plaintiff without serving any copy upon the defendants of the application filed on an off-date i.e. December 2, 1987 got the suit fixed behind their back for peremptory hearing on December 26, 1987, which date had earlier been fixed as a date, for SD and on that date the defendants could not take any step and thereafter January 4, 1988 was fixed for ex parte hearing of the suit. On that date the defendants having come to know that the suit had been fixed for hearing ex parte, filed an application to withdraw the suit from the list of ex parte disposal and to refix for peremptory hearing to a subsequent date. It was also stated therein that the plaintiff in collusion with the bench clerk suppressed the defendant's application for adjournment and did not place the application before the court and by practicing fraud upon the court the plaintiff got the suit disposed of ex parte and that on January 4, 1988 the regular presiding officer of the Court had been on leave and, as such, the defendants reasonably expected, as a matter of practice, that the learned Judge-in charge for the day would not hear the suit ex parte and another day would as usual be fixed for peremptory hearing as prayed for by the defendants and that in the cause list of the court no next date or note of any order had been shown for a long time and that the defendant on February 22, 1988 came to know, for the first time, from Syed Shamsul Haque, learned Advocate for defendant No.3 RAJUK, that the suit had been decreed ex parte on January 4, 1988.

6. Defendant No.3 also filed an identical Misc. Case, being No.18 of 1988 for setting aside the said ex parte decree.

7. The plaintiff by filing a written objection contested the case contending, inter alia, that the aforesaid Misc. Case was barred by limitation, having not been filed within 30 days from the date of decree. The plaintiff denied the allegation of practicing any fraud upon the court in getting the suit heard and decreed ex parte on January 4,1988. According to him, the suit was heard as usual as the defendants, although had knowledge of the date of ex parte hearing, did neither appear in court nor took any step.

8. In the hearing of the case the appellants got the relevant entry in the court's court-fee register on January 4, 1988, being entry No.56/40, marked as Ext.1 and the Register as Ext.2 and examined one Abdur Razzaq as PW 1, and LD Assistant- cum-Typist of the Ministry of Works and another Mr Mizanur Rahman, office assistant of the Government Pleader, as PW 2 and the plaintiff examined only himself as PW 1.

9. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record disbelieved the case of the appellants that they had come to know for the first time the ex parte decree on February 22, 1988 and accordingly dismissed both the Misc. Cases holding, inter alia, that the same are barred by limitation, being filed long beyond 30 days of the passing of the decree. The trial Court, however, found that a fraud seemed to have been practiced upon the court by not placing before the presiding judge the defendant's application dated January 4, 1988 for adjournment of the ex parte disposal of the suit.

10. The aggrieved defendants then preferred FMA No.416 of 1990 in the High Court Division. A Division Bench of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and order of the trial Court holding, inter alia, that the trial Court had rightly held that the Misc. Cases are barred by limitation and that in the absence of holding any enquiry for fixing up the liability for not placing the adjournment application before the presiding Judge, there is no basis for holding the plaintiff guilty of committing fraud upon the Court to manage the exparte decree in question.

11. Leave was granted to consider the following submissions made on behalf of the defendant-appellants :

(i) the High Court Division seriously erred in not considering that Title Suit No. 142 1986 was fixed on 26 December, 1987 for settling the date of hearing, but the plaintiff filed a petition on 2 December, 1987 for fixing the suit for peremptory hearing without serving any copy of that petition upon the contesting defendants and the learned Subordinate Judge illegally fixed the case for peremptory hearing on 26 December, 1987, which date was earlier fixed for settling the date of hearing and that the said order was not shown to the defendants or to their learned lawyer.

(ii) that in spite of the trial Court's own finding that there was collusion and fraud in obtaining the ex parte decree in Title Suit No. 142 of 1986, the court illegally refused to set aside the ex parte decree and directed the defendant to file fresh suit for setting aside the decree. The High Court Division seriously erred in holding that there was no fraud and collusion in the suit and wrongly upheld the trial Court's order.

(iii) the High Court Division wrongly held that the defendants totally failed to make out a case that they had been prevented by sufficient cause from appearing in court on 4 January, 1988 when the suit was called on for ex parte disposal.

12. Mr B Hossain, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for defendant-appellants, submitted that the appellants from the very beginning had been contesting the suit diligently with all seriousness by filing written statement, raising definite objection that the suit property being a declared abandoned property, the suit itself was not maintainable and that the plaintiff beyond the knowledge of the defendants fraudulently got the suit fixed on 26-12-87 for peremptory hearing and then on 4-1-88 for ex parte hearing and that on 4-1-88 as soon as the defendants came to know the said date of ex parte hearing of the suit, immediately filed an application praying for adjournment and withdrawal of the suit from the list of ex parte disposal and to re-fix the date of peremptory hearing to a subsequent date and that although the said petition had been entered in the court-fees Register of the court vide serial No.56/40 dated 4-1-88 (Ext.I) yet the plaintiff in collusion with the bench clerk managed not to place that adjournment petition before the court and thus by practising fraud upon the court the plaintiff got the ex parte fraudulent decree in question and that although the trial Court on consideration of the materials on record, found that some form of fraud, had been practised upon the court in getting the said ex parte decree, illegally refused to set aside the same upon taking an erroneous view that the Misc. Cases were barred by limitation. Mr Hussain finally submitted that the High Court Division on the face of such finding of fraud by the trial Court, wrongly upheld the trial Court's judgment and order upon taking an absolutely erroneous view that without holding an inquiry to fix up the liability of the person who had committed fraud by suppressing the defendant's application dated 4-1-88 for adjournment of hearing of the suit ex parte, the decree in question cannot be set aside.

13. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel appearing for the plaintiff-respondent on the other hand submitted that the trial Court as well as the High Court Division on consideration of the evidence on record rightly held that the Misc. Case was barred by limitation, having been filed beyond 30 days from the date of the ex parte decree. The appellants had admittedly the knowledge of the date of ex parte hearing because on that date they filed an application for adjournment and, as such, the impugned judgment of the High Court Division does not call for any interference.

14. The trial Court found that some sort of fraud had been committed, but ultimately held that the miscellaneous case was barred by limitation as the defendant had knowledge of the date of ex parte disposal of the suit. They filed an application for adjournment of the ex parte disposal of the suit on 4-1-88.

15. The case of the defendants is, that after 4-1-88 there was no entry in respect of the case in the daily cause list. They did not know of the ex parte disposal of the suit and on 22-2-88 they came to know for the first time regarding the ex parte decree and on 6-3-88 they filed the miscellaneous case.

16. The trial Court noticed that the defendants on 4-1-88 filed an appellation for adjournment, Exhibit-1, the court-fee register but the copy of the application had been missing from the record. Moreover, there has been a manipulation in the daily cause list against suit No.142 of 1986 by making the same through overwriting as TS No.242 of 1986. It is also the case of the defendants that the regular presiding Judge of the court had been absent on leave on 4-1-88 and they had a reasonable expectation that the suit in question would be adjourned as usual from hearing ex parte on that date as they had already filed an application praying for adjournment stating reasonable grounds. The plaintiff as O.P.W. 1 admitted in his evidence (page 59 Paper Book) that on 4-1-88 the regular presiding judge of the court was absent and his Advocate asked him to depose before another Judge who was in charge of that court and he did not ask the Bench Officer of the court whether the defendants had taken any step in the suit. Mr B Hussain submitted that the trial Court itself on consideration of the above stated facts held that a fraud had been practised on the court in obtaining the ex parte decree in question, but the learned Subordinate Judge illegally directed the defendants to file an independent suit. The learned Judges of the High Court Division without considering the allegations of fraud misdirected themselves in affirming the judgment of the trial Court only on the ground that the Miscellaneous case was rightly found to be time-barred by the trial Court.

17. It appears that neither the trial Court nor the High Court Division arrived at a finding that the suit in question was shown in the daily cause list so as to show that the defendants had knowledge of the exparte decree before 22-2-88. The trial Court found manipulation in the cause list dated 4-1-88. Both the trial Court as well as the High Court Division have held that because the defendants had filed an application on 4-1-88 praying for adjournment of the ex parte disposal of the suit-it is to be presumed that they had the knowledge of the ex parte decree before 22-2-88. Thus it appears that neither the trial Court nor the High Court Division considered the important question as to whether the defendants had the opportunity of knowing the exparte disposal of the suit from the daily cause list, when the admitted position is, there is no entry in the daily register against Title, Suit No.142 of 1986.

<u>18. It is a cardinal principle of administration of justice that no result of any judicial proceeding should be allowed to receive judicial approval from any court of law whenever it is obtained by practising fraud upon the court; reason being fraud demolishes the very foundation of sanctity of such judicial proceeding. It is also well established principle of law that fraud vitiates all judicial proceedings. Thus contravention of the provision of law cannot be a valid ground for allowing an order obtained by fraud to stand. When the trial Court itself on consideration of the materials on record was obtaining the ex parte decree it was the duty of the satisfied that a fraud had been committed in trial Court to set aside the ex parte decree. The failure of the trial Court in the performance of its legal obligations ought not to have been maintained by the High Court Division in affirming the finding of the trial Court.</u>

19. Fact of fraud is a matter of inference from proved facts and circumstances of each case and the evidence received by the court. Each circumstance by itself may not tell much, but when a bundle of circumstances are taken together they may bring into light a fraudulent or dishonest plan to commit fraud.

20.  It is already noted that the plaintiff got the suit fixed for peremptory hearing on 26-12 87 behind the back of the defendants upon filing an application on an off date although the defendants had been seriously contesting the suit by filing written statements. It is also seen that in the absence of the regular presiding judge of the court suit was disposed of ex parte by another Judge, who on that date was in-charge of the court and that the defendant's application for adjournment of hearing of the suit ex parte was not placed before the Judge concerned before hearing of the suit ex parte and even the said application is missing from the case record and that a manipulation in suit number in the daily cause list has been noted by the trial Court whereby TS No.142 of 1986 was shown as TS to 242 of 1986. It is clear from the materials on record that the defendants successfully proved in the trial Court the elements of fraud as alleged by them for setting aside the ex parte decree and that the plaintiff could not show that the ex parte disposal of the suit had been recorded in the daily cause list against Title Suit No. 142 of 1986 which could lead to a presumption of the defendant's knowledge of such ex parte disposal of the suit on 4-1-88. Thus, it appears that the learned Judges of the High Court Division did not at all consider the defendants against the plaintiff in upholding the gravity of allegations of fraud alleged by the judgment and order of the trial Court.

21. There is another aspect of the matter which can be seen from the statement made by the plaintiff himself in the plaint of the suit. In a suit for specific performance of contract only the contracting parties and in view of the provisions of the President's Order No.142 of 1972, the Government, are the necessary parties. But the plaintiff has made the Joint Secretary.  Ministry of Works and Urban Development, Government of Bangladesh, Bangladesh Secretariat, who looks after abandoned property, as defendant No.4 in the suit making statements in paragraph 9 of plaint as hereunder "that the original owners, defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are not absentee and they are Bangladeshi nationals and the suit property belongs to the Bangladeshi nationals. In order to avoid all complications, the defendant No.4 has been impleaded in the suit so that the suit may be adjudicated in his presence".

22. These statements made in paragraph 9 of the plaint show that the plaintiff had the knowledge that there was some complication in respect of the suit property and that it may have been treated as an abandoned property. The plaintiff as OPW 1 also has admitted in cross-examination (page 60 of the Paper .Book) that he has instituted a case in the Court of Settlement in respect of the suit property. From the order sheet it appears that the suit was filed on 2-6-86 and on the next day ie 3-6-86 defendant No.3 DIT (now RAJUK) appeared by filing-power and the present defendant-appellants filed the written statement before 20-9-86 taking specific defence that the suit property having been declared abandoned property the suit itself was not maintainable inasmuch as it is hit by Article 14(1) of President's Order No.16 of 1972, MLR VII of 1982 and Ordinance No. LIV of 1985.

23. It is a cardinal principle of administration of civil justice that the plaintiff is to prove his case fairly to get the decree in his favour. But it appears that the learned Judge in charge of the trial Court mechanically passed the decree in favour of the plaintiff without even considering the circumstances which necessitated the plaintiff to make defendant No.4, the Joint Secretary, Ministry of Works and Urban Development as a defendant in his suit for specific performance of contract. Had the learned Judge taken note of the plaintiffs statement made in paragraph 9 of the plaint he would have definitely got the clue whether the suit as instituted was maintainable or not. Besides that, in the interest of justice that trial Court in the disposal of the miscellaneous case ought to have taken note of the admitted facts that the plaintiff had instituted a case in respect of the suit property in the Court of Settlement, obviously for releasing the same from the list of abandoned property.

Ordinarily this Division is slow to interfere with concurrent finding of facts of the courts below. But having considered the notorious facts and peculiar aspects of the present case, as noted earlier, under the dictate of judicial conscience we are inclined to see proper and fair adjudication of the suit. Accordingly, for doing complete justice in the matter we allow this appeal without, however, any order as to cost. In the result the judgment of the High Court Division is set aside and the Miscellaneous Case No.14 of 1988 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka is allowed and Title Suit No. 142 of 1986 is restored to its original file and number absence from duty for than 5 years has resulted in respondent No.1’s cessation as a Government Servant under Rule 18 of  the Fundamental Rules.

The appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The impugned of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal is set aside and that of the Administrative Tribunal is restored.

End.
