full_judgment:
This Rule was issued under section 115 of the Code of Civil 'Procedure at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner calling upon the defendant opposite party No. 1, to show cause as to why the judgment arid degree dated 1-7-1991 and 8-7-1991 respectively passed by the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court, Khulna, in Title Appeal No.169 of 1985 setting aside those dated 10-7-1985 and 16-7-1985 respectively, passed by the Munsif, Police Station-Dumuria, in Title Suit No. 15 of 1983, should not be set aside.

2. The plaintiff-petitioner filed a suit being Title Suit No. 19 of 1983 in the Court of Munsif, Second Court Khulna, against the defendant opposite parties praying for declaration of his title in the suit land contending inter alia; that 0.47 acre of land mentioned in the Schedule 1 to the plaint, originally belonged to one Minhaj Gazi whose name was recorded in CS Khatian No. 46 in Plot No. 17 as stated in Schedule 1 to the plaint and 0.11 acre out of 0.46 acres of land stated in Schedule 2 to the plaint, originally belonged to one Nasir Biswas whose name was recorded in CS Khatian No. 45 in Plot No. 16, both the plots situated in Mouza Noakati, PS Dumuria, District Khulna, that Minhaj transferred 0.47 acre of land by registered Kabala dated 11-3-1944 to Shahadat Biswas, the defendant No.3, that Nasim Biswas had four Sons, namely, Dinder Biswas defendant No. 1 (opposite party No.2). Intaj Biswas, defendant No.2 (opposite party No.3). Shahadat Biswas defendant No. 3 and Nabu Ali Biswas, that after the death of Nasim Biswas, his four sons including the defendant No. 3 inherited 0.11 acre of land each; that in this manner the defendant No. 3 became owner of 0.47 acre of land by purchase and 0.11 acre of land by way of inheritance, in total 0.58 acre that the defendant No.3 while in possessions of the aforesaid 0.58 acre, of land, sold the said lands to the plaintiff minor Bashibur Rahman Biswas by a registered kabala dated 11-11-1980, and since purchase the plaintiff is in possession is of the said lands but as the names of the defendant Nos. 1 to 3 were wrongly recorded in SA Khatian No.78 although the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 never possessed the said lands rather, the plaintiff since his purchase on 11-11-1980 is in possessions if the suit lands, The further case of the plaintiff is that the alleged deed of gift by the defendant No. 3 dated 22-3-1975 in favour of defendant No. 5 Babar Ali was never acted upon but the defendant No.5 subsequently on 14-7-1982 sold 0.24 1/2  acres of land to Hanif Ali Biswas, the defendant No. 4 (the son of Nabu Ali Biswas) although he never acquired any right, title or possession in respect of the properties mentioned in the deed of gift, that before selling of the suit land, the defendant No.3-by registered deed dated 11-11-1982 cancelled the earlier deed of gift dated 22-3-1975 but as the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 4 threatened the plaintiff on 15-1-1983 he was constrained to file the instant suit.

3. The suit was renumbered as Title Suit No. 15 of 1983 on being transferred to the Court of Munsif, Dumuria Upazila.

4. Only the defendant No. 4 (opposite party No. 1) contested the suit by filing a written statement, contending inter alia that the suit lands mentioned in the Schedule-1 to the Plaint originally belonged to Minhaj Gazi, that the defendant No. 3 purchased 0.47 acre of lands mentioned on Schedule-1 to the plaint from Minhaj Gazi with common funds from the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, as such, the suit land was recorded in the names defendant Nos. 1 to 3 in SA Khatian, that although the said property was purchase only in the name of defendant No. 3 but since his two other brothers were also owners of the said land their names were correctly recorded in SA Khatian that after such purchase the defendant No. 2 constructed his house in his portion of 0.15 acre of land within the said 0.47 acre, that the lands stated in Shedule-2 to the plaint originally belonged to  Nasim Biswas and after his death it was owned and possessed by four brothers and one sister Baru Bibi, all sons and daughter of late Nasim Biswas but the name of Baru Bibi was mistakenly omitted in SA Khatian, that the defendant No. 3 Shahadat Biswas had no children he reared up one Babar Ali, defendant No. 5 from his early ,childhood and when he grew up, the defendant No.3 also gave him in marriage, that he made, a gift of 0.15 3/4 acre from Schedule-1 and 0.09 acre from Schedule-2 to the plaint, in total 0.24 3/4  acre, in favour of defendant No. 5 by a registered deed of gift dated 22-3-1975 that the defendant No. 5 himself constructed a tin shed house thereon and also after his marriage used to live there, that two of his children died who were buried in the suit land, that he used to pay the ground rents in respect of the suit land, that eventually the defendant No.5 transferred 0.09 acre of land as. stated in Schedule-I to the plaint by a deed registered on 14-7-1982 in favour of the defendant No. 4 and another deed registered on 14-10-1982, transferred 0.6 1/6 acre and 0.09 acre as stated in Schedule-1 and 2 respectively in his favour, the defendant No.4 also became owner to the extent of 0.05 acre as an heir of Nabu Biswas and 0.04 acre by purchase from his sister Baru Bibi bya deed registered on 2-7-1984 in plot No.16 C.S Khatian No. 45, SA Khatian No. 77. In this manner, the defendant No 4 became owner of 0.15 1/4 acre of land in Schedule-1 to the plaint and 0.18 acres in the aforesaid plot No. 16. The further case of the defendant opposite party No. 1 is that Amin Ali Biswas, the son of the defendant No. 1 purchased the suit land in the benami of his five-year-old minor son, the plaintiff, falsely alleging that the suit lands, belonged to the defendant No.3 alone, although he had no subsisting interest in the suit land since his gift dated 22-3-1975, made in favour of the defendant No. 5.

5. After hearing, the learned Munsif found that the defendant No. 3 alone purchased 0.47 acre of land stated in Schedule-1 to the plaint from Minhaj Gazi and also became owner to the extent of 0.11 acre as stated in Schedule-2 to the plaint as one of the four sons of Nasim Biswas and that his deed of gift was not acted upon and possessions of the suit lands were not delivered, presumably to the defendant No. 5 The learned Munsif found title and possession in favour of the plaintiff and decreed the suit. On appeal being Title Appeal No. 169 of 1985, the learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court, Khulna, on consideration of evidence on record found, inter alia, that it is Amin Ali Biswas the father of the miner plaintiff, filed the suit, in the name of his minor son, that the suit itself is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as he did not pray for cancellation of the registered deed of gift dated 22-3-1975made by the defendant No. 3 in favour of defendant No. 5, that the said deed was genuine and acted upon, that the registered deed of cancelling dated 11-11-1982 by the defendant No. 3 was not legal and valid, consequently by the kabala registered on 11-11-1982 by him, the plaintiff did not acquire any right or title in the suit lands. With these findings the learned Appellate Judge set aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif, allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit

6. Mr Syed Shahidur Rahman, Advocate, appears with Mr Moklesur Rahman, Advocate, on behalf of the petitioner while Mr KS Zaman, Advocate, appears with AKM Salahuddin Khan, Advocate, on behalf of the opposite party No. 1.

7. It is admitted that the suit land of 0.47 acre mentioned in Scheduled 1 to the plaint originally belonged to Minhaj Gazi. His name was recorded in CS Khatian 0.17 within CS Khatian No. 46 corresponding to. SA Khatian No.78 Similarly, 0.45 acre of land was recorded in the name of one Nasir Biswas in CS Plot No. 16 within CS Khatian No. 45 the land mentioned in Schedule 2 to the plaint. He had four sons including the defendant No. 3 Minhaj Gazi transferred, his 0.47 acre of Jand by a registered kabala dated 11-3-1944 (Ext 3) in favour of the defendant No. 3. As such, he became owner of 0.47 acre by purchase and also 0.11 acre by inheritance as one of four sons of Nasir Biswas as referred, to in schedule-2 to the plaint The first question is, whether the defendant No. 3 was owner to the extent of 0.47 acre purchased from Minhaj Gazi or he was owner only to the extent of 1/3 .of 0.47 acre as recorded in SA Khatian No. 77. The learned Munsif held that he was the owner of his entire purchased land of 0.47 acre while in appeal the learned Subordinate Judge held that although the aforesaid entire of 0.47 acre of land was purchased in the name of the defendant No.3 alone but, as a matter of fact, it was purchased from the common fund of all the three brothers and accordingly it was so recorded in SA Khatian showing 1/3rd share of each of the three brothers i.e. the defendant Nos.1 to 3.

8. Mr Syed Shahidur Rahman, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff petitioner supports the finding of the learned Munsif in this regard and submits that the defendant No. 3 alone purchased 0.47 acre of land from Minhaj as evidenced from the registered Kabala dated 11-3-1944 (Exhibit 3) and, as such, the concerned SA Khatian showing the names of the defendant Nos. 1 to 3 instead of the defendant-No.3 alone, was obviously wrong.

9. On the other hand, Mr KS Zaman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 1, refers to the different petitions of the deposition of witness of both the sides and supports the finding of the learned Appellate Judge in this regard and submits that admittedly defendant No. 3 purchased 0.47 acre of land from Minhaj Gazi by a kabala registered on 11-3-1944 (Exhibit 3) though in his own ,name but was purchased from the common fund of all three brothers the defendant Nos. 1 to 3, and, as such, on the initiative of defendant No. 3 himself the names of all three brothers are recorded SA Khatian as owner of 0.47 acre of land and each of the three brothers, the defendant Nos. 1 to 3, used to possesses 0.1533 acre of land and had their own homestead in their respective 1/3rd portion of the said purchased land. As such, the learned Advocate submits, the defendant No. 3 in spite of Exhibit-3 was owner to the extent of 1/3rd share out of the aforesaid 0.47 acre of land.

10. It appears from the record and also from the evidence that SA Khatian records the names of all three brothers showing that each of them was owner to the extent of 1/3rd portion of the land.

11. It is true that Exhibit 3 shows the defendant No. 3 as the only purchaser of 0.47 acre of land from Minhaj Gazi but PW 1 Amin Ali Biswas, the father of the plaintiff, admitted in his, deposition that his father, the defendant No 1 had his own house within the suit land. This suggests his possessions in a part of the suit land and, also his consequent ownership thereon in derogation to the alleged exclusive ownership of the defendant No. 3 alone. Similarly, the DW 2 Imtaz Biswas (the defendant No. 2) also stated in his deposition that he has his own house in a portion of the suit land and possesses part of it PW 1 also admitted in his cross-examination that the defendant No. 3, was alive at the time of SA operation but he did not take any step to correct the name and record the entire 0.47 acre in his own name alone instead of the names of his three brothers as recorded in the SA Khatian although he lived for 11 long time after the aforesaid SA operation. PW 3 Nurul Islam, a neighbour also admitted in his cross-examination that the purchased land of 0.47 acre was divided in three parts and each 1/3rrl part was owned, possessed and enjoyed by the defendant Nos. 1 to 3 separately. He also said that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 used to possess and enjoy their respective shares in the suit land. PW 5 Abdul Barek Sheikh also stated in his deposition that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 used to possess their respective shares in the purchased property of 0.47 acre. The defendant No. 4 Hanif Ali Biswas deposed as DW 1. He is the son of Nabu Ali Biswas, one of the four sons left by Nasim Biswas. He stated in his deposition that the defendant No.3 purchased the suit land and shared with his other two brothers and accordingly, the names of all three brothers were recorded. The DW 4 A Halim stated in his deposition that defendant No. 3 used to possess only 1I3rd of the total land of 0.47.acre and defendant No.2 Intaj Biswas also used to possess his portion of the said purchased land.

12. These evidence together with the record of rights belie the claim of the plaintiff and clearly shows that although 0.47 acre of land in plot No. 17 in CS Khatian No. 46 corresponding to SA Khatian No. 78 as referred to in schedule-1 to the plaint, was purchased in the name of the defendant No.3 alone but, as a matter of fact, it was owned possessed and enjoyed by the defendant Nos. 1 to 3, in their respective 1/3rd shares and consequently, defendant No. 3 was owner to the extent of only 0.1533 acre of lands in Schedule-1 to the plaint.

13. The next question is whether the gift was made by the defendant No. 3 in favour of Babar Ali, the defendant No. 5, by the deed of gift registered on 22-3-1975 (Exhibit Uma and Exhibit 6) was valid and acted upon or not.

14. In this regard, Sayed Shahidur Rahman, the learned Advocate, submits that although the defendant No. 3 reared up Babar Ali but the alleged gift made by him in favour of Babar Ali was never acted upon and possession was never delivered in his favour, consequently Babar Ali never acquired any right, title or possession of the suit land, as such, the purported sale to the defendant No.4 was also illegal, Besides, he further submits, only after revocation of the earlier deed of gift Exhibit-6 and (Exhibit-Uma) by a registered deed of cancellation, the defendant No.3 executed and registered a deed of sale in favour of the plaintiff on 11-11-1982 and also transferred possession in his favour, as such, the said transfer was legal and valid.

15. In reply, Mr Zaman submits that Babar Ali was reared up by the defendant No.3 from his very early childhood and by a deed of gift registered on 22-3-1975 (Exhibit Uma) he transferred 0.242/3  acre of his land in favour of the said Babar Ali, that he went into possession of the gifted properties and enjoyed the same till he sold the said properties by registered deeds dated 14-7-1982 (Exhibit-Ka) and 15-11-1982 (Exhibit-Kha) in favour of defendant No. 4 and also delivered possession in his favour. He further submits that since the said Babar Ali as owner transferred his said properties in favour of the defendant No. 4, the alleged revocation of the gift by a deed of conciliation registered on 11-11-1982 allegedly by defendant No. 3 was illegal and without any lawful effect, consequently the deed of sale (Exhibit 4) did not confer any right, title or interest in favour of the plaintiff which is nothing but a mere paper transaction and made even without any consideration.

16. It is on evidence that from the very childhood Babar Ali was reared up by the defendant No.3 as his own son. He gave him in marriage, after marriage all of them used to live together in the same homestead. Eventually, by a deed of gift dated 22-3-1975, (Exhibit-Uma) the defendant No. 3 transferred 0.24⁡〖2/3〗 acre in favour of Babar Ali and all of them continued to live together.

<u>17. The law in this respect is well settled, A Mohammedan may dispose of all his properties by way of gift in favour of anybody, even to it stranger. But a gift in order to be valid and complete, there should, firstly, be a declaration of gift by the donor in favour of the donee, secondly, an acceptance of the said gift expressly or impliedly by the donee and thirdly, delivery of possession of the subject matter of the gift by the donor to the donee.</u>

18. Although there was no requirement of' writing or registration for a valid gift to be effective, still in this case, Exhibit-Uma, the deed of gift registered on 22-3-1975, shows that the defendant No.3 transferred his  0.24⁡〖2/3〗  acre of land in favour of the defendant No. 5. This is admitted. Now let me consider the evidence of physical delivery of possession by the defendant No. 3 to the defendant No.5. PW 1, the father of the minor plaintiff in his cross-examination admitted that defendant No.1 reared up .Babar Ali and gave him in marriage and they used to live together before the cancellation of the gift dated 11-11-1982 and the said Babar Ali used to look after the defendant No.3. PW 3 Nurul Joarder, a neighbour, stated in his cross-examination that Babar Ali buried his two sons in the suit land. PW 4 Md Afzal Shaikh stated in his deposition that defendant No. 3 and Babar Ali used to possess the suit lands together. Similarly, defendant No. 2 Intajuddin, a brother of defendant No. 3, stated in his deposition as DW 2 that the defendant No. 3 made a gift of his properties in favour of the said Babar Ali and Babar Ali while was in possession sold the said lands to the defendant No. 4 Hanif and thereafter Hanif went into possession of the suit lands. Baba Ali, the defendant No. 5, himself deposed as DW5 and stated in his deposition that he was reared up by the defendant No. 3 since his age of three months.

19. It appears that although there was no direct evidence of physical delivery of possession by the defendant No.3 to the defendant No.5 but from the conduct of the defendant No. 3 the donore and the defendant No. 5 the donee, as appears from the evidence discussed above, their intention was clear that after the gift, the defendant No.3 acknowledge the ownership of the defendant No. 5 in his concerned properties and the defendant No. 5 also exercised his rights as the owner of the said properties. It is, no doubt, of the essence of a gift that it should be completed by the delivery of possession. The Holy Prophet has said "A gift is not valid unless possessed" (Inayah, Vd. IV page-24). The law contemplates that the possession required to be given to the donee must be such as the nature of the property permits and the circumstances wound around it. If the donor has done all that he could do under the circumstances, to complete the contemplated gift, the transfer is valid. The mode by which the possession is delivered to the donee depends upon the nature and character of the property and the question has to be considered keeping in mind all the facts and circumstances of the case. The evidence on record show that the defendant No. 3 reared up the defendant No. 5 from his very early childhood, gave him in marriage when he grew up and the defendant No. 5 along with his family looked after the defendant No.3 and continued to live with him in the same homestead. Exhibit-Uma shows the bonafide intention of the defendant No. 3 to divest himself of his concerned property and to confer it on the defendant No. 5. The defendant No.5 also possessed and treated the said property as his own even buried his own children in a portion of the suit land. Besides, he by the deeds of sale registered on 14-7-1982 and 15-11-1982, transferred the said very lands of 0.242/3 acre, received from the defendant No. 3 by way of gift, in favour of the defendant No. 4. As such, there can hardly be any doubt that the deed of gift, Exhibit Uma was acted upon including delivery of possession in favour of the defendant No.5 as was necessary and practicable under the facts and circumstances of the case and he was owner to the extent of  0.24⁡〖2/3〗   acre of land since 22-3-1975. In this regard, it is worthwhile to quote West in the case of Shaik Ibrahim vs Shaik Suleman 9 ILR Born 146;

"as to the delivery of the house, the principle is to be borne in mind, that when a person is present on the premises proposed to be delivered to him, a declaration of the person previously possessed puts him into possession. He occupies certain part, and this occupation becoming actual possession by the will of the parties, extends to" the whole which is in immediate conception with such part where the possession is rightfully, though not where it is wrongfully taken Exparte Fletchar, An appropriate intention where two are present on the same premises may put the one out as well as the other into possession without any actual physical departure or formal entry, and effect is to be given, as far as possible, to the purpose of an owner whose intention to transfer has been unequivocally manifested."

<u>20. The next question is, whether the deed of gift dated 22-3-1975 (Exhibit-Uma) was validly revoked by the defendant No. 3 by his deed of cancellation registered on 11-11-1982 (Exhibit 5) a gift can only be revoked before it is acted upon. But once the possession is delivered in favour of the donee and he exercises his right of ownership, as in this case, the gift cannot be revoked. In this case PW 1 and PW 2 admitted in their cross-examination that the deed of gift made in favour of Babar Ali was cancelled by the defendant No.3 only when the said Babar Ali sold the properties, as such, apart from other evidence of ownership exercised by the defendant No. 5, his transfer even of a part of the properties by a registered deed dated 14-7-1982 (Exhibit-Ka) in favour of the defendant No. 4, is enough to invalidate any attempt even by the defendant No. 3, the donor, to revoke his earlier gift of the said properties in favour of the defendant No. 5. Besides, once possession of an immovable property is delivered in favour of the donee, specially when the gift is by a registered instrument, nothing short of a decree of the Court is sufficient to revoke the gift-mere revocation by a registered deed of cancellation is not at all enough.</u>

21. Under such circumstances, the deed of cancellation by the defendant No.3 registered on 11-1l-1962 (Exhibit 5) is invalid and ineffective in the eye of law, consequently, the deed of sale registered sale on 11-11-1982 (Exhibit 41 in favour of the plaintiff is also invalid too and does not confer any right, title or ownership on him and the appeal was rightly allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif.

22. Another point requires consideration. The plaintiff was fully aware that the defendant No. 3 had already transferred his concerned properties in favour of the defendant No.5 by a deed of gift registered on 22-3-1975, still simple suit for declaration of title was filed, without praying for cancellation of the said deed of gift dated 22-3-1975 (Exhibit-Uma) although he knew that, such cancellation is required because PW 1, the father of the minor plaintiff, himself admitted in his cross-examination that he prayed for cancellation of the earlier deed of gift also which is not correct. Under such circumstances this suit for simple declaration, without a proper prayer for decree for cancellation of the deed of gift dated 22-3-1975 (Exhibit-Uma), is also-barred under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and, as such, not maintainable.

23. In the result I find nothing to interfere with the judgment and decree passed by the learned Appellate Judge.

24. Before parting with the case, I would like to observe that at the time of delivery of judgment on 8-8-1999, it was detected the date of drawing up of the decree in Title Suit No.15 of 1983 was wrong, as such, the records were sent to the court of Assistant Judge, Dumuria, Khulna, for correction of the date of decree. The learned Assistant Judge corrected the date in the decree but though the corrections were made in two places, he put his signature in one place only instead of both the places, the learned Judge ought to have put his signature with date of actual correction in all the places of corrections.

25. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged but without any order as to cost.

Send down the records forthwith.

End.

full_judgment:
Gour Gopal Saha J: This Rule is directed against the order dated 18-3-98 passed by the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Sadar Chittagong, in Partition Suit No. 88 of 1981 rejecting the plaintiffs application for determination of the value of 1/3rd share of the suit property for buying up purposes.

2. Short facts leading to the case are that, the petitioners as plaintiffs instituted a suit for partition of the suit property with a prayer for buying up the share of the stranger purchaser who had purchased the same from their full brothers Chiranjib Sen, before the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong being Partition Suit No. 88 of 1981, alleging, inter alia, that the suit property is a dwelling house bounded by pucca boundary walls within the city of Chittagong and it contains an area of 5 gondas and 2 karas of land, Defendant Opposite Party No. 1 purchased the suit property by sale deed between 15-5-81 and 21-5-81 whereby Chiranjib Sen purportedly sold the entire suit property to defendant No. 1 although he had only 1/3rd share therein, It has been alleged that the suit property was the Streedhan property of Smt Madhabi Lata Sen, mother of the plaintiff petitioners and defendant Chiranjib Sen, the only son of late Madhabi Lata Sen. The suit property is an undivided homestead and, as such, the plaintiffs are entitled to buy up the same from defendant No. 1.

3. Opposite party No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaint and contended, inter alia, that the suit property was purchased by the father of the petitioners late Promoda Ranjan Sen in the benami of his, wife Madhabi Lata Sen, and therefore their son Chiranjib Sen, Alone inherited the suit property and his daughter a the plaintiffs did not inherit anything in it and consequently the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. On the above-noted pleadings of the parties the suit proceeded arid ultimately reached the stage of peremptory hearing when both the parties adduced evidence in support of their respective cases.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge by this judgment dated 17-8-98 dismissed the suit with the finding that the plaintiffs could not prove that their mother Madhabi Lata Sen was the real owner of the Suit property.

6. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree the plaintiffs petitioners took an appeal before High Court Division, being FA No. 257 of 1991.(Dhaka) =FA No, 31 of 1988 (Chittagong) and a Division Bench of this Court after hearing the parties allowed the appeal and decreed, the suit by judgment dated 20-6-96 with the finding that the suit property was the Streedhan property of Madhabi Sen and as such, plaintiffs inherited 2/3rd share of the suit property. It was also found that the plaintiffs were entitled to buy up 1I3rd share of the suit property which was earlier purchased by defendant opposite party No. 1, in terms of section 4 of the Partition Act read with section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act.

7. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division, defendant opposite party, No. 1 filed a Civil Petition for-Leave to Appeal before the Appellate Division in Civil Petition No. 598 of 1996 but the same was ultimately dismissed by order dated 2-2-97, After the records of the suit reached the trial Court the plaintiff petitioners on 10-4-91 filed an application before the learned Subordinate Judge praying for determination of the value of the 1/3rd share of the suit property out of the total amount of Taka 2,80,000.00 as the price of the entire suit property shown in the impugned sale deeds so as to enable the plaintiffs to deposit the same before the Court towards the buying up process.

8. Defendant opposite party No. 1 resisted the aforesaid application for determination of the price of 1/3rd share of the suit property by filing written objection contending, inter alia, that at the time of purchase of the suit property the value of the land was much more than the value shown in the kabala of the year 1981 when the price of one gonda of land stood at Taka 2 lac whereas the present market price is Taka 4,50,000.00. It was also contended that the value of the 1/3rd share of the suit property should be made as it prevails at the time of the final decree and not as it prevails now or as it prevailed at the time of the impugned purchase.

9. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing parties rejected the plaintiffs application holding, inter alia that the valuation of the 1/3rd share of the suit property should be made at the time of filing of the report by the Advocate Commissioner while effecting the final decree. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid impugned order the petitioners moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

10. Mr SR Paul the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners, submits that in view of the fact that the plaintiff-petitioners opted for buying up the 1/3rd share. of the undivided family dwelling house and filed Partition Suit No. 88 of 1981 before the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong on 2-7-81 i.e. within two months of the purchase of the same by the stranger purchaser the proper time for determination of the value of the buying up share is the time of filing of the suit as envisaged under section 4 of the Partition Act and, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge was manifestly wrong in passing the impugned order on an erroneous view of law and the same has occasioned failure of justice.

11. Mr HN Nondy, the learned Advocate appearing for opposite party No. 1, on the other hand, submits that the value of the buying up share of the suit property under section 4 of the Partition Act can be determined only at the time of the final decree when the Advocate Commissioner allots sahams to the contending parties and not before that and consequently, the learned Subordinate Judge committed no error of law in passing the impugned order occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that the value of the buying up share of the suit property is made on the basis of the Commissioner's report after allotting sahams to the contending parties when shares of the parties are determined and value thereof assessed i.e. only at the stage of final decree and not before that and, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge was perfectly justified in passing the impugned order and it suffers from no illegality or legal infirmity. The learned Advocate further submits that the rights of the parties in a suit for partition are determined at the preliminary decree but sahams are determined and effected at the time of the final decree and, as such, the proper time for determination of the value of the buying up share is the final decree and consequently, the learned Subordinate Judge committed no error of law in passing the impugned order occasioning failure of justice justifying interference by this Court exercising revisional power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

12. Mr Paul has placed before us the impugned order as well as the application dated 10-4-97 praying for determination of the value of the buying up share of the suit property and the written objection filed by the contesting defendants against it.

<u>13. It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge passed the impugned order essentially on the basis of a case reported in AIR 1973 Allahabad 548 (Kashinath Bhatt and others vs Atma Ram and others) in which a Single Judge of the Allahabad High Court took the view that the proper time for determining the valuation of the share of the stranger purchaser to an undivided homestead would be at the time of filing of the Advocate Commissioner's report while allotting specific sahams to the parties in effecting partition by metes and bounds.</u>

<u>14. In support of the contention Mr Paul has placed reliance on the case of Sayesta Bibi and others vs Juma Shah and others reported in 42 DLR (AD) 53 wherein it has been held that the claims of the parties in a suit under section 4 of the Partition Act are to be determined with reference to their respective possessions existing at the time of filing of the suit. It is to be noted in this connection that in this case impartibility of the suit property is undisputed when the suit was filed by the petitioners in 1981. In this case it is found that the suit was filed almost immediately after the purchase of the same by stranger defendant opposite party No. 1. Mr Paul also placed reliance on the case of Mrs Malati Ramchandra Raut and others vs Mahadebvasudes Joshi and others, reported in AIR 1991 (SC) 700 in which case it has been held in a suit for partition shares of the parties have to be valued as they existed on the date of filing of the suit for buying up the share of the stranger purchaser. In this case, it is not disputed fact that the plaintiffs filed the Partition Suit on 2-7-81 for buying up the undivided share of the stranger purchaser.</u>

<u>15. Mr Nondy, on the other hand, has placed reliance on the case of Kashinath Bhatt vs Atma Ram and others, reported in AIR 1973 Allahabad 58, Mr Nondy then cites the case of Sree Jugal Kishore Sarker vs Azizur Rahman and others, reported in 40 DLR (AD) 150. In support of his contention Mr Nondy also cites the case of Subal Chandra Modak vs Gostha Bihari Das, reported in 60 CWN 829. Mr Nondy then cited before us the case of Kshirode Chunder Ghosal and another vs Saroda Prosa Mitra reported in 12 CLJ 525.</u>

<u>16. On perusal of the cited decisions we find that only in the case reported in AIR 1973 Allahabad 58 a Single Judge took the view that the proper time for valuation of buying up share under section 4 of the Partition Act is at the time of the final decree. Other decisions relied on by Mr Nondy have reference to the time for determining the value of the buying up share of the stranger purchases but the facts and circumstances of those cases are quite distinguishable from the facts of the present case and consequently, these are of no assistance to the opposite parties. In the case of Sayesta Bila and others vs Juma Shah and others reported in 42 DLR (AD) 53 our Appellate Division took the view that the time for determination of the value of buying up share shall be the time when the parties opt for purchasing the share of the stranger purchaser.</u>

<u>17. Section 4 of the Partition Act was enacted to afford a special opportunity to a co-sharer of an undivided homestead or dwelling house against a stranger purchaser for buying up his share through the Court. The-object of this legislation is to preserve the sanctity of an undivided dwelling house against the intrusion of a stranger on the basis of purchase of a portion of such a dwelling house from a co-sharer or some of the co-sharers. This was obviously to safeguard the interest of the existing co-sharer or co-sharers against forcing entry into an undivided dwelling house by a stranger by providing an opportunity to buy up the share purchased by a stranger thereto. This is indeed a beneficial legislation for the co-owners of an undivided homestead or dwelling house against the onslaught of an outsider. The object of this legislation is reasonable and it is quite in consonance with the principle of equity, justice and, good conscience. Since in the instant case the plaintiff petitioners opted to purchase the share of the stranger purchaser in the undivided homestead in question immediately after the purchase of the same by the stranger defendant, we are of the view that the proper time to determine the value of the buying up share is the time of filing of the suit when the plaintiff ostensibly opted to buy up the share of the stranger purchaser in the undivided dwelling house. The principle of law enunciated by their Lordships in 42 DLR (AD) 53 fully applies to the facts and circumstances of the present case and we are bound to be in respectful agreement with the view taken therein.</u>

<u>18. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record we are of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in holding that the proper time for determination of the value of the buying up share of an undivided homestead is at the time of the final decree and not before that. We are, therefore, unable to accept the contentions raised by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties. In the facts of the case, we hold that the proper time for determination of the value of the suit property is at the time of filing of the suit for partition when the co-owner seeks the protection of, the Court for buying up the share of a stranger purchaser in the undivided dwelling house, The submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioners are thus found to have sufficient substance and these are accordingly sustained.</u>

19. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost and the impugned order dated 18-3-98 passed on 18-3-98 by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Sadar Chittagong in Partition Suit No. 88 of 1981 is set aside. The learned Subordinate Judge is hereby directed to determine the valuation of the buying up share of the suit property with reference to the price prevailing at the market on the date of filing of the, suit on 2-7-81.

20. In view of the fact that this is a very old case, the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong is directed to dispose of Partition Suit No. 88 of 1981 within a period of six months positively from the date of receipt of the order of the Court.

Communicate the order to the learned, Court below immediately for his information and necessary action.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment dated 18-01-96 passed by this Court in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 36 of 1995)
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman J: This appeal by leave by the pre-emptee appellant by way of review is against the judgment and order passed on 18-1-96 in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 36 of 1995 dismissing the leave petition by this Division.

2. Respondent No.1 as pre-emptor filed three cases for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. The pre-emption cases were filed in respect of three kabalas on the assertion that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer of the land.

3. The pre-emptee contested the cases stating that respondent Nos. 2-4 got saham in Partition Suit No. 36 of 1975 and they sold the same by the disputed three sale deeds and thereafter the pre-emptee got his name mutated and also spent a substantial amount of money for improvement of the case land. Hence the pre-emptor is not a co- sharer.

4. The trial Court dismissed the three pre-emption cases by a common judgment holding that ,in view of the final decree passed in Title Suit No. 36 of 1975 (Partition suit) the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the case land.

5. On appeal the lower appellate Court reversed the judgment of the trial Court and allowed the pre-emption cases on the ground that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the land as the partition decree was not executed in full and that the tenancy of the pre-emptor and the vendors were still ejmali and that there was no evidence that the ejmali property was separated. A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division affirmed the judgment of the lower appellate Court.

6. In Leave Petition Nos. 36-38 of 1995 the main question was, whether the pre-emptor is still a co-sharer in the land transferred.

7. In our Original Judgment it was held that a decree no doubt finally determines the status of the parties to the suit but unless it is fully executed co-sharership in the land transferred does not change automatically along with final decree, and that it was further held that the pre-emptee having failed to prove that the case land was partitioned by Advocate Commissioner and his vendor got possession therein the co-sharership of the pre-emptor in the land continues and, in that view, we allowed the pre-emption Nos. 36-38 of 1995.

8. Leave was granted in the review petition to consider the submission of Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee-appellant, to consider whether in view of the provisions of section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 24(11) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in affirming the decision of the court of appeal below which was based on the reasoning’s that the final decree of partition passed in Title Suit No. 36 of 1975 had not been fully executed and whether this material aspect of this case has not been considered by this Division in disposing of the petition for leave to appeal.

9. Leave was further granted to consider the question of law as to the effect of a final decree in a partition suit on the co-sharership of the pre-emptor in a pre-emption proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949.

10. The pre-emptor Abdul Karim and his father Momin Biswas purchased five kathas i.e. 0.0825 Ajutangsha of land from CS Plot No. 968 in equal share by registered deed on 24-4-60 and thereafter on the death of his father the pre-emptor filed partition suit against the other heirs of his father in the court of Sub-Judge, 1st Court, Faridpur being TS No. 36 of 1975 and the said suit was decreed in preliminary form on 30-11-77 and thereafter an Advocate Commissioner was appointed for distributing and separating the boundary of the saham of the ejmali land to the parties of the said partition suit and the Advocate Commissioner. accordingly distributed and separated the saham and filed his statement on 2-10-78. Thereafter, the final decree was passed on 23-12-78 and the suit property fell in the saham of respondent Nos. 2, 3 and 4 and they possessed the property in their respective share in khas. Respondent Nos. 2-4 sold the suit property on 29-12-84 to the Appellant long after the final decree was passed in Title. Suit No. 36 of 1975 and thereafter the pre-emptor respondent No. 1 filed the pre-emption Miscellaneous Cases on 28-9-85 on the ground of co-sharership.

11. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee-appellant, submitted that the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division wrongly considered that pre-emptor respondent No.1 was a co-sharer in the suit land without considering the final report of the Advocate Commissioner who according to the preliminary decree distributed the saham of the parties in the ejmali property by separating the boundary of the saham and by putting the parties in their saham land and thereafter the Advocate Commissioner Mr Gazi Abdul Hakim filed the report along with the case map, field book, saham list on 3-10-78 which are, in fact, separation of the ejmali property between the parties terminating the co-sharership in the land.

12. It appears to us that passing of final decree in a partition suit implies that all the directions in respect of distributing and separating the Saham of the parties contained in the preliminary decree was complied with and nothing remains to be executed after the passing of the final decree. The final decree only affirms the completion of the direction of the court contained in the preliminary decree. Therefore, it is wrong to imply that the final decree has to be executed for the separation of the saham land.

<u>13. Further, we find that after passing of the final decree in a partition suit it is effective between the admitted co-sharers and for the purpose of a pre-emption proceeding where the transfer is made by a co-sharer to a stranger, this question of execution of the final decree between the co-sharers is not relevant and necessary.</u>

14. A reference to section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure shows that a decree may be either preliminary or final. Explanation to section 2(2) provides that "a decree is preliminary when further proceedings have to be taken before the suit can be completely disposed of. It is final when such adjudication completely disposes of the suit". In a suit for partition, after filing of the report along with the case map, field book, saham list by the Advocate Commissioner final decree takes effect and thereafter remains nothing to be done. In a pre-emption proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the question of co-sharership in the tenancy is relevant, but in section 24(1) of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act the co-sharership in the land is material. In that view of the matter, the passing of the final decree in a partition suit finally determines the rights of the co-sharers in the land. Hence, the application for the pre-emptor-respondents on the basis of co-sharership is not maintainable.

Accordingly, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque J: This appeal by leave is at the instance of the plaintiff against judgment dated 3-8-1998 passed by the Admiralty Court in Admiralty Suit No.48 of 1996 dismissing the suit.

2. Plaintiff filed the aforesaid suit for recovery of damages and compensation of US $ 22,631.80 equivalent to Taka 9,50,535.60 at the conversion rate of Taka 42.00 per US dollar from the principal defendant-respondent Nos. 1 to 5. The case of the appellant was that he is a businessman carrying on the business of ship repairer and ship chandler, watchman, chipping and painting, engine store and bunker supplier under the name and style of SOVHAN MARINE SYNDICATE. Defendant No.1 is a merchant vessel named MV Forum Power. Defendant No.4 as agent of the said vessel wanted supply of (i) Vertical centrifugal Main cool SW pump complete with Motor, VDK 440E (ii) fire/GS pump complete with Motor, type VSK 951 (iii) Bearing Unit complete, blower side, VTR 200 (iv) Bearing Unit complete turbine side, VTR 200 and (v) Lubricating disc for VTR 200 for the defendant No.1 who was lying in distress at the port of Mongla and for want of those machines and parts was unable to discharge her cargo. Defendant No.4 by fax message dated 1-10-1996 asked for quotation for supply of those items to defendant No.1 from the plaintiff and the plaintiff by telex message dated 3-10-1996 gave their best price including installation cost and on 22-10-1996 informed the specification by another telex message. Plaintiff by fax message gave his terms of supplying the items minimum 30 days credit and advance 50%. By fax message dated 23-10-1996 defendant No.4 confirmed to supply the vessel at Mongla port the aforesaid items at the rate, terms and conditions of the plaintiff. Defendant No.4 gave supply orders to the plaintiff as agent of defendant No.1 to be delivered and installed on board of defendant No.1, cost for installation, transportation and labour shall be borne by the defendant Nos.1 and 4 and by fax message dated 24-10-1996 the plaintiff also informed defendant No.4 actual cost for such works. Thereafter plaintiff supplied those items to defendant No.1 on 29-10-1996 and defendant Nos.2 and 3 acknowledged receipt of the same in writing by issuing a certificate. Those defendants issued another certificate stating that those items have been installed by the plaintiff on board of' defendant No.1. Plaintiff duly submitted his bill for US $ 14,851.00 for those items. Defendant No.2 in the meantime sent a list of spare parts to the plaintiff for supplying to defendant No.1 numbering 17 by telex dated 27-10-1996. Plaintiff informed defendant No.4 quoting rate for the same by fax message dated 9-11-1996. Defendant No.4 requested plaintiff to supply those 17 items of spare parts at the rate given by the plaintiff and accordingly the plaintiff supplied those items to defendant Nos.2 and 3 who acknowledged receipt of the same issuing a certificate on 18-11-1996. Plaintiff sent his bill to defendant No.4 for those items amounting to US $ 4,289.67. Defendant No.2 requested the plaintiff for supply of food (provisions) and laundry service and accordingly, plaintiff supplied provisions and provided laundry service to the officers/crews of defendant No.1. The bill for provisions amounted US $ 2,138.52 and bill for laundry service amounted to US $ 536.61. Defendant No.1 along with the steward of defendant No.2 acknowledged receipt of those provisions and laundry service by issuing certificate. Plaintiffs sent those bills to the defendant No.4. On the request of defendant Nos.2 and 3 the plaintiff also supplied stationery amounting to US $ 134.00. Plaintiff demanded payment of the bills for the aforesaid goods supplied by him from the defendants who in spite of promises did not pay the same. After coming to learn that the vessel may leave Bangladesh at any time plaintiff issued a notice on 2-12-1996 demanding immediate payment of the dues with 20% interest but defendants paid no heed to the demand of the plaintiff. So the plaintiff was compelled to file the suit for realisation of the amount mentioned hereinbefore.

3. Defendant No.6, the local agent of defendant No.1 against whom no claim was made in the suit, contested the suit by filing a written statement stating, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable in the present form and that the plaintiff has no cause of action and that the plaintiff filed the suit with the malafide intention and vexatious pleas to harass the defendant; the suit is also bad for misjoinder and non-joinder of parties. Further case of the defendant is total denial of alleged supply made by the plaintiff of any spare parts or provisions and laundry service and that the plaintiff is not entitled to any amount. Further case of defendant No.6 is that they never forwarded any requisition for the items allegedly supplied on board the vessel by the plaintiff and the plaintiff is required to obtain agreement on shipping export bill from the customs authority against supply of those requisitioned items. Their further case is that no supply was made in presence of customs officer on board the ship and no shipping export bill was used/ sealed and signed by the master of the vessel and customs officer. So the plaintiff is not entitled to any decree in the suit.

4. After considering the evidence adduced by the parties learned Admiralty Judge dismissed the suit by the impugned judgment dated 3-8-1998 on the view 'that plaintiff has not in fact supplied the spare parts, provisions and provided laundry service in accordance with law and I very much doubt that if the plaintiff himself fabricated and/or manufactured those spare parts in his workshop and supplied the same to the defendant No.1 vessel. Therefore I find that the plaintiff has failed to discharge its onus of proving that he had supplied spare parts, provisions and provided laundry service to the defendant No.1 vessel. In fact, the plaintiff has failed to prove his case by adducing sufficient and reliable proper evidence. Accordingly, I am of the opinion that the plaintiff is not entitled to a decree as prayed.

5. Aggrieved by the impugned judgment plaintiff sought leave to appeal and leave was granted to consider the following submissions:

"That the petitioner having proved to have supplied the spare parts and provisions and rendered laundry service to the vessel. defendant No.1 which has not been denied by the principal defendants and the present suit being an action in rem as well as in person defendant Nos. 1 to 5 are liable to satisfy the claim of the plaintiff and a bank guarantee having been furnished to deposit the amount of the claim made by the plaintiff in the event of a decree being passed against the ship and/or other defendants, the learned Judge of the High Court Division acted illegally in dismissing the suit against defendant Nos. 1 to 5 although they did not contest the suit."

"That the High Court Division having itself clearly found that the plaintiff had supplied 17 items of spare parts, beside (i) Main Cool SW Pump complete with motor type; VDK 440E. (ii) Fire and GS pump complete with motor type; 95J (iii) Bearing Unit complete blower side VTR 2000. (iv) Bearing Unit complete turbine side VTR 2000 and (v) Lubricating Disc for VTR 200 has fallen into an error of law in not decreeing the suit upon an erroneous view that the plaintiff could not make the supplies to the foreign ship without obtaining any permission from the Custom Authority. He maintains that the learned Judge misread and misinterpreted the various provisions of the Customs Act in taking such a view."

"That there being no legal bar for the plaintiff to release his claim for supply of spare parts, provisions and laundry services from the defendants in the admiralty jurisdiction the High Court Division was wrong in dismissing the suit."

"That the High Court Division having itself noted the oral evidence of DW 1 that "DW 1 has stated that the money that was deposited with the bank was furnished by the owner of the vessel" and there being no evidence that defendant Nos. 1 to 5 had ever denied the claim of the plaintiff, defendant No.6 was not competent to deny the claim of the plaintiff on any ground whatsoever and therefore, the plaintiff was entitled to the decree prayed for in the suit."

6. Plaintiff prayed for decree against the defendant Nos. 1-5 and not against the local agent defendant No.6. In spite of the same defendant No.6 contested the suit by filing a written statement mainly on the grounds that no requisition for supply of the machineries, spare parts, provisions and laundry service was made by the defendant No.6 as local agent of defendant No. 1 and no clearance was obtained from the customs authorities for supply of the said goods and services to the defendant Nos.1-5.

7. In addition to the evidence of PW 1 plaintiff relied on the documents marked Exts. 1-18 in support of his case. It appears that Exts. 1 to 1(d) are the fax and telex correspondence between the plaintiff and the defendant No.4, foreign agent of the defendant No.1 vessel for supply of some machineries and parts and terms and conditions including price were settled through the said correspondence. Exhibits 2 and 2(a) are the fax messages by the plaintiff to the defendant No.2 informing about supply of those machineries and parts to defendant No.1. Exhibits 3 and 3(a) are the certificates issued by the Master and Chief Engineer of the vessel defendant No.1 acknowledging receipt of the said machineries and parts. Exhibit 4 is the fax message communicating the bill of US $ 14,851.00 towards the price of aforesaid machineries and parts, installation cost and labour cost. Exhibit 5 is a fax message communicating price quotations by the plaintiff for supply of some spare parts requisitioned by the defendant No. 2, Master of the vessel. Exhibit 6 is the fax message by which defendant No.4 gave confirmation for supply of the said spare parts at that rate. Exhibit 7 is the certificate granted by the defendant No. 2, Master of the vessel acknowledging receipt of the spare parts supplied by the plaintiff. Exhibit.8 is the bill for US $ 4,289.67 submitted by the plaintiff to defendant No. 4 for the aforesaid spare parts. Exhibit 9 is a fax message by which defendant No. 2 requested the plaintiff to supply provisions to the vessel and laundry service and another fax message by defendant No.4 confirming the said requisition by the defendant No. 2. Exhibit 10 series are the certificates issued by the defendant No. 2 acknowledging receipt of the provisions supplied by the plaintiff. Exhibit 11 series are the bills submitted by the plaintiff for US $ 2,138.52 for the supply of provisions to the defendant No. 1. Ext. 12 is the certificate issued by the defendant No.2 acknowledging receipt of the laundry service provided by the plaintiff. Exhibit 13 is the bill for US $ 536.61 submitted by the plaintiff for the laundry service provided to the defendant No.1. PW1 in his deposition stated that on the request of the Master they supplied some stationery to the vessel for which bill for US $ 134. Exhibit 14 was submitted by the plaintiff. But Exhibit 14 is not the bill for the said amount. However assertion of the PW 1 about the said amount has not been specifically denied by the DW1. Exhibits 14 to 17 are the subsequent communications between the parties about the aforesaid transactions. Exhibit 18 is the bill for US $ 682.00 spent for telex, fax and telephone for the "correspondence and communication. On consideration of the pleadings, oral evidence of the parties and aforesaid documents it appears that plaintiff supplied machineries, spare parts, provisions, stationeries and laundry services worth US $ 21,949/80 and also spent US $ 682.00 for sending fax, telex, telephone to the defendants. Thus plaintiff spent- US $ 22,631.80 as claimed in the plaint and the same at the rate of Taka 42/00 per US $ was equivalent to Taka 9,50,535,60 at the time of institution of the suit. At present per. US $ is equivalent of Taka 51.25. So US $ 22,631.80 is equivalent to Taka 11,59,882.25.

8. Let us consider whether the plaintiff- appellant is entitled to recover the aforesaid amount from the defendant-respondent Nos. 1 to 5. Defendant-respondent Nos.1 to 5 did not contest the claim of the plaintiff-appellant by filing any written statement denying the claim of the plaintiff-appellant. There is nothing on record to show that defendant Nos. 1 to 5 instructed defendant No. 6 to contest the suit denying the claim on their behalf. On the other hand, it appears that defendant Nos. 1 to 5 furnished the claimed amount to defendant No. 6 to deposit the same in the bank to give a bank guarantee to satisfy the claim of the appellant in the event of a decree in the suit.

9. It is true that defendant No. 6 local agent of the vessel, defendant No. 1 did not give any requisition to the plaintiff-appellant for supply of the goods and services but it appears from the evidence on record that defendant No.4 the foreign agent of the ship defendant No.1 as well as defendant Nos.2 and 3 Master and Chief Officer of the vessel gave orders to the plaintiff-appellant for supply of the aforesaid goods and services. There is no legal bar on the part of defendant Nos. 2 to 4 to give orders for the supply of goods and services for the use of the vessel, its officers and crews. So absence of any order from defendant No. 6 for supply of the aforesaid goods and services to the ship cannot be said to be illegal. It has already been noticed that all the supplies of the goods and services have been acknowledged by the Master, Chief Engineer and other Officers of the ship. Defendant Nos. 1 to 5 having not denied the claim of the plaintiff and the officers of the ship having acknowledged the receipt of the aforesaid goods and services, we find no reason on the part of the defendant No. 6 to deny the claim of the plaintiff appellant for recovery of the value of the said goods and services from defendant Nos. 1 to 5.

10. Learned Judge of the High Court Division held that supply of spare parts, provisions and laundry services should be provided to the vessel through the customs authority and the plaintiff did not supply the same with the approval of the customs authority. In coming to the above conclusion learned Judge relied on the provisions of sections 50, 64, 66 and 67 of the Customs Act, 1969.

11. Section 50 of the said Act is as follows:

Order for entry outwards or loading of goods to be obtained before export goods are loaded-(1) No goods other than passengers baggage and mail bags shall be loaded on a conveyance until-

(a) in the case of vessel, a written application for entry of such vessel outwards, subscribed by the master of such vessel has been made to the appropriate officer and an order has been given thereon for such entry; and

(b) in the case of any other conveyance a written application for authority to load the goods subscribed by the person-in-charge of the conveyance has been made to the appropriate officer and an order has been given thereon authorising the loading.

(2) Every application made under this section shall specify the particulars as prescribed by the Board.

12. The aforesaid provision speaks of obtaining order before entry of a vessel outwards or loading of the goods in the vessel other than passengers, baggage and mail bags. This provision has no manner of application to supply of machineries, spare parts, provisions and necessaries to a vessel in distress.

13.	Section 64 is as follows:

Goods not to be loaded or unloaded or waterborne except in presence of officer- Save where general permission is given under section 67 or with permission in writing of the appropriate officer, no goods other than passengers, baggage or ballast urgently required to be loaded for the vessels safety, shall be shipped or water-borne to be shipped or discharged from any vessel, in any customs-port, nor any goods except passenger, baggage shall be loaded in or unloaded from any conveyance other than a vessel at-any customs- station or customs-airport except in the presence of an officer of customs.

14.	Section 66 is as follows:

Goods not to be loaded or unloaded except at approved places-Save where general permission is given under section 67 or with permission in writing of the appropriate officer, no imported goods shall be unloaded or goods for export loaded at any place other than a place duly approved under clause (b) of section 10 for the unloading or loading of such goods.

15.	Section 67 is as follows:

Power to exempt from sections 64 and 66-Notwithstanding anything contained in section 64 or section 66, the Board may, by notification in the Official Gazette, give general permission for goods to be loaded at any customs-station from any place not duly appointed for loading and without the presence or authority of an officer of customs.

<u>16. The above provisions relate to loading and unloading of export goods in a vessel and exception therefrom. Those provisions have no manner of application in case of supply of spare parts, machineries, provision and necessaries to a vessel in distress. Defendant No.1 was in distress condition at Mongla port and required the supply of machineries and spare parts for proper maintenance of the said vessel. It also required provisions and laundry services for the use of its officers and crews. There is no legal bar to our knowledge in the Customs Act to the supply of such goods and services to the ship in distress and anchored at any port in Bangladesh. Commissioner of Customs has been impleaded in the suit as defendant No.9 but he did not enter appearance nor raised any objection to the supply of machineries, spare parts, provisions and laundry service to the vessel by the plaintiff. His silence shows that the supply of above goods and services to a ship in distress was not objectionable. So the learned Judge of the High Court Division was not justified to refuse a decree to the plaintiff-appellant on the ground that the goods and services were not supplied with the approval of the customs officer on board the vessel.</u>

17. It has already been noticed that the defendant Nos. 1-5 did not contest the suit. On the other hand they sent money to the defendant No.6 to enable him to furnish a bank guarantee for release of the vessel from attachment. DW1 admitted in his deposition: "It is a fact that the money we have deposited with the bank guarantee in this suit was given to us by the owner. I do not know whether there is paper in my office from the defendant Nos. 1 and 4 ever denied or disputed the claim of the plaintiff." From the above admission it is clear that the defendant Nos. 1-5 did not dispute the claim of the plaintiff rather sent the claimed amount to furnish bank guarantee for the release of the vessel. So there is no scope for the defendant No.6 to be adversely effected in the least by the decree passed in the suit.

18. Learned Judge of the High Court Division found fault with the plaintiff for his failure to adduce evidence to show he either purchased the machineries and spare parts from the market or fabricated the same in his factory. When defendant Nos.1-5 acknowledged the receipt of the same there was no necessity of adducing evidence to show from whom those were purchased or from where those were fabricated. That was not an issue in the suit. Learned Admiralty Judge misdirectioned himself to enter into such an enquiry unnecessarily. When the supply of the machineries and spare parts are admitted by the principal defendants against whom decree has been sought there was no necessity of enquiring about the origin of the same. We are of the view that failure of the plaintiff to adduce evidence as to from whom those were purchased or from where those were fabricated cannot deprive the plaintiff from recovering the price of the same from the defendant Nos.1-5.

19. In the facts and circumstances and discussion made above we find merit in this appeal.

In the result the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. Impugned judgment is set aside and the suit is decreed in full for realisation of Taka 11,59,882.25 with cost against the defendant- respondent Nos. 1-5 as prayed for.

End.
