full_judgment:
MM Ruhul Amin J : This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and decree dated 18- 4-2000 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 92 of 1971 allowing the appeal.

2. Short facts are that, one Abdus Salam Chowdhury, the predecessor-in-interest of the respondents, instituted Title Suit No. 80 of 1966 in the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Rangpur for establishment of title and recovery of khas possession in the suit property stating, inter alia, that he had some properties in the district of Jalpaiguri in India and also some shares in the Nipuchapur Tea Estate, Jalpaiguri. One Satyabati Devi and her co-sharers had properties in the Rangpur town as described in schedule A to the plaint. Satyabati Devi and her co-sharers were desirous of leaving this country for good and negotiated with the original plaintiff to exchange the property described in schedule A to the plaint with the plaintiff's properties situated at Jalpaiguri in India along with 30 shares of Nipuchapur Tea Estate described in schedule-B to the plaint. Thereafter, a deed of agreement was drawn up and signed by the parties in September, 1960 and in terms of the deed of agreement a deed of exchange was executed on behalf of Sudhir Kamal Sen and his co-sharers through their constituted attorney Abu Siddique Mazumder (defendant No.7) on 30-12-1960. The further case of the plaintiff was that Abu Siddique Mazumder was friendly with the plaintiff from before and since the plaintiff could not come to Rangpur from India at the relevant time for the purpose and since he had none to look after his properties the plaintiff appointed Abu Siddique Mazumder (defendant No.7) as his attorney by a power of attorney dated 21-1-1961 to manage and look after his property at Rangpur. It was also the case of the original plaintiff that at the time of exchange the property in suit was under requisition of the Government and occupied by the Manager, Employment Exchange, Rangpur, Thana Agriculture Officer, Rangpur and one Ashraf Hussain. Thereafter, on 2-9-1961 the property was de- requisitioned and he got vacant possession with respect to a portion described in schedule-C to the plaint and allowed the remaining portion of schedule-A property to be in possession of the said Agricultural Officer as a tenant under him and in this way the plaintiff became absolute owner of schedule-A property by exchange. The plaintiff asserted that he allowed his attorney Salamatullah who is defendant No. 6 to occupy and reside in a portion of the property described in schedule-C on behalf of the plaintiff as his licensee on condition that he would vacate the premises when demanded by the plaintiff. The plaintiff thereafter permanently left India and came to live in the then East Pakistan on 25-3-1961 and on his demand said Salamatullah promised to leave the disputed property soon. In April, 1962 Salamatullah was transferred to Karachi but he left for Karachi without handing over possession to the plaintiff. The plaintiff further asserted that defendant Nos. 1-5 illegally entered into the premises as described in schedule-C without any knowledge of the plaintiff. The original plaintiff mutated his name with the Municipality and has been paying rent to the Government after duly registering his name in the Govt. records and he revoked the power of attorney earlier granted in favour of defendant No. 6 as he found that his interest at the hands of his attorney was not safe. Thereafter, the original defendant No. 1 claimed the property in suit asserting the original plaintiff as his benamder and hence the suit.

3. Defendant Nos. 1-5 and 7 contested the suit by filing written statement and their case, in a nut shell, is that defendant No. 1 is the father of defendant Nos. 2-4 and defendant No.1 used to live at Jalpaiguri in India and was connected with several Tea Estates and in 1951 he became the Secretary of Rahimia Lands and Tea Company (Private) Ltd which was a concern of Nawab Mosharraf Hossain's family and the original plaintiff went to Jalpaiguri from Noakhali immediately after partition of India and when he was in difficulty he sought help from original defendant No.1 and was appointed a Munshi in the Longarkhana of the Nawab family where the defendant No. 1 used to reside and he earned confidence of defendant No.1. The further case of the original defendant No. 1 is that sometime after partition of the Sub-Continent, the defendant No.1 sent his son, who is defendant No.2, in January, 1951 to Rangpur and when he himself was living at Jalpaiguri at that time. He was subsequently transferred to Calcutta office of the Rahimia Land and Tea Company (Private) Ltd and at that time he came in contact with the owners of the suit property and they agreed to exchange the same with the property of the defendant No. 1 in India and for expediency defendant No. 1 made the plaintiff his benamder as he was a man of defendant's confidence and the exchange deed was finalised accordingly and prayer was made for de-requisition of the property in the name of the plaintiff who is the benamder of defendant No.1. The further case was that there was no negotiation with Satish Kamal Sen for the exchange of the property with the plaintiff who is only a benamder of defendant No.1 in relation to the disputed property. The further case is that defendant No. 1 is the real and beneficial owner of the suit property and the same was never possessed by defendant No. 6 on behalf of the plaintiff as a licensee.

4. The trial Court on consideration of the materials both oral and documentary dismissed the plaintiff's suit. On appeal being First Appeal No. 92 of 1971 the High Court Division after hearing the parties allowed the appeal. Being aggrieved the heirs of defendant No. 1 preferred the civil petition for leave to appeal before this Division.

5. Leave was granted to consider the submissions that the impugned judgment of the High Court Division is not a proper judgment of reversal inasmuch as it does not conform to the long established principle that in reversing the judgment of the trial Court the appellate Court must fully apply its judicial mind to each and every finding of the trial Court and the decision based and the reasons given therefor and those findings and reasoning are required to be set aside with cogent reasons but these well established principles of dispensation of even handed justice have been glaringly violated in the impugned judgment of the High Court Division to the great prejudice of the appellants resulting in miscarriage of justice and further submission that the High Court Division committed illegality in deciding the case in a causal and indifferent manner as the impugned judgment ex facie bears ample testimony of non-application of judicial mind by the High Court Division to the most relevant issues in the case and the findings arrived at by the trial Court and the further submission that while interfering with the judgment of the trial Court the High Court Division failed to notice that the trial Court's judgment was based on totality of the factual findings on the relevant issues of facts that normally crop up as pertinent questions in a case of benami transaction and not a single issue in isolation and also the submission that the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), was not aware of the legal position as to on whom lay the onus of proof in a case of benami transaction though with little care could have found that the trial Court was quite conscious with regard to the onus of proof in benami transaction, and the further submission that the High Court Division failed to appreciate the long established principle, criteria and factors pertaining to benami transaction such as motive for the benami, how and by whom the consideration was paid, the conduct of parties both during and after the transaction, custody of the title deeds possession of the property, negotiated deal and various other matters connected with the transaction and held that original defendant No. 1 successfully discharged the onus that lay on him and established that he was the real and beneficial owner of the property in suit and that the original plaintiff was his benamder with respect thereto and the further submission that the High Court Division ought to have discussed the elaborate evidence relating to the topic of custody of the basic documents but has not applied its Judicial mind in this regard, and the further submission that the High Court Division it appears tried to say that in a benami transaction only possession of the title deed is the main criteria which is not at all correct and the submission that the High Court Division in this case though is a final Court of fact discarded the judgment of the trial Court and its finding in a very superficial and summary fashion in one sentence stating that the defendant failed to discharge his onus regarding exchange and such hasty and abrupt procedure can hardly be countenanced by the Appellate Division which would upset the whole jurisprudence as to the judicial duties and obligations of the appellate Court and negation of justice, and the further submission that the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) had the advantage of observing the demean our of the witnesses and, as a matter of fact, assessed the credibility and reliability of DW 3 Mahtabuddin Khan, Advocate who drafted the exchange deed at Rangpur and relying on his testimony along with other reliable evidences held that the basic document of title was with defendant No. 1 when the same was shown to DW 3 a few days before September, 1965 lndo-Pak War and the said document was handed over to the plaintiff while a boundary dispute arose. But the High Court Division failed to appreciate this aspect of the matter and also the evidence of DW 3 which has caused miscarriage of justice.

6. We have heard Mr TH Khan, the learned Counsel for the appellants and Mr Md Fazlul Karim, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-respondent Nos. 1-7 and perused Judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers.

7. The case of the plaintiff was that he was the real owner of the disputed property and purchased the same with own money and for his own benefit, whereas the case of the defendant No.1 was that the plaintiff was his benamder and the defendant No. 1 purchased the suit property with his own money and for his own benefit. The vital point for consideration in this case is whether the plaintiff was the real owner or he was the benamder of defendant No.1, in respect of the disputed 'A' schedule property situated in the centre of Rangpur town. The deed of agreement Exhibit 3 dated 1-9-1960 was executed by admitted owners of disputed property Satyabati Devi, Sudhir Kamal Sen and other co-sharers in Calcutta in favour of the plaintiff Abdus Salam Chowdhury as well as the deed of exchange Exhibit 1 executed by defendant No. 7 Abu Siddique at Rangpur on 31-12-1960 on the basis of the power of attorney, Exhibit 2 dated 5-9-1960 executed by Satyabati Devi and her co-sharers in Calcutta regarding the suit property were by the original plaintiff from his custody.

8. It was the case of the plaintiff that he purchased 10 decimals of land in Jalpaiguri town, india from defendant No. 1 by kabala dated 4-4-1960 Exhibit A (3) and also acquired 39 shares of Nipuchapur Tea Estate of Jalpaiguri and effected exchange with Kusum Kamini in lieu of 3-1/3 decimals of land and 9 shares of Nipuchapur Tea Estate and thereby obtained the property named Kusumalaya at Rangpur and the remaining shares and lands were given to Satyabati and her co-sharers by way of exchange and obtained' the disputed property. The case of the defendant No.1, on the other hand, was that he made an ostensible transfer of his 10 decimals of land out of 15 decimals of land in Jalpaiguri town and 30 shares of Nipuchapur Tea Estate in favour of the plaintiff at Jalpaiguri without any consideration only to facilitate the exchange of the disputed property with Satyabati Devi and her co-sharers and the other house, Kusumalaya with Kusum Kamini at Rangpur. By the aforesaid two exchanges defendant No. 1 became the real owner of the disputed property and house therein and the plaintiff became beneficial owner of the house Kusumalaya.

<u>9. The trial Court observed that in the circumstances of the case the onus, rather heavy onus, lies on the defendant No. 1 to establish his assertion that the plaintiff was his benamder in respect of the disputed property. The trial Court further held that in all cases of benami transaction it is necessary to consider the motive for benami, how and by whom the consideration was paid, the conduct of the parties both during and after of the transaction, custody of the title deeds, possession of the property and various other matters connected with the transaction.</u>

<u>10. The High Court Division at the very outset of the judgment observed that the learned trial Court was not aware of the legal position as to on whom lay the onus of proof in a case of benami transaction like the present one. We must observe that the trial Court was quite aware of the ingredients of benami transaction and the onus to prove the same and other matters connected with benami transaction as it appears from trial Court's judgment. It is unfortunate that the High Court Division without considering the judgment of the trial Court made a sweeping remark that the trial Court was not aware of the legal position regarding onus of proof in a case of benami transaction. The trial Court, it appears, made sincere endeavor in deciding the question of benami transaction and took into consideration the relationship of the parties from long before the transaction, the documents produced by the defendant No.1, namely, the passport of his wife Exhibit Y(9), the certified copy of income tax assessment order Exhibit EE and other connected papers to arrive at a conclusion that the defendant No. 1 was at the relevant time the Secretary of Rahimia Land and Tea Company (Private) Ltd, Jalpaiguri and he paid income tax on his salary of Taka 10,282 and on dividend of Taka 214 respectively during the period from 1-4-1960 to 31- 3-1961. It further appears that the plaintiff admitted in his examination-in-chief that defendant No. 1 purchased considerable properties in the name of his eldest son defendant No.2 by the kabalas, Exhibit A series at Rangpur. The total value of the properties thus purchased by defendant No. 1 through his son defendant No.2 at Rangpur in 1959-60 comes to Taka 19,199. The trial Court also considered the life insurance policy of defendant No. 1 for Taka 15,000 and the declaration made by him at the end of 1959 before the Martial Law Authority regarding an amount of Taka 30,000-35,000 lying with Muslim Commercial Bank and Lloyd's Bank, Dhaka. All these matters the trial Court considered to arrive at the conclusion that the defendant No. 1 had sufficient means to acquire property at Jalpaiguri and also the disputed property. In this connection the trial Court had also taken into consideration the evidence of DW 9 (defendant No.2), son of defendant No.1, who corroborated his father in all material particulars on the above matters.</u>

11. The trial Court found that the defendant No. 1 Nurul Huq attended the 43rd Annual General Meeting of the Indian Tea Planters Association held on 12th April, 1958 as Secretary of Rahimia Land and Tea Company (Private) Ltd. Exhibit Z. The trial Court also found Exhibit EE, the assessment order to be a genuine document and in this connection considered SRO 128(R) 65 and Postal Circular Exhibit 28. From all these the trial Court concluded that the defendant No. 1 was a man of sufficient means and, as such, at the relevant time he was not required to transfer 10 decimals of land in Jalpaiguri town and 30 shares of Nipuchapur Tea Estate in India in favour of the plaintiff for his sustenance as claimed by the plaintiff. The definite case of the defendant No.1 was that 10 decimals of land and 30 shares in Nipuchapur Tea Estate belonging to him was transferred to the plaintiff without any consideration only to facilitate the exchange of the disputed property and Kusumalaya in the name of the plaintiff.

12. The trial Court next considered the circumstances leading to the exchange deed regarding the disputed house.

13. In this connection it is to be mentioned here that Satyabati Debi and Sudhir Kamal Sen and their co-sharers were residents of Calcutta. The trial Court found that the plaintiff could not show that he was at the relevant time residing in Calcutta or visited Calcutta with passport and visa. It is not disputed that the defendant No.1 left India for good on 1-8-1965 with Indian passport. The case of defendant No. 1 was that from Jalpaiguri he was transferred as Secretary of Rahiinia Land and Tea Company (private) Ltd to their Calcutta office at 6 Rowdown Street, Calcutta and at Calcutta he negotiated the transaction with Satish Kamal Sen and others. The defendant No. 1 also filed papers Exhibit Y (9) to 1s how that he also lived at 155 Park Street, Calcutta in connection with his service.

14. It is undisputed that DW 8 Ashraf Hossain at the relevant time was an occupant in a portion of the disputed house at Rangpur town. He stated that he had talk with DW 1 at Rangpur in 1959 about the exchange of the disputed property and he gave first information to the defendant No. 1 at 6, Rowdown Street, Calcutta by a letter. This DW 8 is a competent and disinterested witness. The further case of the defendant was that though the disputed property was shown to have been exchanged in lieu of 10 decimals of land in Jalpaiguri and 30 share of Nipuchapur Tea Estate but, in fact, he got back 10 decimal of land at Jalpaiguri and 30 share of Nipuchapur Tea Estate from Satish Kamal Sen and others afterwards on payment of cash money to Satyabati Devi, Satish Kamal Sen and other co- sharers and the owner of Kusumalaya. The defendant No. 1 filed Exhibit EE and AA to show that later on he sold the shares in Nipuchapur Tea Estate to Babulal Agarwala and 10 decimals of land to Arun Kumar Nandi. It is in the evidence of defendant No. 1 that he paid Taka 11,995 to Sudhir Kamal Sen and others and got back the share certificates of Nipuchapur Tea Estate and 10 decimals of land in Jalpaiguri town and transferred the same to others as stated above.

15. Defendant's case is that at the request of the plaintiff he exchanged Kusumalaya with his own money for the plaintiff out of love and affection and the disputed property with his own money for his own benefit in the benami of the plaintiff.

16. It is on record that in respect of Kusumalaya, Kusum Kamini executed the power of attorney in favour of elder brother's son of the defendant No. 1 and the case of the defendant No.1 is that his son defendant No.2 bore all expenses in respect of execution of document for Kusumalaya in favour of the plaintiff under his instruction. It is in the evidence of plaintiff that he received the original document in respect of Kusumalaya from his attorney, Lutfor Rahman, elder brother's son of defendant No.1.

17. The learned Advocate for the respondents argued that Exhibit CC and AA are forged documents and no reliance can be placed on these documents. Exhibit CC is the certified copy of mutation register book in respect of 48 shares of the Nipuchapur Tea Estate, Jalpaiguri. It is clear that one G. Momen of Jalpaiguri was owner of the shares in the Nipuchapur Tea Estate and in respect of some shares the name ofthe plaintiff was mutated i.e. in respect of 10 + 38 = 48 shares and subsequently those were transferred to Babu Lal Agarwala of Jalpaiguri. This exactly supports the case of the defendant No. 1 and not the plaintiff as it is the consistent case of the defendant No. 1 that as owners of both the disputed property and Kusumlaya were not willing to sell the property for cash money he had to make exchange deed but later on he paid cash money to them and got back 10 decimals of land and the share certificates and sold the same to one Arun Kumar Nandi and Babu Lal Agarwala by Exhibit AA and cc.

18. Exhibit 2 is the power of attorney executed by Sudhir Kamal Sen and others in respect of the disputed property. In this power of attorney defendant No.6 Abu Siddique Majumder, brother-in-law of defendant No. 1 was appointed on 5-9- 1960 as a constituted attorney for doing the needful in the matter. It is undisputed that Abu Siddique Majumder is not related to the plaintiff nor a close man of the plaintiff. Exhibit 2(b) is another general power of attorney executed on 25-1-1961 by plaintiff Abdus Salam in favour of Abu Siddique Majumder, brother-in-law and Salamatullah, full brother of defendant No. 1 in respect of disputed property and other properties. It is to be noticed that normally the plaintiff is supposed to appoint his close relation as attorney by the power of attorney relating to the disputed property. But he appointed the close relations of the defendant No. 1 as attorneys. The learned Advocate for the appellants argued that this goes to show that, in fact, the close relations of defendant No. 1 were appointed as attorneys as the defendant No. 1 was the real owner and the plaintiff was benamder. The trial Court held that the plaintiff did not adcillce any evidence to corroborate him regarding tlie transaction but the defendant No.1, on the other hand, examined DW 9 (defendant No.2), the constituted attorneys DWs 2 & 5 of the plaintiff in respect of the disputed property and DW 3 Mahatabuddin Khan, a Senior Advocate of Rangpur Bar and Vice-Chairman of Rangpur Pourashava and DW 8 Ashraf Hossain who admittedly, occupied a portion of the disputed property at the relevant time and gave initial information to the defendant No. 1 regarding intention of the owners of the disputed property to sell the same. These witnesses corroborated him regarding the transaction and custody of the original documents.

19. We have also noticed that DWs 2 and 5, Salamatullah and Abu Siddique Majumder respectively constituted attorneys of the plaintiff in respect of the disputed property and DWs 3,6, 8, 9 in their evidence supported the 'Case of defendant No. 1 and, in our view, their evidences, especially the evidence of DW 3, were rightly taken into consideration by the trial Court regarding custody of the original documents by the defendant No. 1. The trial Court gave importance to the evidence of DW 3 Mahatabuddin Khan, a Senior Advocate practicing in the civil side at Rangpur Bar and Vice-Chairman of Rangpur Municipality since 1939. He joined the Bar on 7th August, 1925. He stated that he drafted the deed of exchange Exhibit 1 at the instance of DW 2 Salamatullah and DW 5 Abu Siddique, full brother and brother-in-law respectively of the defendant No. 1 regarding the house in suit. He further stated that power of attorney and agreement executed in Calcutta were placed before him in connection with .preparation of the draft and DW 2 Salamatullah told him that his brother (defendant No.1) was purchasing the house in suit in the name of the plaintiff. He further stated that long after that the deed of exchange was shown to him by defendant No.1, Nurul Haque and Abu Siddique. He further stated that defendant No. 1 pointed out some mistakes in the number of some shares as written in the deed of exchange and this meeting with defendant No.1. Nurul Haque, took place few days before September War of 1965. He saw the deed of exchange and other documents Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 with Nurul Haque, defendant No. 1, on that occasion. The defendant's case is that when boundary dispute arose with Dr T Rahman he handed over original title deeds to the plaintiff to file a case through Mr Taleb Ali, Advocate. We have also gone through the evidence of DWs 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8 and 9. We are of the view that the trial Court has rightly placed reliance on their evidence, and specially the evidence of DW 3, and, in our view, the plaintiff could not dislodge the evidence of DW 3 regarding the custody of the original documents by the defendant No. 1 till the boundary dispute with Dr T Rahman when those were handed over to the plaintiffs.

20. Both parties claim that they bore all expenses of the documents in connection with the deal. The evidence of the plaintiff is that total cost of the same was more than Taka 2,000 whereas the defendant No. 1 deposed that he spent Taka 282 towards the cost of the documents in Calcutta. The trial Court with reference to the documents found that cost of stamps used in the aforesaid 4 documents comes to Taka 116 and further found that some other incidental costs in connection with the 4 documents such as Advocate's fees, Notary Public's fees etc. were also incurred. The plaintiff could not account for as to how he spent an amount of Taka 2000 for the same as claimed by him. The defendant No. 1 had given a figure which corresponds with the expenditure. The plaintiff could not say how much he paid as registration costs and how much for income tax clearance certificate in respect of transfer of the disputed property whereas the defendant No. 1 gave a vivid account of the expenditure incurred in this connection.

21. Exhibit 2 (b) executed by the plaintiff in respect of the disputed property and Kusumalaya at Robertsonganj, Rangpur shows that the plaintiff authorised Salamatullah and Abu Siddique Majumder, two attorneys, to do everything including sale, etc. in respect of the suit property but they i.e. the attorneys, would have no power to sell! mortgage etc., in respect of Kusumalaya which the defendant stated was acquired for the plaintiff by the defendant No. 1 out of love and affection for him. But the plaintiff authorised the attorney to deal with the disputed property in whatever manner they liked without any reservation including sale but he was very particular regarding Kusumalaya in respect of which he was cautious enough not to delegate power of sale or mortgage to the attorney. The trial Court found that the disputed property is at least three times more valuable, if not more than that of Kusumalaya. From the differential treatment in respect of the two properties as discussed above the trial Court rightly found that this is a sufficient indication of the fact that the plaintiff was all along dealing with Kusumalaya as an owner and did not deal with the disputed property as an owner as he had no interest in the disputed property.

22. It is on record that the plaintiff got his name mutated in respect of Kusumalaya immediately after the transaction whereas he got his name mutated in respect of disputed property when trouble arose between him and the defendant No.1, that is, on 27-5-1966. From this the trial Court concluded that the plaintiff was vigilant regarding Kusumalaya from the beginning but he was indifferent regarding the disputed property and this indicates that he was not the owner of the disputed property rather the defendant No.1 was the real owner and the plaintiff was his benamder.

23. The defendant No.1, Nurul Haque as DW 1 in his evidence stated that at the time of agreement Exhibit 3 dated 1-9-1967, Satyabati and others handed over some papers including three dakhilas to him and he filed those dakhilas on 10-5-1967 i.e. few days after the filing of the written statement before the trial Court, and those three dakhilas were marked Exhibit P, P(1) and P(2). The three dakhilas relating to payment of rent for the year 1363 BS to the Government Acquired Estate are in respect of the disputed property. The plaintiff did not give any satisfactory explanation as to how these dakhilas went to the custody of the defendant No.1. The normal presumption is that those were handed over to the defendant No. 1 by the original owners at the time of negotiation of the transaction.

24. It is not disputed that the application for de-requisition of the disputed property was filed by DW 2 Salamatullah, brother of defendant No.1 who himself signed the name of the plaintiff in the application for de-requisition and got the property de-requisitioned.

25. It is undisputed that the disputed property was under requisition when it was purchased. It is also undisputed that Salamatullah, brother of defendant No.1, who was at that time serving as Superintendent of Customs and Excise at Rangpur, was residing in a portion of the disputed property and when he left for Karachi on transfer in March, 1966 the power of attorney in his favour was revoked. It is also admitted that even after his transfer from Rangpur to Karachi his family occupied a portion of the disputed property. It is on record that the defendant No.2 Aminul Haque (DW 9), son of defendant No. 1, also lived in a portion of the disputed property. The trial Court disbelieved the plaintiffs contention that as the activities of Saiamatullah was suspicious he revoked the power of attorney and believed the contention of Mr Salamatullah that as he was transferred to Karachi from Rangpur at his request, the power of attorney in his favour was revoked. The trial Court held that Salamatullah and defendant No.2 Aminul Haque, son of defendant No.1, initially entered upon a portion of the disputed property, in their own right and not as licensee of anyone.

26. It is an admitted case of both parties that an amount of Taka 10,000 was in deposit as compensation of the disputed property for the period of requisition and the plaintiff withdrew the entire amount from the requisition department sometime after his arrival at Rangpur from Jalpaiguri. The trial Court on consideration of the materials on record arrived at the conclusion that the withdrawal of this amount from the office of Deputy Commissioner by the plaintiff does not prove anything conclusively or that he is the real owner of the property. The trial Court also held that since the title deeds stood in the name of the plaintiff, it was rather natural that he would withdraw the amount. In our view, the above findings of the trial Court are based on the materials on record.

27. The plaintiff's case is that he got delivery of the deed of exchange (Exhibit 1) from scribe Bazlur Rahman after his arrival at Rangpur. The case of the defendant, on the other hand, is that the receipt of the document was with Abu Siddique (DW 5) who executed the same as constituted attorney of the plaintiff and he endorsed the same to the scribe and got back the original document from the scribe and kept the same in his custody and later on handed over to defendant No. 1. It is undisputed that at the time of execution and registration of the document plaintiff was not at Rangpur and he came to Rangpur afterwards. The trial Court accordingly, concluded that the plaintiff was not known to scribe, Bazlur Rahman from before and, as such, unless the plaintiff was introduced to the scribe by DW 6 Abu Siddique the scribe was not supposed to hand over the original document to a stranger and this fact belies plaintiff's story that he got delivery of the original deed of exchange from the scribe. The defendant's case that Abu Siddique, who as attorney executed the deed, got delivery of the same and kept in his possession and later on handed over to the defendant No.1 appears to be probable.

28. It is on record that the plaintiff filed a criminal case on 10-5-1966 against defendant No. 1 and others. The trial Court found that only after getting possession of the original title deeds the plaintiff filed the criminal case and the present suit against the defendant No. 1 and others.

29. Therefore, from our above discussion, it is clear that the trial Court meticulously considered the evidences both oral and documentary, the facts and circumstances of the case and all other relevant aspects and then came to the conclusion that the defendant No. 1 having sufficient means acquired the disputed property with his own money and for his own benefit in the benami of the plaintiff, his trusted man and the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the original deeds and only in May, 1966 when trouble arose with neighbor Dr T Rahman regarding boundary, the defendant No. 1 handed over the title deeds to the plaintiff to file an application before the Deputy Commissioner through Mr Taleb Ali, Advocate and getting possession of the original title deed the plaintiff got his name mutated on 27-5-1966 in respect of disputed property.

30. The observation of the High Court Division that for non-examination of Mr Taleb Ali the presumption under section 114(g) of Evidence Act is against the defendant No. 1 is not at all sustainable because Mr Taleb Ali was not ill possession of the documents rather defendant's case is that documents were handed over to the plaintiff for filing an application regarding boundary dispute with Dr T Rahman through Mr Taleb Ali, Advocate.

31. It is to be mentioned here that the High Court Division without adverting to the reasoning given by the trial Court for believing or disbelieving evidence of plaintiffs witness and defendant's witness reversed the findings of the trial Court and did not at all discuss the evidence adduced by the parties. We have already pointed out that the High Court Division was in error in observing in omnibus manner that the trial Court was not aware of the legal position as to on whom lay the onus of proof in case of benami transaction. We have also indicated earlier that the trial Court thoroughly discussed all aspects of benami transaction and arrived at its findings. The sweeping remark by the High Court Division regarding judgment of the trial Court is really unfortunate.

32. Regarding taking the disputed property in the benami of the plaintiff, the defendant No. 1 offered an explanation stating that transfer could not be made in his name as he was then an Indian national and his brother-in-law Abu Siddique was served with a notice by the Indian Government to quit India and his father-in-law, Md Aminur Rahman Haq, who was then a Manager of another Tea Estate, advised him not to take the document in the name of Abu Siddique in that situation and accordingly, the document was taken in the name of plaintiff who was his trusted man. The explanation appears to be reasonable.

33. In the facts and circumstances of the case and in view of the discussion above, we are of the opinion that the High Court Division as the final Court of fact without considering the evidence and the materials on record and without adverting to the reasoning given by the trial Court reversed the findings of the trial. Therefore, the impugned Judgment of the High Court Division is not at all a proper Judgment of reversal. Accordingly, the same is liable to be interfered with.

The appeal is thus allowed with cost.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the defendants is against the judgment and decree of affirmance in a suit for partition.

2. The plaintiff-opposite-party instituted the suit for partition on the averments that the original owner Haider Ali had 6 sons, 4 daughters and a wife and on his death and on the death of his wife each son inherited 1/anna, 9 pai and each daughter inherited 10 gondas, 4½ pai share in the suit property. In the suit being Other Suit No. 132 of 1942 of the Court of Munsif, North Rouzan, Chittagong the aforesaid share of the heirs of Haider Ali in the disputed land was declared. Accordingly, the plaintiffs who are heirs of Haider Ali got 16-2/3 গন্ডাশেয়ার and the principal defendants (the petitioners before me) are daughters of Bacha Mia, son of Osi Mia, son of Haider Ali, that is to say, grandson of Haider Ali. According to the plaintiffs, the aforesaid daughters of Bacha Mia had 3-1/3 gonda share in the suit property. The principal defendants under the influence of their respective husbands held out threat for disturbing peaceful possession of the plaintiffs therein. Accordingly, they instituted the suit for partition there being no partition earlier made regarding the property in suit. As the defendants refused to partition amicably, hence the suit

3. The suit was resisted by the present petitioners (defendant Nos. 1 2 and defendant Nos. 13-22) by filing separate written statements. The case of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is that the plaintiffs had no cause of action for the present suit. It suffers from defect of parties and all the properties of Haider Ali were not brought into hotchpot of the partition suit. Their specific case, however, was that they inherited 2⁄3 rd share of Bacha Mia, 1⁄8 the share of Saira Khatun, widow of Bacha Mia. They made out a case that Saira Khatun orally gifted her share to the petitioners and the petitioners are in possession and enjoyment of the aforesaid lands. It was the further case of the petitioners that the plaintiffs did not bring into the hotchpot the land of Osi Mia and Bacha Mia of the partition suit. They further made out a case that Waiz Khatun gifted her share in the disputed land to the petitioners orally and the petitioners are in possession and enjoyment of the aforesaid lands. It was the further case of the petitioners that the plaintiffs did not bring into the hotchpot the land of Osi Mia and Bacha Mia of the partition suit. They further made out a case that Waiz Khatun gifted her share in the disputed land to the petitioners orally and in support of the said gift a memorandum was executed by her on 1.11.1966. The petitioners accordingly were also in possession thereof. They further stated that the plaintiffs' statement that they are owners-in-possession of 162⁄3 gonda share of the land is not correct.

4. Mr. Mostafa Kamal Pasha, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submitted that DW 1 having had proved that defendants got 2/3rd. share from Bacha Mia and 1/8 the share from Saira Khatun and the land of Waiz Khatun, the learned Courts below misread the evidence of DW 1 in dismissing the claim of the defendants. He further argued that the Courts below also misread and misinterpreted Exhibit-1 and 1(a), the judgment and decree of Other Suit No. 132 of 1942, and upon such misreading and misinterpretation, the Court below committed serious error of law in the decision in decreeing the suit occasioning failure of justice. He contended further that the Courts below failed to consider the affect of the result of Other Suit No. 12 of 1970 and Other Appeal No. 291 of 1970 arisen therefrom. He submitted that the Court of appeal committed error in accepting the statement of PW 1 who is the plaintiff No. 1, inasmuch as he is vitally interested in the result of the suit and not accepting the statement of DW 1 who is a disinterested and neutral witness. He further submitted that the petitioners having been in peaceful possession of 2⁄3rd share of Bacha Mia, 1⁄8 the share from Saira Khatun and the land gifted by Waiz Khatun beyond the statutory period of limitation, the Courts below committed serious error of law in decreeing the suit occasioning failure of justice. He further contended that both the Courts below failed to consider the RS Khatians which stood in the names of the plaintiffs and the defendants and, as such, non-consideration of these material documents led to occasioning failure of justice.

5. Mr. Anwarul Azim Khair, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1, on the other hand, submitted that the Courts below on proper assessment of evidence on record held that the defendants failed to prove their claim with regard to the land gifted to them both by Saira Khatun and Waiz Khatun. He also argued that it is not correct, as contended by the learned Advocate for the petitioners, that the Courts below failed to consider the judgment of Other Suit No. 12 of 1970 and the judgment on appeal therefrom. He further repelled the contention of the petitioners that Exhibits Kha series, the RS Khatians, have been held by the Courts below rightly that those do not relate to the land of Haider Ali, rather it is owned independently by the recorded owner thereof. Therefore, according to Mr. Anwarul Azim Khair the contention of the petitioners that the Courts below erred in not dismissing the partition suit on the ground that all the properties of Haider Ali were no brought into the hotchpot of the partition suit does not stand.

6. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners has taken me through the judgments of both the Courts below. On perusal of the same I find that admittedly Haider Ali was the original recorded owner of the land in suit. It is also admitted that Haider Ali had 6 sons, 4 daughters and one wife. It appears that the trial Court found on the basis of the judgment and decree made in Other Suit No. 132 of 1942, Exhibits- 1 and 1(ka), that the land described in the schedule of the plaint of the present suit is covered by the land of the Other Suit No. 132 of 1942. It further found in that suit the plaintiffs' title and possession and the title and possession of Haider Ali therein was confirmed and declared. The learned Judge who delivered the judgment in Other Suit No. 132 of 1942 also held that RS Khatian was not correctly prepared. Against the Judgment of that suit it is seen from the record that no appeal was taken. The Court of appeal below has also in affirming the judgment of the trial Court referred to the aforesaid judgment of Other Suit No. 132 of 1942 and observed that on the death of Haider Ali the shares of his heirs were decided in the said suit. Thus, it is difficult to uphold the contention of Mr. Mostafa Kamal Pasha that the Courts below did not consider Exhibits-1 and 1 (ka). So far as the contention of improper and illegal institution of the present suit on the plea that it does not include all the properties left by Haider Ali and, as such, the suit fails for not including all the properties of Haider Ali in the hotchpot has got no substance either in law or on practice. This contention is found on the basis of Exhibits 'Kha' series. On reference to the judgment, of the trial Court it appears that Exhibits 'Kha' series were considered by the Court who observed that the land in suit claimed by the plaintiffs belonged to Haider Ali is not found from the aforesaid exhibits. It observed:

“প্রতিবন্ধি বিবাদী পক্ষে মোকাদ্দমাটি হচপট দোষে বারিত প্রমানের উদ্দেশ্যে জংগল গোমরা মৌজায় এবং পাহাড়তলী মৌজায় বেশ কয়েকটি আর, এস, খতিয়ান প্রদর্শনী খ সিরিজ) দাখিল করে, কিন্তু বাদী পক্ষে নালীশি বূমি হায়দার আলীর দাবী করা হয় এবং হায়দার আলী ওয়ারিশ বা ক্রমিক ওয়ারিশ হিসাবে দাবী করে। কাজেই হায়দার আলী ত্যক্ত কোন সম্পত্তি অত্র মোকদ্দমায় হচপটে আসা হয় নাই। উহা বিবাদী পক্ষ প্রমান করিতে ব্যর্থ হইয়াছে। প্রমতাবস্থায় প্রতিদ্বন্ধি বিবাদীর কথিত মতে অত্র মোকদ্দমাটি পক্ষাভাবে দোষে বারিত গন্য করিবার কোন যুক্তি সংগত কারন দেখি না। কাজেই মোকদ্দমাটি হচ্পট দোষে বারিত গন্য করা যায় না।"

7. On this finding the Court of appeal below equally referred to those Exhibits and observed that:

“প্রতিযোগী বিবাদীগন মোকদ্দমাটি হচ্পট দোষে বারিত প্রমানের জন্য জংগলকুমকড়া মৌজা এবং পাহাড়তলী মৌজার কয়েকটি খতিয়ান দাখিল করিয়াছে। বাদীগণ নালিশী ভূমি হায়দার আলীর ওয়ারিশ বা ক্রমিক ওয়ারিশ বলে দাবী করেছে। বিবাদীগণ হায়দার আলীর কোন সম্পত্তী অত্র মামলার হচ্পটে আনায়ন করা হয় নাই। তাহা প্রমান করিতে সক্ষম হয় নাই।”

8. Thus, on facts the contention of the petitioners that all the ejmali properties were not brought into the hotchpot of the partition suit fails.

9. The decision cited by Mr. Mostafa Kamal Pasha in the case of Mainuddin Biswas & others 5 vs. Sohrab Ali Mir & others, 5 DLR 544 in support of his contention also does not help him. It is true, as held therein, that the general rule which governs a suit for partition is that it should include the entire joint property of the co-sharers. But that rule is not inflexible and merely for such principle a suit for partition cannot be held to be not maintainable. It is settled principle of law that precedent is to be applied or followed to the facts of a given case. The facts of Mainuddin Biswas's case seem to me different from the facts of the present case and accordingly, it is a distinct one.

<u>10. The next decision in the case of Md. Shahidul Alam Khan vs. Md. Gulzar Alam 36 DLR 290 cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioners does not help him rather it helps the opposite party. In this decision the case, of 5 DLR 544 was considered but the Court on somewhat similar fact to the present case held that in a, case where all the joint properties were not brought into hotchpot of the partition suit, such omission will not defeat the partition suit. It held that a rule of equity as opposed to a rule of law shall be applied on the convenience of the parties concerned and may be relaxed from time to time for ends of justice in the interest of the parties concerned without causing prejudice to anyone. The aforesaid expression more so effectively applies in a case like the present one.</u>

11. So far as the contention as built on the judgment of Other Suit No. 12 of 1970 and the judgment on appeal therefrom it seems that the trial Court has duly considered Exhibits-Ga, Ga (1) and Ga (2) respectively. On consideration of those exhibits it found that the suit was a suit for permanent injunction against the opposite parties. The suit for permanent injunction relates to protection of possession in the suit property and hardly deals with title. In the present suit which is a suit for partition determination of title of the respective parties and their shares in the suit land are necessary. The trial Court in this regard took the view that because of the judgment in the aforesaid Other Suit No. 12 of 1970 which was affirmed on anneal, the partition suit does not fail. In a suit for permanent injunction and in a suit for partition the reliefs sought for are quite different and distinct from each other and the result of the suit in the permanent injunction shall not operate as res judicata in a suit for partition wherein the question of title of the respective parties and their shares are to be ascertained and declared. It is true that the Court of appeal below, which is a last Court of fact, is to assess evidence independently to come to its own finding. But where the last Court of fact agrees with the finding of the trial Court on fact a detailed examination of the evidence on a particular point is not necessary. If the appellate Court agrees with the finding of the trial Court with reason that is sufficient. Here on reference to the judgment of the Court of appeal below I find that absence of such detailed examination of documents is no ground for setting aside the finding on this point reached in favour of the petitioners, it appears from the judgment of the Courts below that the defendant-petitioners failed to prove that gift by evidence on record. It has considered' the memorandum dated 1.11.66, Exhibit-ka, an unregistered document. On perusal of the same the trial Court found that the defendants failed to prove the genuineness of the document by adducing independent witness and accordingly, it held that by and under such memorandum no gift made by Waiz Khatun could be proved nor it could prove the oral gift earlier made. So far as the gift made by Suira Khatun is concerned, the trial Court also found that before making the gift Saira Khatun transferred the property covered by the alleged gift in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by a registered kabala on 10.11.1943. Having had considered these two documents the trial Court held that at the time of making gift by Saira Khatun had no transferable interest in the gifted property as claimed by the defendant petitioners. Thus, in view of the aforesaid discussions on various evidence led by the parties to the suit, the Court of appeal below and the trial Court ultimately found that the partition suit is maintainable and accordingly decreed.

12. In view of my aforesaid discussions, I do not find any reason to interfere with the judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below which is a judgment of affirmance in this revision.

Accordingly, I discharge the Rule with a cost of Taka 1,000.00 (Taka one thousand only).

End.

full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Choudhury J: This petition for leave to appeal is against judgment and order dated 18th November 1999 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2757 of 1999 making the Rule absolute rejecting the plaint of Title suit No. 42 of 1999 of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka who earlier rejected the defendants' prayer for rejection of the plaint under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil procedure.

2. The short fact leading to this petition is that the petitioners as plaintiffs earlier instituted Title Suit No. 177 of 1994 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for declaration of their title and partition of the suit properties. That suit on contest was dismissed by the trial Court which decree was affirmed up to the Appellate Division where a review petition was also filed which too was rejected. The petitioners then instituted Title Suit No. 42 of 1999 in the 5th Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka praying for declaration that the decree passed in earlier Title Suit No. 177 of 1994 is illegal and invalid and is not applicable in respect of 'Ga' schedule land of the present suit. Their further prayer is that the land described in 'Kha' schedule measuring about 94 decimals was purchased by defendant No. 1 from defendant Nos. 2 to 6 and these defendants filed an application under Order 7 rule 11 read with Order 14 rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint or in the alternative for hearing on law point first which prayer was rejected by the learned Subordinate Judge by Order dated 27-7-1999. The present petitioners 40 in number previously filed Title Suit No. 92 of 1991 which was subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 177 of 1994 wherein they prayed for declaration of title in respect of 'Ka' and 'Ka' schedule land and for partition. In that suit defendant Nos. 2 to 7 of the present suit were also defendants. With regard to schedule 'Ka' land of the earlier suit there was no dispute but dispute is only in respect of 'Kha' schedule land of the previous suit for self-same plaintiffs filed the present suit. In the 'Kha' schedule land of the plaint of the earlier suit under plot No. 371 of CS Khatian No. 4300 (Jha) area was shown as 94 Satangsha and the plaintiffs claimed that out of 94 Satangsha defendants purchased only 0090 Ajutangsha by several documents in the year 1954-55 and since the defendants purchased a small portion of land by several documents, the plaintiffs prayed for declaration of title as well as partition in the earlier suit. In the previous suit the plaintiffs claimed that the defendants purchased 0090 Ajutangsha land but the claim of the defendants was that they purchased 94 Ajutangsha. In the earlier suit defendants claimed entire CS plot No. 371 and they mutated their names and they are in possession all through. And in that suit the trial Court as well as the appellate Court on consideration of the materials on record found that the defendants purchased the entire land measuring 90 Satangsha. The plaintiff in that suit tried to prove that CS plot contained 94 decimals of land on production of CS Khatian which the trial Court as well as the High Court Division found to be forged and fabricated and ultimately the suit filed by plaintiffs was dismissed by the trial Court which was upheld upto the Appellate Division. It is now the case of the plaintiffs in the present suit that after dismissal of the earlier suit upto the Appellate Division the defendants of that suit who are defendant Nos. 2 to 6 in the present suit sold land measuring .90 Satangsha of CS Plot No. 371 to defendant No. 1 by registered Kabala which is the cause of action of the present suit. The plaintiffs filed the present suit with the following prayer:

(ক) ..... বিনীত প্রার্থনা এই যে, ২৯-৩-৯৫ তারিখের ডিক্রী সম্পূর্ণ বে-আইনী, অকার্য্যকর ও বাদীগণের  গ’ তপছিলে বর্নিত সম্পত্তির ক্ষেত্রে প্রযোজ্য নহে মর্মে এক ঘোষণা মূলক ডিক্রী দিতে,

(খ) ‘ঘ’ তপছিলে বর্নিত দলিল মূলে  খ’ তপছিলে বর্নিত ৯০ অযুতাংশ সম্পত্তি ছাড়া ‘গ’ তপছিলে বর্নিত সম্পত্তিতে ২-৬ নং বিবাদীগণের নিকট হইতে খরিদ মূলে ১নং বিবাদীর কোন প্রকার সত্ত্ব সার্থ উপজাত হয় নাই মর্মে এক ঘোষণা মূ��ক ডিক্রী দিতে,

(গ) বাদীগণ ‘গ’ তপছিলে বর্নিত সম্পত্তির মালিক মর্মে ঘোষণা করতঃ ১নং বিবাদীকে ‘গ’ তপছিলে বর্নিত সম্পত্তির দখল ৩০ দিনের মধ্যে বাদীগনের বরাবরে বুঝাইয়া দেওয়ার নির্দেশ দিতে। ব্যর্থতায় বাদীগণ আদালত যোগে ‘গ’ তপছিলে সম্পত্তির দখল নিতে পারিবে মর্মে এক ডিক্রী দিতে,

(ঘ) মোকদ্দমার যাবতীয় খরচ বাদীপক্ষের অনুকূলে ও বিবাদীগণের প্রতিকূলে ডিক্রী দিতে,

(ঙ) আইন ও ন্যায় সঙ্গত ভাবে বাদীগণ আরো যে ভাবে যে যে প্রতিকার পাইতে পারে সেই মর্মেও ডিক্রী দিতে মহোদয়ের মর্জি হয়।

3. It appears that the plaintiffs of the present suit prayed for a declaration that the judgment and decree dated 23-3-1995 passed in the earlier suit is illegal and not binding upon the plaintiffs and not related to 'Ga' schedule land of the plaint and that for a declaration that defendant No. 1 has not acquired any right, title and interest over 90 decimals of 'Kha' schedule land and further declaration that the plaintiffs are the owners of 'Ga' schedule land and that defendant No. 1 be directed to hand over vacant possession to the plaintiffs within 30 days from the date of the decree.

4. Before the trial Court the present defendants entered appearance and filed an application under Order 7 rule 11 read with Order 14 rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint of Title Suit No. 42 of 1999. The learned subordinate Judge then by his judgment dated 27-7-1999 rejected the defendants prayer for rejection of the plaint against which the defendants moved the High Court Division in Revision No. 2757 of 1999 and a Division Bench by judgment dated 18th November, 1999 made the Rule absolute, set aside the judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and rejected the plaint of the present suit under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The plaintiff-petitioners then filed this petition for leave to appeal.

5. Dr Kamal Hossain, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the respondents in the earlier suit obtained a decree practicing fraud upon the court by placing that area of the disputed land was 0090 acre (90 Ajutangsha) and not 9400 acre (94 Satangsha) as had all along been asserted by the present petitioners. He submits that the defendants not only practiced fraud upon the trial Court but also upon both the Divisions of the Supreme Court and got decree in their favour deliberately suppressing the material fact and this suppression of fact came to light when after the disposal of the matter before the Appellate Division they transferred the suit land to defendant No. 1 of the present suit mentioning 90 decimals in the kabala and not 0090 acre ie 90 Ajutangsha, and when the plaintiffs came to know of this transaction they instituted the present suit on the ground that fraud was practiced upon the court in the earlier suit and the defendants are not entitled to enjoy the fruit of the fraud they have practiced. He submits that the High Court Division failed to appreciate that while disposing of the petition filed under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure only the plaint may be looked into and not any other material ,not even the petition filed under the said provision but the High Court Division disregarding this settled proposition entered into the merit of the suit itself as to the maintainability of the same. Dr Kamal Hossain strenuously argued and argued with full force at his command that when palpable fraud has been committed in the earlier suit the civil Court can interfere even though the earlier suit went upto the Appellate Division and ended in favour of the defendants. In support of his claim Dr. Kamal Hossain placed before us the plaint of the present suit as well as the schedule of the kabala by which defendant No. 1 purchased the suit land from defendant Nos. 2 to 6. He submits that a plain reading of this schedule would indicate that the defendants earlier practiced fraud upon the court in the previous suit arid obtained a favourable decree.

6. Dr Kamal Hossain further submits that the plea of res judicata ought to have been agitated and decided at the time of trial on taking evidence which is not connected with the question of rejection of plaint under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

7. In this matter the submission made by Dr Kamal Hossain has also been supported by Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed and Mr Mahmudul Islam. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed added that in this case when the fraud has been practiced upon the court, the present suit may be proceeded with and the allegation of fraud may be decided at the time of trial on evidence. The plaintiffs have succeeded in making out a case of fraud in the suit itself. Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Advocate added that when the fraud has been alleged the limitation will be of three years from the detection of fraud. In the present case the plaint disclosed a cause of action and it will be not proper to reject the plaint without taking evidence in support of the plaintiffs' contention.

8. Mr Nurul Huq, learned Counsel appearing for respondents, on the other hand, submits that over the self-same suit land appertaining to CS plot No. 371 the self-same plaintiffs earlier instituted Title Suit No. 177 of 1994 praying for declaration of their title and also for other reliefs including partition. It is submitted that in the earlier suit respondents disclosed that their predecessor purchased the entire CS plot No. 371. There is no suppression of fact and this fact has been clearly asserted in the written statement of the earlier suit which was known to the present plaintiffs from before and the land covered by CS plot No. 371 has been recorded in the name of these respondents. He further submits that the earlier suit was not filed by the present respondents but was filed by the present plaintiffs and it is well settled that the plaintiffs are to prove their own case adducing evidence, they can not bank upon the defects, if any, in the defence version of the case, In the previous suit the plaintiff failed to prove their title and possession over CS plot No. 371 and this finding was affirmed upto the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court when the plaintiffs' title over CS plot No. 371 has not been declared even upto the Appellate Division in their own previous suit they can not now re-open the matter in the present suit. The plaintiffs adduced all their evidence in the earlier suit to prove that only about 2 decimals of land have been purchased by the present respondents from CS plot No. 371. As against this, defence version is that they purchased 90 decimals of land ie the entire CS plot No. 371. In that suit all the courts found that the entire plot No. 371 was purchased by the predecessor of defendant Nos. 2 to 6. The fact now alleged in the present suit was known to the plaintiffs from long before. These defendants in their sale deed to defendant No. 1 has clarified certain facts on wrong recording which can not be construed as practicing fraud upon the court. In the earlier suit they have clarified the matter and in their sale deed no new fact has been introduced. Mr Nurul Huq submits that the present litigation is nothing but an act of gambling in the form of a suit. He further submits that when on the very face of the plaint it appears that the same is barred under law this should be nipped in the bud. He further submits that since their purchase these respondents are in possession of the entire CS plot No. 371 which has been admitted by the respondents in their present suit when they prayed for recovery of Khas possession. The property was purchased by the predecessor of the defendants in 1954-55 and in such a situation it will be evident that the suit is barred by limitation. He further submits that the matter in issue in the two suits are substantially the same. He also contended that there is no suppression of fact from the side of the defendants in the earlier suit. Repelling the submission made by Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Mr Nurul Huq submits that in view of admitted pleadings of the parties in the earlier suit the allegation of fraud can not stand. There was no fraudulent conduct of the respondents in the earlier suit. They placed all their cards before that court and it was decided-accordingly.

9. It is well settled now that a plaint may be rejected under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure merely on a plain reading of the plaint but in exceptional circumstances the court may invoke its inherent jurisdiction and can throw the plaint out in limit. It is also well settled that the plea of implied bar should be decided on evidence unless the fact disclosed in the plaint clearly indicate that the suit is not maintainable. In exceptional cases recourse may be taken even under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It is also well settled that in an application for rejection of plaint on the ground of undisclosed cause of action the court should not dissect the plaintiff's case part by part.

10. Admittedly these 40 plaintiffs earlier instituted Title Suit No. 177 of 1994 in the third court of subordinate Judge, Dhaka for declaration of their title in the suit property specifically described in schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' attached to the plaint wherein CS plot No. 371 was incorporated in schedule 'Kha' measuring 94 decimals equivalent to 9400 Ajutangsha and also prayed for partition and recovery of possession. It has been alleged by the plaintiffs that the predecessor of defendant Nos. 1 to 8 purchased only about 1 decimal of land out of CS plot No. 371 which was necessary for them to have their path-way for ingress and egress to their other purchased land. In that suit defendant Nos. 1 to 8 entered appearance and filed their written statement. In paragraph 25 the defence disclosed their case claiming that their predecessor purchased 'Ka' and 'Kha' schedule land in 1954 and they got delivery of posssession. In that suit both sides adduced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective cases. The suit was dismissed on contest which was affirmed upto the Appellate Division. Thereafter contesting defendants sold CS plot No. 371 to defendant No. 1 of the present suit. On seeing this transfer the petitioners as plaintiffs instituted the present suit alleging that though the predecessor of the defendants purchased 0090 Ajutangsha they sold 94 decimals of land to defendant No. 1 which indicate that by practicing fraud upon the court in the earlier suit the defendants got that suit dismissed. In the present suit plaintiffs prayed for a declaration that the decree passed in the earlier suit in respect of 'Ga' schedule land is illegal, void and not related to 'Ga' schedule land of the plaintiffs and they also prayed for a declaration that excepting the land mentioned in 'Kha' schedule land defendant No. 1 had not acquired any title over the remaining 'Ga' scheduls land and they also prayed for declaration of their title over 'Ga' schedule land and recovery of khas possession of this land.

11. We have gone through the plaints of both these suits and it appears that in both the suits plaintiffs prayed for declaration of their title over CS plot No. 371 minus of course 0090 Ajutangsha of land. The plaintiffs in their earlier suit prayed for declaration of their title which was rejected upto the Appellate Division. Now in the present suit also the plaintiffs prayed for the same relief only alleging that in the earlier suit fraud was practiced in getting the same dismissed. But it appears from the perusal of the available materials that in the earlier suit also the defendants claimed purchase of the entire CS plot No. 371. There was no ambiguity in the defence version of the case. Their case is that during SA operation the land was not properly recorded and for that matter they had to give an explanation in the kabala of defendant No. 1 about wrong recording which can not be a fraud practiced upon the court in the earlier suit. From the perusal of the plaint as well as the written statement of the earlier suit it appears that everything was placed in that suit and it was decided upto the Appellate Division against the plaintiffs. It is well settled that in such a suit the plaintiffs must prove their case by adducing their evidence, they can not bank upon any defect in the defence version of the case. In the earlier suit defendants placed their case and also produced their documents claiming entire CS plot No. 371 which was accepted by the courts.

<u>12. It is well settled that a plaint may be rejected on a plain reading of the same. In the plaint of the present suit it has been alleged that by suppression of certain facts as regards area of the lands which tantamount to practicing fraud upon the court, the defendants got the earlier suit dismissed. The plaintiffs have relied upon certain recitals in the kabala of defendant No. 1 and they have incorporated the same in the plaint itself and they have further stated in paragraph 8 that predecessor of the defendants purchased 0090 Ajutangsha of land from CS plot No. 371 for having a path-way leading to plot No. 115. Their specific case is that CS plot No. 371 is measuring 94 decimals and in that suit the defendants asserted that they only purchased 0090 Ajutangsha from CS plot No. 371 but from the perusal of the defence case it appears that their claim is over the entire plot No. 371 which was purchased by the predecessor of the defendants. The claim of the plaintiffs over that land was rejected even upto the Appellate Division and when that is the position the plaintiffs can not maintain the present suit. It is well settled that where a plaint can not be rejected under Order 7 rule 11 Code of Civil Procedure the court may invoke its inherent jurisdiction and reject the plaint taking recourse to section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Here in the present case from the available materials particulary the plaint itself it appears that they failed to get their title declared over this land in their earlier suit wherein the defence also claimed the entire CS plot No.371 which was accepted and affirmed upto the Appellate Division. The plaintiffs therefore can not now be allowed to proceed with the present suit simply because that in the kabala of defendant No. 1 certain explanations have been given for inclusion of certain lands. It appears that no fraud has been practiced upon court by the defendants in the earlier suit. The onus of proving their title and possession rest with the plaintiffs which they failed to discharge in their suit even upto the Appellate Division. When this is the position the present suit cannot be allowed to be proceeded further. As the ultimate result of the suit is as clear as day light such a suit should be properly buried at its inception so that no further time is consumed in a fruitless litigation when the ultimate result is clear, the plaintiffs can not be allowed to re-open the same matter afresh after losing upto the Appellate Division. This is merely a gambling in litigation which can not be allowed. The High Court Division thoroughly considered every aspect, of the matter and rightly found that the present suit is barred by law. The learned Advocates who appeared on behalf of the petitioners failed to point out any legal infirmity in the judgment of the High Court Division which may call for our interference. The judgment of the High Court Division is based on proper and correct appreciation of both law and fact. There is therefore no merit in this petition.</u>

The petition is accordingly dismissed.

End.
