full_judgment: Mahmudul Amin Choudhury J: This Rule was issued calling upon the Opposite Party Nos. 1, 2, 4-12 and 14 to show cause why the Judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge, Nawabganj in Title Appeal No. 107 of 1989 affirming the Judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Nawabganj in Other Class Suit No. 169 of 1989 shall not be set aside. 2. The plaintiff-petitioner's case, in short, is that he instituted OC Suit No. 169 of 1985 against the opposite parties praying for establishment of title and confirmation of possession contending, inter alia that the suit land was auction purchased by Haji Yunus Mollah with the ejmali fund of brothers and sisters. Thereafter the suit land along with other lands were partitioned amongst the co-sharers in terms of the Solenama filed in Title Suit No. 157 of 1957 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi and in accordance with the terms of the solenama the plaintiff got the suit land. It is also the case of the plaintiff that during RS Operation the suit land was recorded in the names of Haji Yunus Molla and the Government of Bangladesh which has clouded his own title and for removal of that cloud the plaintiff had to file the aforesaid suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession. But during the proceeding of the Suit the plaintiff had to amend the plaint when the Advocate Commissioner found 2.35 acres of land out of the possession of the plaintiff. The plaintiff then by way of amendment prayed for recovery of khas possession of this land from defendant No. 14. 3. Before the trial Court defendant Nos. 1, 2-12 and 14 contested the suit by filing separate written statements and their case is that the suit land was auction purchased by Haji Yunus Mollah by his own money and for his own interest. Their further case is that Haji Yunus Mollah was a very rich man and he acquired some properties in the benami of others and he adopted a device for keeping the suit property in benami by a solenama filed in Title Suit No. 157 of 1957. Their further case is, that this Haji Yunus Mollah transferred 2.35 acres of land out of the suit property by gift dated 27.2.1983 to defendant No. 14 who is possessing the same by constructing Fulkuri School Mahila Madrassa, Mosque, etc. thereon. It is also the case of the contesting defendants that the decree in the said partition suit has not been acted upon and the possession of the suit land was not delivered to the plaintiff who is merely a benamder of aforesaid Haji Yunus Mollah. 4. Before the trial Court both the parties adduced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective cases. The learned Subordinate Judge then by his judgment dated 27.8.1989 dismissed the suit on contest against the defendant Nos. 1-12 and 14 and ex parte against the rest holding that the plaintiff is the benamder of Haji Yunus Mollah in the suit property and that the-decree in the partition suit has not been acted upon which is still not complete in the eye of law and the suit filed in the present form is not maintainable. 5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the Judgment and decree the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 107 of 1989 before the learned District Judge, Nawabganj who though found the suit maintainable but dismissed the appeal on merit and affirmed the Judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge holding that the plaintiff-appellant failed to prove his right, title and possession in the suit property. He also found that Haji Yunus Mollah auction purchased the suit property by his own money and that the plaintiff-appellant is the benamder of Haji Yunus Mollah in the sole decree in respect of the suit land. The appellant then moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 6. Mr. SS Halder, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioner, submits that both the Courts below failed to appreciate the evidence correctly and, as such, came to a wrong finding. He submits that the decree in the aforesaid partition suit, the record of right, rent receipts and the return submitted to the authority supported the plaintiffs case. He further contended that the Courts below failed to appreciate the oral evidence adduced from the side of the parties but they based their decision only on the evidence of PW 1. It is submitted by Mr. Halder that though the Courts below found that the plaintiff is the benamder of Haji Yunus Mollah, the basis of this finding is the sale decree but sole decree cannot be construed as a benami transaction and the partition suit was not filed by Haji Yunus Mollah but by Taimus and others in which Haji Yunus Mollah was one of the defendants and in the solenama it cannot be found that the plaintiff acted as a benamder of Haji Yunus Mollah. He argued that a partition decree cannot decide the benami and this cannot also decide who is the benamder and for whom. The learned Advocate contends that such benami transaction takes place only in case of transfer of certain land. The concept of benami cannot be made available in suit for partition and the Courts below decided the case on a wrong concept. He further argued that benami is to be proved on framing specific issue which has not been done in the present case. 7. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of opposite party 1, 2, 4-12 submits that both the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff was the benamder of Haji Yunus Mollah which is a finding of fact and as such this Court will be reluctant to interfere in the matter. He further submits that the plaintiff-petitioner has failed to point out any wrong in the procedure and law or any error committed by the Courts belows. This Court is not sitting as a Court of appeal and, as such, it cannot enter into the facts concurrently decided by the trial Court, unless there is a gross illegality in procedure or non-appreciation of evidence. He further submits that though the plaintiff relied mainly on the sole decree in the partition suit but that was not a decree at all, only a solenama was filed by the parties which was accepted by the concerned Court but no decree was drawn up. So the matter is still pending and there is no evidence that on the basis of solenama the plaintiff got possession of the suit property. That the plaintiff was not in possession of the suit property will be evident from the fact that during the lifetime and after this sale decree Haji Yunus Mollah made a gift of 2.35 acres of land in favour of defendant No. 14-and delivered possession to them. The definite case of the defendants is that the plaintiff was the benamder of Haji Yunus Mollah. The learned Advocate contends that when the plaintiff is the benamder the return was rightly submitted in his name who is the ostensible owner, the real owner was Haji Yunus Mollah. The learned Advocate argued that the suit for partition is a method or device adopted for keeping the land in the benami of the plaintiff and there is no legal bar in it. The learned Advocate contends that both the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff failed to prove his possession in the suit property and when there is such concurrent finding of fact this court may not interfere in the matter. 8. Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of opposite party No. 14, submits that they got delivery of possession of 2.35 acres of land of the suit property from Haji Yunus Mollah and they constructed a School, a Mahila Madrassa and a Mosque over the same and they are enjoying the usufructs and the pleader Commissioner found their possession in the same which has been admitted by the plaintiff when he amended his plaint and prayed for recovery of khas possession of this portion of the land. The learned Advocate contends that as defendant No. 14 is in possession of the suit property on the basis of a gift for over 12 years and during that period when the plaintiff has not laid his claim over the same the suit is barred by limitation. The learned Advocate contends that there is no proof that after the Judgment in the partition suit the plaintiff got possession over the suit property and thereafter he was dispossessed either by Haji Yunus Mollah or by opposite party No. 14 and he brought this suit within 12 years from the date of dispossession. It has been also contended that though according to the plaintiff the partition suit was disposed of on 26.10.57 and though the record of right was published in 1983 the plaintiff has not come within 12 years from either years which made the suit barred by limitation. 9. The petitioner filed the aforesaid OC Suit No. 169 of 1985 for declaration of title and confirmation of possession. Subsequently, he had to amend the plaint and sought recovery of khas possession from opposite Party No. 14 from 2.35 acres of land. His specific case is that the suit land was purchased by Haji Yunus Mollah with the ejmali fund of the brothers and sisters. Subsequently, Title Suit No. 157 of 1957 was filed for Partition and a solenama was filed and on the basis of the terms of the solenama the plaintiff got the suit land. As against this the defence case is that this plaintiff was merely a benamder of Haji Yunus Mollah who himself purchased the property with his own money but for keeping the property from being taken over by the Government he adopted a method by way of getting a suit filed for partition wherein a solenama was filed in which the land was shown to have been allotted to plaintiff though, as a matter of fact, the land continued to remain with Haji Yunus Mollah and as the plaintiff was the benamder, no step was taken by the parties in the suit for drawing up of a decree. 10. Admittedly, this is an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and we have to decide the matter within the four comers of the procedure and while disposing of this application we cannot act or suppose to act as an appellate forum. 11. It is the consistent view of our Appellate Division that concurrent finding of fact by the Courts below cannot be interfered with by this Court in a revisional application filed under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The consistent view of the Appellate Division is that the High Court Division is not competent to interfere with the finding of facts arrived at by the lower Appellate Court which is based on appreciation of evidence, however wrong the same may appear in the absence of error of law or procedure affecting the merit of the case. This is the view of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in the decisions reported in 28 DLR (AD) 57 [Ramjan Khan @ Ramjan Ali Khan vs. Obaidul Huq Chowdhury and others], 30 DLR (SC) 81 [Akbar Ali & others vs. Zahiruddin Kari and others] 38 DLR (AD) 201 [Abdul Mannaf Khan & others vs. Bangladesh and another], 1990 BLD (AD) 209 and in many other decisions. With the backdrop of this legal position of our jurisdiction, let us now examine whether the plaintiff has succeeded in making out a case for our interference. 12. The plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title over 4.8525 decimals of land and also confirmation of possession. Initially defendant No. 14 was not a party in the suit. This defendant No. 14 was impleaded by the trial Court's order dated 28.3.88 and thereafter a commission was taken for tocal investigation and the Commissioner found defendant No. 14 in possession of 2.35 acres out of the suit land for which the plaintiff had to amend the plaint and prayed for recovery of khas possession of this portition of the suit land. In such circumstances, the plaintiff is required to prove that since the disposal of the partition suit or since purchase by Haji Yunus Mollah the plaintiff continued to possess the suit land till the filing of the suit on 29.9.85. The plaintiff before the trial Court examined 3 witnesses and also produced the order passed in the partition suit, rent receipts, copy of the return and khatian to prove his possession in addition to the oral evidence. It appears that the plaintiff himself was not examined but his son appeared as PW 1 in support of the claim of the plaintiff. 13. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that though both the Courts below found that the plaintiff is the benamder of Haji Yunus Mollah but no such issue was framed. It is true that no specific issue on benarnder has been framed by the trial Court but in the judgment it appears that the trial Court found that the only point at issue is whether the plaintiff was the benamder of his brother Haji Yunus Mollah and the plaintiffs case is that this Yunus Mollah purchased the suit property from the common fund of the family. Whereas the specific defence case is that Haji Yunus Mollah was a rich businessman having sufficient fund and he purchased the property with his own money for his own interest and since before purchase he was living in separate mess from his other brothers. It appears from the Judgment of the trial Court that PW 1 admitted that Haji Yunus Mollah was a rich businessman and he was in a separate mess. This fact was also admitted by DW 1 who is another brother of Haji Yunus Mollah. From the Judgment of the trial Court it appears that DW 1 deposed that for keeping the property in benami Haji Yunus Mollah got the partition suit No. 157 of 1957 filed and he also got the solenama filed. The decree was mere a paper transaction which was not acted upon. The trial Court opined that had the decree or order been acted upon the possession of the suit property would have been definitely with the plaintiff. On consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case the trial Court found that the plaintiff was merely a benamder. The trial Court also found that the plaintiff was a benamder will also' be evident from the fact that this Yunus Mollah made a gift of 2.35 acres of the suit property to opposite party No. 14 after the filing of the solenama and the plaintiff filed the suit claiming possession over the entire suit property including this 2.35 acres where admittedly there is a School, a Madrassa and a Mosque from which the trial Court came to the finding that for all practical purposes the plaintiff was a benamder of Haji Yunus Mollah. This finding of fact has also been accepted by the appellate Court on appreciation of evidence. The trial Court it appears considered the oral and documentary evidence of the parties and came to the finding that the plaintiff was benamder of Haji Yunus Mollah. 14. Now the question arises whether by a partition suit can one be treated as benamder of the other. 15. Mr. SS Halder, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submitted that the concept of benamder is only available in case of land transferred but not in a suit for partition. As against this Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate submits that the whole benami transaction is a device to keep the property with the real owner though it stands in the name of an ostensible owner. This device may be by way of a sale-deed, a gift or any other transaction or even by a suit and here in this present case for keeping the property from being taken over by the Government Haji Yunus Mollah used this device in connivance with his brothers and sisters and got a sole decree within three months from the date of filing of the suit and thereafter no step was taken from either side for the drawing up a decree though in a partition suit both plaintiffs and defendants are treated as plaintiffs. 16. We have carefully gone through the record and it appears that the documents of purchase of the suit property and so also other papers are all coming from the side of the heirs of Haji Yunus Mollah. Excepting the copy of the order passed in the aforesaid partition suit, a Copy of the return, khatian, and two rent receipts nothing has been produced from the side of the plaintiff and the two rent-receipts are of the period after the institution of this suit. So this coupled with the gift with delivery of possession made in favour of opposite party No. 14 Haji Yunus Mollah clearly indicate that the partition suit is a device to keep the property with Haji Yunus Molla and the Courts below rightly found that the plaintiff was a benamder which is a concurrent finding of fact and in arriving at this decision the courts below have not committed any illegality or wrong. 17. Now as regards possession the plaintiff himself is not coming but he has sent his son PW 1 and it appears that two other witnesses have also been examined from the side of the plaintiff. The defendant also examined some witnesses and the trial Court as well as the appellate Court considered the evidence and came to the concurrent finding that Haji Yunus Mollah was al through in possession of the suit property and he actually made a gift in favour of opposite party No. 14 and handed over possession to them. Had the entire suit land not been in possession of Haji Yunus Mollah how he can transfer the property and handover possession to opposite Party No. 14 by way of a gift? From this circumstance the Courts below concurrently came to the finding that Haji Yunus Mollah was in possession of the suit property and after him his heirs are in possession of the entire suit property along with opposite party No. 14 who is possessing 2.35 acres out of the same. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner failed to point out any illegality in procedure as well as in the appreciation of the evidence committed by the Courts below. The consistent view of our Appellate Division is that the finding of facts arrived at by the lower appellate Court which is based on appreciation of evidence, however wrong the same may be, cannot be interfered with in revision in the absence of error of law or procedure affecting the merit of the case or that the Judgment of the Courts below are perverse in nature. No such case has been made out by the petitioner before this Court. We have carefully gone through the judgments of the Courts below and it is found that they, on proper and careful appreciation of the evidence on record both oral and documentary, came to the concurrent finding of fact that the plaintiff was a benamder of Haji Yunus Mollah and that he was al-through in possession of the suit property right from his purchase till his death and after him his heirs are in possession. 18. Relying on a decision reported in AIR 1961 (SC) 1655 [Javer Chand and others vs. Pukharaj Suranei, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner contends that once a document is taken into evidence this cannot be brushed aside even though it has not been stamped. The learned Advocate contends that when the solenama was taken into evidence the same cannot be brushed aside from consideration and this solenama indicates that the plaintiff got the suit property in his saham. In this decision it has been held that when an unstamped document has been marked as exhibit in the case and used by the parties in examination and cross-examination of the witnesses the order admitting the document in evidence cannot be subsequently reviewed or revised. There is no dispute on this point. But fact remains that in the present case a solenama was filed in the partition suit which was only accepted by the trial Court. But on the basis of the solenama no decree was drawn up and such a partition suit culminates with the drawing up of a decree which is sealed and signed by the Court. So the final act, that is, drawing up of the decree has not yet been done. Only there is an order of acceptance of solenama and unless the solenama is made part of the decree on drawing up of the same it cannot be construed that the whole act has finished. But in the present case the decree has not yet been drawn up. It is well settled that in a suit for partition if the decree is not drawn up it should be construed that the suit is still pending. This is the consistent view of the higher Courts of this subcontinent. The plaintiff or any of the defendants or the parties in the suit have not taken any step for drawing up of a decree. In a suit for partition when the defendants claim a saham in the suit property he may take step drawing up of a decree even when the plaintiff failed to take any step. Haji Yunus Mollah took no step for drawing up of the decree and so is the case with the present plaintiff who was party though he is claiming the suit land on the basis of the earlier partition suit. In that view of the matter, we hold that mere acceptance of the solenama is not sufficient to hold that the plaintiff has acquired full title and possession over the suit property and the conduct of the plaintiff of the parties in that suit clearly indicate that actually the property belonged to Haji Yunus Mollah who adopted a device for keeping the property with him. 19. As regards the points raised by opposite party No. 14 on the limitation, it appears that this has been seriously asserted either before the trial Court or before the appellate Court by opposite party No. 14. In spite of that the Courts below came to the finding, that the suit is not barred by limitation. It is true that even though the matter was not asserted seriously before both the Courts below but there is no bar in agitating the same before this Court as that is, a point of law. Admittedly the suit property was purchased by Haji Yunus Mollah but nowhere in a plaint the petitioner has stated on which date he actually got delivery of possession of the suit property. The learned Advocate for the petitioner tried to impress that the date of filing of the solenama may be construed as the date of actual possession of the suit property. But by adducing oral and documentary evidence the plaintiff-petitioner failed to prove that he got actual physical delivery of possession or he continued to possess the suit property. Both the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff-petitioner had or has no possession over the suit property. Further, it appears that opposite party No. 14 got delivery of possession of a part of the suit property from Haji Yunus Mollah and from that date the suit was not filed within 12 years. Opposite party No. 14 got the property after the acceptance of the solenama in the aforesaid partition suit. So, if the date of solenama be construed as the actual date of possession then the suit has not been filed within 12 years from the date of dispossession by opposite party No. 14. The plaintiffs cause of action of this suit is that when he came to know of the wrong recording of the suit property in the name of Haji Yunus Mollah and the Government he had to file the suit. Admittedly, the record of right was published in the year 1963 and the suit was filed on 29.9.1985 which shows that this suit was not filed within 12 years from the date of publication of the ROR. So this suit is hopelessly barred by limitation. 20. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has not pressed this petition on any other ground. 21. Thus, after consideration of the materials on record and after hearing the learned Advocates of both the sides we hold that the Courts below have not committed any illegality or wrong which may call for any interference by this Court in this revisional application. 22. There is, therefore, no merit 10 this application and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 23. The Rule is accordingly, discharged without any order as to costs. Send down the lower court records at once. End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 973 of 1999.
lawyer:
Rokanuddin Mahmud, Senior Advocate instructed by Sharifuddin Chaklader; Advocate-on-Record------For the Petitioner.  
Not represented------The Respondents,
parties:
Sultana Jute Mills Limited  ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Court of Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat and others  ------ Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 29-6-1999 passed by the High Court Division in WP No. 1862 of 1997).
full_judgment:
M Amin Choudhury CJ: This petition for leave to appeal is against judgment and order dated 29-6-1999 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1862 of 1997 discharging the Rule.

2. The short fact leading to this petition is that respondent No. 2 instituted Mortgage Suit No. 21 of 1990 in the Artha Rin Adalat No. 1, Chittagong claiming an amount of Taka 8,89,94,800.22 only against the petitioner and proforma respondent Nos. 4 to 7 who filed written statement denying the claim and pleaded set off. During pendency of the suit the parties settled the dispute amicably and the Board of respondent No 2 approved the settlement in its meeting held on 28-1-1995 which was communicated to the petitioner by letter dated 25-2-1995 of respondent No. 2. The terms and conditions included that a compromise decree would be passed in the aforesaid suit accordingly. The petitioner by a letter dated 19-3-1995 suggested some modifications but respondent No. 2 by his letter dated 14-6-1995 intimated the petitioner on non-acceptance of the modification and requested the petitioner to take step according to its earlier letter dated 25-2-1999. The petitioner then by letter dated 25-6-1995 communicated its unconditional acceptance of the offer contained in letter dated 25-2-1999 and signed a copy of the same and sent it back to respondent No. 3 as per terms and conditions proposed by them for compromise. Thereafter the petitioner filed an application on 27-10-1996 before respondent No. 1 under Order XXIII rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure for a compromise decree in terms of Board resolution of respondent No. 2 as contained in letter dated 25-2-1995 which was accepted by the petitioner. Letters dated 25-2-1995 and 14-6-1995 of respondent No. 2 and letter elated 25-6-1995 of the petitioner were submitted in the court. But respondent No. 2 filed written objection on certain untenable grounds and on hearing the parties the Adalat by order dated 15-3-1997 rejected the petition for compromise decree. It is the case of the petitioner that the Artha Rin Adalat was wrong in holding that respondent No. 2 was not agreeable to compromise. But in the letter dated 25-2-1995 respondent No. 2 set down the terms and conditions of the compromise and have asked the petitioner to sign the letter if those were acceptable, The petitioner accepted the terms of compromise proposed by respondent No. 2 and accordingly it became a lawful agreement but the Adalat wrongly refused to accept the compromise which terms are lawful and there is no allegation of fraud in the same, It is the further case of the petitioner that when the terms offered by respondent No. 2 was accepted there is a binding agreement between the parties and, as such, the petitioner was entitled to a compromise decree. No one contested the Rule before the High Court Division, The Rule was discharged on 29-6-1999.

3. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that having regard to the fact that the Agrani Bank by letter dated 25-2-1995 set down the terms of compromise which was accepted by the petitioner in letter dated 25-6-1995 compromise between the parties was proved by signing document of both the parties forming lawful agreement but the Artha Rin Adalat acted without lawful authority in refusing to pass decree in accordance with the terms and conditions set down by respondent No. 2 and the Artha Rin Adalat was also wrong in holding that respondent. No. 2 was not agreeable to the terms and conditions of the compromise. It is submitted that the High Court Division was wrong in drawing adverse reference from non-filing of earlier application, as the petitioner could have easily produced the same if adjournment was granted. It is submitted that the High Court division rejected the petitioner's plea on the ground of non-filing of earlier application filed before the Adalat on 7-9-1996. The High Court Division found on going through the letter dated 25-2-1995 that the petitioner was required to comply with certain conditions and fulfilling those terms and conditions the suit was to be compromised by reducing 1/3rd of the claim and rescheduling the pledged amount of the claim. The High Court Division found that in the written objection the respondent-Bank specifically stated that the petitioner failed to fulfill the conditions of the sanction letter and even did not express its concurrence to a draft compromise petition prepared by the lawyer of the plaintiff bank. The High Court Division held that mere acceptance of the terms and conditions of the letter dated 25-2-1995 by 14-6-1995 by the petitioner without fulfilling the terms and conditions of that letter cannot entitle the petitioner to get a compromise decree in terms of that letter Learned Advocate submits that the High Court Division discharged the Rule on a mere technical ground without going into detail of the matter in question.

<u>4. We have gone through the judgment of the High Court Division and heard the learned Advocate for the petitioner. It appears that the whole petition is based on letter dated 25-2-1995 issued by respondent No. 2 Bank and the petitioner's case of acceptance of terms and conditions set forth in this letter. It is the definite case of the petitioner that the terms and conditions set forth in this letter were accepted by the petitioner who specifically intimated respondent No. 2 on the acceptance of the terms. In such a situation Mr Mahmud submits that there ought to have been a compromise decree. It appears that the High Court Division on a very technical ground discharged the Rule that whether letter dated 25-2-1995 has been written to the petitioner by the plaintiff-bank and whether the same has been accepted by the petitioner are matters of evidence. The points at issue now before us can well be decided at the time of trial of the suit but on a writ jurisdiction this question cannot be decided. Defendants will be at liberty to adduce evidence on this point and may also confront the plaintiff Bank on the question of compromise as set forth in bank's letter dated 25-2-1995 and there is no bar in it. If at all on evidence it can be proved that actually the Bank's offer of compromise was accepted by the petitioner then result may follow. So, relief for the petitioner is now before the trial Court and they are at liberty to agitate the matter before the trial Court. In such a situation we find that no useful purpose would be served in granting leave in this case. The petitioner may agitate his case of compromise before the trial court with liberty to adduce evidence.</u>

With that observation this petition is disposed of on condonation of delay.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Aziz J: This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff has been filed against the decree passed by the learned subordinate Judge. First Commercial Court at Sadar Chittagong in Mortgage Suit No. 73 of 1983

2. This appeal arises out of the facts, in short, that the plaintiff-Bank filed the Mortgage Suit against the defendants-respondents stating, inter alia,that, its predecessor the Eastern Mercantile Bank Limited, granted cash credit facilities of taka five lac to the defendant No.1 the partnership firm, against the pledge of oil seeds and other stock-in-trade. The defendant Nos. 2 to 4, the partners of the defendant No. 1 also executed collateral security. Defendant No. 3 mortgaged his property as further security for the loan. The charge documents were executed on 27-5-1963.The defendants enjoyed the loan but they did not liquidate the same despite calls and reminders. Fresh charge documents were executed in the year 1965 and also in subsequent years. But the outstanding loan amount was not paid by the defendants. The plaintiff thereafter served a legal notice and ultimately filed the suit for recovery of the said-outstanding loan amount with interest.

3. The defendant No. 5 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint contending, inter alia, in short, that, the suit is not maintainable in the present form, the suit is barred.by limitation, the suit is barred by principle of waiver, estoppel and acquiescence and that the suit is false and fabricated. The defendant No. 5 further stated in his written statement that during pendency of the suit the defendant-respondent No. 2, who is also defendant No. 6, died on 9-7-1977, the defendant- respondent No. 3 died on 24-4-1982 and defendant-respondent No. 4 died on 15-3-1984. But no steps were taken for substitution of their heirs and legal representative in the suit that the contesting defendant did not enjoy the cash credit facilities in the way alleged by the plaintiff. That the loan was sanctioned against the defendant-respondent No. 1 against pledge, hypothecation and mortgage of the mill, factory machinery, godown and the stock-in-trade of defendant No.1 and those were under the administration, control, custody and management of the plaintiff. That the entire stock-in-trade and valuable machineries were lost and ruined during the war of liberation in 1971, including fixtures, fittings and stock from the custody of the plaintiff and for that the' defendant made GO entry wit-h the local police station. That the bank was not dutiful and vigilant to protect those valuable goods and materials of the defendants under its (plaintiffs) custody and for that the defendants suffered huge loss, that the plaintiff has not accounted for the same and that the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The trial Court on consideration of the facts, evidence and materials on record, dismissed the suit finding that the suit is not maintainable. This has resulted into filing this appeal.

5. Mr. Abdur Razzak, the learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant, assailed the judgment and decree of the trial Court on threefold grounds namely:

(1) Notwithstanding the fact of death of defendant-respondent Nos. 2 to 4 and 6, the suit can be proceeded with against the surviving defendant-respondents although the deceased have not been substituted;

(2) the defendant-respondent Nos. 2 to 4 and 6 having been dead, the defendant-respondent Nos. 1 and 5 can be proceeded with who are liable to repay the loan on their own admission vide Exhibit 10(j), and lastly,

(3) the trial Court has dismissed the suit illegally and without any specific finding and without applying his judicial mind and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside.

6. Mr. Khan Saifur Rahman, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the contesting defendant No. 5. On the other hand, supports the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court and resists the appeal on the ground that;

(1) The trial Court has rightly dismissed the suit as not maintainable as the pledged goods have not been accounted for by the plaintiff- Bank;

(2) the heirs and legal representatives of the deceased defendants having not been brought on record of the suit by the plaintiff under Order 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the trial Court has rightly dismissed the suit;

(3) the plaintiff-Bank cannot get a decree of the unpaid loan neither against dead persons nor against the contesting defendant- respondent No. 5 when the Bank is unable to return the goods and stock-in-trade kept in pledge to the bank and lastly,

(4) the appeal having been filed against and in the name of the dead persons, is not maintainable.

7. We have heard the learned Counsels of both the appellant and respondent No. 5 and perused the pleadings, evidence and exhibits on record of the case. Both sides argued the case in length and cited decisions.

8. Admitted positron in the suit is that, in 1963 the plaintiff-bank granted a cash credit upto the limit of taka five lac to the defendant-respondent No. 1 and against the security of the said loan the defendant No. 1 mortgaged' its factory mills, machinery, godown worth more than taka ten lac and also pledged and' hypothecated the entire stock-in-trade comprising of rape seeds, finished products, oil cakes, containers, etc. The keys of the godown containing storage of entire stock-in-trade as aforesaid were kept by the plaintiff-bank the goods were absolutely under the control and custody of the bank and process of delivery/redemption of the goods processed through day-to-day cash payment. The defendant-respondent Nos. 2 to 4 gave collateral securities. The defendant No. 5 came as partner later. The limit was extended upto 1974. But the defendants having failed to repay the loan on several requests, the plaintiff-bank served legal notice Exhibit (E) dated 9-5-1972 and ultimately filed the suit on 30-9-1974 being Mortgage Suit No. 91 of 1974 renumbered as Mortgage Suit No. 73 of 1984.

9. The contesting defendant-respondent No. 5 in his written statement contended, in short, that the goods and stock-in-trade hypothecated and pledged to the plaintiff-bank were in custody and under the care, control, possession and supervision of the plaintiff who was the absolute custodian of the goods as a bailee having the keys of the godown with them. But the bank was not dutiful and vigilant and did not discharge its responsibility to protect the valuable goods of the respondents and those were lost and looted away from their custody during the liberation movement in 1971, for which the bank did not even make a report to the police. The plaintiff-bank being the custodian as bailee of the pledged goods and having not accounted for the same in the suit the suit is liable to be dismissed and has rightly been dismissed by the trial Court.

10. The learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant referred to sections 2(a), 4, 18, 22, and 45 of the Partnership Act 1932 and argued that the defendant-respondent No. 5 having admitted the liability of the loan is bound to repay the debt and the trial Court has erred in law in not decreeing the suit. The learned Counsel virtually relied on Exhibit 10(J), which is a reply of the defendants to the legal notice Exhibit (E) of the plaintiff, for decreeing the suit. The learned Counsel further argued that the defendant-respondent No.5 having admitted the loan vide Exhibit 10(J), has accepted the liability and cannot escape from the same and is liable to pay. He further argued that, the defendant-respondent No. 5 has also not denied or objected to the amount of loan or statement of account which is admissible under section 4 of the Banker's Book Evidence Act 1891. The learned Counsel further argued that notwithstanding the fact of death of defendant Nos. 2 to 4 and 6 and non-substitution of their heirs, the defendant-respondent No. 5 having admitted the liability is bound to pay the debt with interest as per his own admission and the suit can be proceeded with against him as per provision of law quoted above. As such, the trial Court was wrong in dismissing the suit. In support of his submission, the learned Counsel referred to two decisions reported in PLD 1966 (Karachi) 55 and 27 DLR 200.

11. The learned Counsel for the respondent No. 5, on the other hand, contends that the suit lies on very simple principle of law and equity. As this is a suit for recovery of loan outstanding amount of loan granted against defendant-respondent No. 1 against equitable mortgage as cash credit, as a running business capital on pledge of its business goods and stock-in-trade along" with other mortgaged properties and additional collateral securities, the realization of loan depends upon the simple principle "take money return the pledged goods" or vice versa, that is, 'return goods take money'. He submits that the Bank has the concurrent and corresponding responsibility and liability to return the goods on payment by the defendants. The mode of recovery of the loan is" based on the aforesaid simple principle, but in this case as the plaintiff is admittedly unable to return the goods they are not entitled to the decree as per sections 176 and 177 of the Contract Act 1872.

12. Secondly, the plaintiff in paragraph 4 of the plaint having admitted that "in terms of the letter of sanction, defendant Nos. 2 to 4 in their personal capacity executed three separate guarantee forms guaranteeing and undertaking to pay the said amount with interest in case of default of defendant-respondent No. 1", the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 5 continues, the heirs of the deceased partners, defendant-respondent Nos. 2 to 4 and 6 having not been brought on record under the provision of Order 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure with the surviving partners in the suit, the suit has abated and cannot be proceeded with under sections 42 and 45 of the Contract Act. He further submits that, in view of the provisions of section 42(c) of the Partnership Act. 1932, the defendant-respondent No. 1, the partnership firm, must be taken and treated as dissolved and non-existent by operation of law with their deaths followed by non-substitution of the heirs of the deceased partners as aforesaid. Mr. Khan further submits that the appeal is liable to be dismissed having been filed against dead persons.

13. The learned counsel for the respondent No. 5 has put much emphasis on sections 176 and 177 of the Contract Act.

Sections 176 and 177 run as follows:

Section 176-Pawnee's right where pawnor makes default: If the pawnor makes default in payment of the debt, or performance, at the stipulated time of the promise, in respect of which the goods were pledged, the pawnee may bring a suit against the pawnor upon the debt or promise, and retain the goods pledged as a collateral security; or he may sell the thing pledged, on giving the pawnor reasonable notice of the sale.

If the proceeds of such sale are less than the amount due in respect of the debt or promise, the pawnor is still liable to pay the balance. If the proceeds of the sale are greater than the amount so due the pawnee shall pay over the surplus to the pawnor.

Section 177.-Defaulting Pawnor's Right to Redeem: If a time is stipulated for the payment of the debt, or performance of the promise, for which the pledge is made, and the pawnor makes default in payment of the debt or performance of the promise at the stipulated time, he may redeem the goods pledged at any subsequent time before the actual sale of them, but he must, in that case, pay, in addition, any expenses which have arisen from his default."

14. Facts of the case show that the plaintiff served a legal notice Exhibit (E) on 9-5-1972 to defendant No. 1 only for payment of loan money. The legal notice Exhibit E clearly stated that; unless the defendant No.1 clears its outstanding liabilities in terms of the legal notice, the bank would be obliged to dispose of the pledged goods at best available price that is, by sale of the pledged goods. It clearly spells out that, the pledged stock-in-trade was still under the custody of the bank. Section 176 of the Act also clearly speaks that the pawnee may retain the pledged goods as collateral security. Section 177 gives the pawnors a statutory right of redemption of the pledged goods before sale of the goods subject to certain conditions. But the admitted fact is that the plaintiff had no pledged goods of the defendants with them when Exhibit (E) was issued for their redemption. This is a total violation of the mandatory provision of law.

15. The provisions of sections 176 and 177 of the Contract Act further provide that sale of pledged goods is a condition precedent before institution of the suit. Again, according to the said provisions, the defendants have a statutory right to redeem the pledged goods before such sale and that they are entitled to a mandatory notice of sale of the pledged goods beforehand. It is thus clear that, the plaintiff is entitled to file a suit in the given situation only after the plaintiff had complied with the provisions of sections 176 and 177 of the Contract Act and the defendants were still in default to comply accordingly. But the plaintiff of this suit did not comply with the same before bringing the suit. The suit having thus been filed in total violation of the mandatory provisions of law has rightly been dismissed by the trial Court as not maintainable.

16. It further appears in the present case that the plaintiff-appellant not only failed to comply with the provisions of sections 176 and 177 of the Contract Act as aforesaid before bringing the suit, they also made an incorrect and deceitful statement in its legalnotice about the selling of pledged goods which were not under their custody at the relevant time. PW 1 Mr. Abdur Razzak has admitted in his deposition that those were lost and looted away during war of liberation in 1971. This fact was also not disclosed in their plaint. The defendant- respondent No. 5 has stated the same fact which has been admitted by the PW 1. The plaintiff also did not account for the pledged goods arid stock-in-trade and has not given any valuation statement of the same either in its plaint or in the deposition of the PW 1. The legal notice gives an impression that those goods were under their custody at the relevant time which was not true. By giving out an incorrect statement in the legal notice and suppressing the true state of affairs of the pledged goods in legal notice and plaint, the plaintiff practised fraud upon the defendants as well as upon the statute and the court. On the other hand, the plaintiff has made and used the said legal notice, Exhibit (E), and the sincere reply there by the defendant, Exhibit 10(1), as basis of the suit. As such, the plaintiff is not entitled to any discretionary or equitable relief as they have not come before the Court with clean hands.

17. Again a close reading of the provision of sections 176 and 177 of the Contract Act as quoted above, reveal that, in order to bring such a suit the plaintiff must serve a notice to the pledgers as provided therein keeping the pledged goods intact, so that the plaintiff can return the same to the pledgers on payment by them before sale. In support of his contention Mr. Khan has relied on two decisions reported in PLD 1966 (Lahore) 1 and 27 DLR 523.

18. In the case between AM Burq and another vs Central Exchange Bank Ltd and others reported in PLD 1966 (Lahore) 1, their Lordships held that:

"that the principle in equity is that the creditor is not entitled to recover the amount of his secured debt when he cannot return the security."

19. In the case between Md. Obaidul Akbar vs East Pakistan Provincial (now Bangladesh) Co- operative Bank Limited reported in 27 DLR 523 their Lordships has held that:

"The pawnor having had the right conferred by section 177 to redeem his property at any time before the actual sale"

<u>20. In view of the aforesaid provisions of sections 176 and 177 of the Contract Act and in view of the decisions quoted above, it appears that, where the pawnee is not in possession of the property pledged to him as security for the payment of the Joan nor did he prove that it had been damaged or destroyed at the risk of the defendant (pawnee), the pawnee is not entitled to recover the debt because the pawnor had the right conferred by section 177 to redeem his property at any time before the actual sale prior to filing of the suit.</u>

21.We have given our anxious consideration to the submission made by the learned Advocates and it appears that admittedly the pledged goods and stock-in-trade have been lost from the custody of the plaintiff and they are unable to return the same. In that view of the matter the submission of the learned Counsel for the defendant-respondent No.5 that the plaintiff being unable to return the goods to the defendants for redemption, they are not entitled to repayment of the debt appears logical to us. Law is nothing but a codified common sense. When we cannot compel the pledgee to return the pledged goods to the pledgers how can we direct the defendant No. 5 either to repay the loan himself; or on behalf of the other defendants, who (defendant Nos. 2 to 4) have executed three separate guarantee forms in their personal capacity which has also been admitted by the plaintiff in its plaint as stated above. Law does not permit us to do so.

22.This is also not the case of the plaintiff that the pledged goods were lost and looted away or destroyed despite taking proper and adequate care of the same as a man of ordinary prudence would have taken of his own goods. The plaintiff also did not deny the custody of the pledged goods but failed to protect the same. The plaintiff was under legal obligation to protect the pledged goods of the defendant-respondent under section 151of the Contract Act. Section 151 of the Contract Act runs as follows:

Section 151-Care to be taken by bailee: In all cases of bailment the bailee is bound to take as much care of the goods bailed to him as a man of ordinary prudence would under similar circumstances take of his own goods of the same bulk, quality and value as the goods bailed."

23. Here in this case the materials on record show a total lack of care on the part of the plaintiff-appellant in respect of protection of the pledged goods. In the case of DP Goenka vs Governor- General of Pakistan and another reported in 7 DLR 134 it has been held by their Lordships that;

"care which a bailee is bound to take is co- extensive with that of a man of ordinary prudence."

24. In view of the said decision we have no hesitation in the given facts of the present case to hold that the plaintiff has shown gross negligence and carelessness and own fully failed in discharging statutory obligation imposed on it under section 151 of the Contract Act.

25. The learned Counsel for the respondent No.5 further submits that the plaintiff having not accounted for the loss of the pledged goods the trial Court has rightly dismissed the suit on the findings that:

"As we have already found that the plaintiff-Bank was the custodian of the pledged-goods and as the loss of the pledge-goods has not been ascertained and shown in the statement of account by the pledgee or, the plaintiff-Bank. So, the plaintiff-Bank is hot entitled to get a decree for the money as claimed by it by brushing aside the admitted loss of the pledged goods.

26. In support of his submission, Mr. Khan has cited an unreported decision dated 11-2-1997 of our Appellate Division delivered in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 644 of 1994 in the case between Pubali Bank Limited. Vs Satania Iron and Steel Industries and another wherein the Appellate Division, dismissed the leave petition affirming the judgment of the High Court Division, on the finding as follows:

"The trial Court on consideration of the evidence dismissed the suit on the grounds that the plaintiff could neither account for the loss of the pledged goods kept under its custody nor could it prove that the defendants Were notified before the auction sale of the goods in question,"

27. We find that the aforesaid decision is applicable in the facts and circumstances of the case before us.

28. In view of the same and in consideration of the materials on record we are of the opinion that the appeal must fail. We hold that the trial Court has rightly dismissed the suit.

29. The submission of the appellant that the defendant-respondent No.5 is bound by his own admission vide Exhibit 10(J) and cannot escape the liability and is bound to repay the loan, does not have any leg to stand and must fail. We have already observed that the said admission was obtained by the plaintiff on deceitful means by making false and untrue statement in Exhibit (E) suppressing the actual fact and Exhibit 10(J) has been used as a basis for filing the suit.

30. The submission of the learned Counsel for the appellant that the suit can be proceeded with against the surviving partners without substituting the heirs and legal representative of the deceased defendant Nos. 2 to 4 and 6, has also no merit.

31. Mr. Khan Saifur Rahman, the learned Counsel appearing for the defendant-respondent No. 5, referred to sections 42 and 45 of the Contract Act and submits that the heirs and legal representative of the deceased defendant having not been brought on record in the suit, the suit cannot proceed. The provision of sections 42 and 45 of the Contract Act runs as follows:

Section 42-Devolution of joint Liabilities:

When two or more persons have made a joint promise, then unless a contrary intention appears by the contract, all such persons during their joint lives, and after the death of any of them, his representative jointly with the survivor or survivors, and after the death of the last survivor, the representatives of all jointly, must fulfil the promise.

Section 45-Devolution of joint Right:

When a person has made a promise to two or more persons jointly, then, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract, the right to claim performance rests, as between him and them, with them during their joint lives, and after the death of any of them, with the representative of such deceased person jointly with the survivor or survivors, and after the death of the last survivor, with the representatives of all jointly.

<u>32. Here the suit was filed during the lifetime of all the partners of the firm, but defendant-respondent Nos. 2 to 4 and 6 died during the pendency of the suit. Provisions of sections 42 and 45 of the Contract Act as quoted above clearly indicate that, when a person or two or more persons made a joint promise to two or more persons they are jointly liable for the performance of the same and the right to claim performance of the same rests as between him and them during their lifetime and if any of them died their representative must be brought on record to enable them to perform the contract. But in the present case admittedly defendant Nos. 2 to 4 and 6, partners of firm, died during pendency of the suit before the trial Court and no step was taken for their substitution in the suit. Therefore, in view of the provision of the aforesaid sections, the suit must fail as it cannot proceed against dead persons.</u>

33. Moreover, it appears from the aforesaid fact that, in view of the provision of section 42 (c) of the Partnership Act, the defendant-respondent No. 1,the partnership firm, has also been dissolved automatically by operation of law and became nonexistent with the death of its aforesaid partners.

Section 42.-Dissolution on the happening of certain contingencies:

Subject to contract between the partners a firm is dissolved

(a).................

(b)................

(c) by the death of a partner: and

(d)................

34. Therefore by the death of the partners, the partnership firm, defendant-respondent No.1, has already automatically been dissolved by operation of law and, as such, the suit against it cannot proceed.

35. It further appears that the appellant has brought this appeal against the aforesaid dead persons as defendant-respondent Nos. 2 to 4 and 6 and also against the dissolved and non-existent defendant-respondent No.1, and, in that view of the matter the appeal is also not maintainable.

36. In view of our above discussions, we are of the view that the appeal has no merit. The trial Court has rightly dismissed the suit. We find no illegality in the judgment and decree passed by the Court below for our interference.

The Court fees paid is correct.

In the result, this appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree passed by the trial Court is hereby affirmed.

Send down the lower court records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioners is against judgment and decree dated 12-5-1990 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Chittagong on Other Appeal No. 207/1978-78/78 allowing the appeal and setting aside judgment and decree dated 13-12-77 passed by the Munsif, Satkania, Chittagong in Partition Suit No. 34 of 1973.

2. Plaintiffs filed Partition Suit No. 98 of 1970 claiming 11 kanis 14 gandas of land or the quantum of land decided by the Court in their share out of 24.78 acres of the suit land by partition initially on payment of fixed court-fee and subsequently on payment of ad valorem court-fee on 26-11-77 in course of hearing argument of the suit in the court. Plaintiffs claimed title and possession in the said land by successions and transfers asserting that RS Khatian in respect of the suit property was wrong and that they purchased in the benami of another person.

3. Suit was contested by the defendant Nos . 1-6, 7 10, 11, 17 to 19 by filing separate written statements except defendant Nos. 17-19 and other defendants prayed for saham. Those saham praying defendants also made certain allegations like the other contesting defendants in their respective written statement asserting that plaintiffs have no rights, title and interest in the suit property and denying title and possession of the plaintiffs. Upon the aforesaid pleadings trial Court, amongst others, framed issue No.3 which was as follows:

3. Have the plaintiffs their alleged right, title and interest in the land and, if so, to what extent?

4. On consideration of the materials on record trial Court decreed the suit in preliminary form holding that plaintiffs have their title in the suit jote and entitled to get saham of 11 kanis and 14 gondas of land.

5. Being aggrieved by the same defendant Nos. 10 and 11 preferred Partition Appeal No. 207 of 1978 and defendant Nos. 17-19 preferred Partition Appeal No. 78 of 1978. Both lie appeals were heard analogously and by the impugned judgment both lie appeals were allowed and dismissed the suit.

6. Mr Abdul Momen Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, after placing the impugned judgment and other materials on record, submitted that Court of appeal below acted illegally in holding that trial Court was wrong in passing the decree of partition as complicated question of title was involved in the suit when no prayer for establishment of title was made by the plaintiffs. Mr Kamal-UI Alam, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 4 and 5 (Defendant Nos. 10 and 11), submitted that his clients preferred Partition Appeal No. 207 of 1978 being aggrieved by the quantum of sahamalloted to his clients. But the Court of appeal below acted illegally in allowing the appeal without modifying the decree increasing their quantum of saham and in dismissing the suit itself.

7. Mr Omar Farook, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 10-12 (defendant Nos. 17 to 19) supported the impugned judgment contending that Court of appeal below correctly held that a simple suit for partition without prayer for declaration of title was not maintainable.

8. It appears from the opening sentence of the trial Court's judgment that it is suit for establishment of title and partition. It further appears from trial Court's judgment that in view of the question of title involved in the suit plaintiffs paid ad valorem court-fee with a prayer for establishment of title.

9. It appears from paragraph 'Ka of the plaint is as follows:

"(ক) বাদীর পূর্ববর্তী আকবর আলীর বন্দোবস্তীকৃত ১৪ গন্ডা জমি দিয়া বা বাদীর যে পরিমাণ জমি আইনতঃ সাব্যস্ত করেন তাহা বাদীর অংশে দিয়া বাদীকে গোলাভাগের প্রাথমিক ডিক্রি দিবার আজ্ঞা হয়।”

10. It appears from the order-sheet of the trial Court that trial was closed on 25-11-77 and 26-11-77 was fixed for hearing argument. On that date argument was heard and court-fee of Taka 400.00 was also paid. Thereafter judgment was delivered on 3-12-77 and on that date plaintiffs were directed to deposit the deficit court-fees of Taka 10. 35. Thereafter on 10-12-77 plaintiff paid the deficit court-fee which also finds support from the sharistader's note dated 10-12-77 recorded on the Ist page of the plaint.

11. Trial Court decided the case on merit treating the same as a suit for establishment of title and for partition on realising ad valorem court fees on the value of the suit raised on the basis of contested order passed on 28-8-1976. Though the trial Court observed that plaintiffs paid ad valorem court-fees with a prayer for establishment of title in the judgment it does not appear from the record that any such application was filed at any time for amending the prayer of the plaint. But the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner contends that prayer 'Ka' quoted hereinbefore contains the essential elements of declaration of title. It appears from the said prayer 'ka' of the plaint that there is alternative prayer for granting saham in respect of 11 kanis 14 gandas of land or for the quantum of land legally found by the court.

<u>12. A simple suit for partition is to be filed with a fixed court-fee under article 17(V-A) of the Schedule II of the court-fees Act if the plaintiff alleges that he is in possession of the suit property. When a suit is filed for partition and for recovery of possession by the plaintiff alleging that he is out of possession then he is to pay ad valorem court-fee on the value of his share of the suit property under section 7(VI-A) of the Court-fees Act. Even if the plaintiff claims to be in possession of his share of the suit property but prays for declaration of his title and partition then also he is to pay ad valorem Court fee on the value of his share of the suit property under section 7(IV)(C) of the Court-fees Act as partition in such a suit is a consequential relief to the prayer for declaration of title in his share of the suit property as in the present suit.</u>

13. It appears from the plaint that plaintiffs claimed that they are in posession in schedule No. 2 of the suit property claimed by them and they made an alternative prayer for declaration of their title in the suit property on the allegation that RS Khatian was wrong, etc. So the plaintiffs suit was not a suit for partition and possession as they did not allege that they are out of possession. So ad valorem court-fee was not realised from the plaintiffs on the ground that they filed the suit for partition being out of possession. Trial Court rightly observed that plaintiffs paid ad valorem court-fees as question of title was seriously involved in the suit with a prayer for establishment of title. Court of appeal below without considering the above erroneously held that the trial Court erred in decreeing the simple suit for partition. From the alternative prayer in the plaint and payment of ad valorem court-fee by the plaintiffs it cannot be doubted that plaintiffs' suit was for declaration of title and partition.

<u>14.Court of appeal below did not at all consider the evidence, both oral and documentary, adduced by the parties and considered by the trial Court. Thus the Court of appeal below shirked its responsibility in deciding the appeal on merit. In the facts and circumstances stated above Court of appeal below acted illegally in allowing the appeal and dismissing the suit without reversing any finding of the trial Court regarding title of the plaintiffs and some of the defendants in the suit property and the sahamalloted to the respective parties. In such circumstances impugned judgment is liable to be set aside and case remanded to the Court of appeal below to decide the appeal on merit. Since the partition appeal No. 207 of 1978 was allowed without giving proper relief to the opposite party Nos. 4 and 5 (defendant Nos. 10 and 11) the said appeal should also be heard on merit.</u>

15. In the result, the Rule is made absolute with cost and the impugned judgment and decree are set aside and both the appeals remanded to the Court of appeal below to decide the appeals on merit. Court of appeal below is directed to dispose of the appeals expeditiously within 3 (three) months from the date of receipt of the lower court record.

Let the lower court record be sent down to the Court concerned expeditiously.

End.
